a15_1084300csm.text: Endeavour, this is Houston. Over.

a15_1084300csm.speaker: Worden
a15_1084300csm.text: Hello, Houston; Endeavour.

a15_1084300csm.speaker: Fullerton
a15_1084300csm.text: Okay, you've been loud and clear. We've been balled up on a site configuration problem here, but I think we're back with it, and we have one question. You're by T-stop for the Pan Camera now, we wondered if you went to Mono on the Pan Camera at 3 minutes and 20 seconds before T-stop. Over.

a15_1084300csm.speaker: Worden
a15_1084300csm.text: Negative, Gordo. I got tied up in that VHF check.

a15_1084300csm.speaker: Fullerton
a15_1084300csm.text: Roger.

a15_1084300csm.speaker: Worden
a15_1084300csm.text: Want me to go Mono now [on the Panoramic Camera]?

a15_1084300csm.speaker: Fullerton
a15_1084300csm.text: Go [to] Standby now, Al. We're past the T-stop time. [Pause.]

a15_1084300csm.speaker: Worden
a15_1084300csm.text: Okay, Gordo. Sorry about that. We're in Standby now.

a15_1084300csm.speaker: Fullerton
a15_1084300csm.text: No problem. That was our fault for the comm problem. We - we heard the comm checks and it sounded good. You're clear to go back to normal configuration on the VHF whenever you get a chance.

a15_1084300csm.speaker: Worden
a15_1084300csm.text: Okay. [Long pause.]

a15_1084300csm.speaker: Irwin
a15_1084300csm.text: Okay, Joe. I have some frame counts for you.

a15_1084300csm.speaker: Allen
a15_1084300csm.text: Roger, Jim. Standing by.

a15_1084300csm.speaker: Irwin
a15_1084300csm.text: Roger. Mag L (also known as AS15-85) is reading 33. Mag K (Mag 87) is reading 66. And Mag Metro (Mag 84) is reading 20.

a15_1084300csm.speaker: Fullerton
a15_1084300csm.text: Endeavour, Houston. We'd like the Gamma-ray, Gain Step switch one step up. Over.

a15_1084300csm.speaker: Allen
a15_1084300csm.text: Roger, Jim. Thank you. Sounds like we got some beautiful shots already.

a15_1084300csm.speaker: Worden
a15_1084300csm.text: Roger. Gamma-ray Gain Step, one step up, now.

a15_1084300csm.speaker: Fullerton
a15_1084300csm.text: Okay, Al. Thank you.

a15_1084300csm.speaker: Irwin
a15_1084300csm.text: Beautiful scenery.

a15_1084300csm.speaker: Worden
a15_1084300csm.text: Okay. And if you want to let me know on the Pan Camera power; whether the lens is in or not.

a15_1084300csm.speaker: Allen
a15_1084300csm.text: It sounds it! [Long Comm Break]

a15_1084300csm.speaker: Fullerton
a15_1084300csm.text: Okay. The lens is tucked in...

a15_1084300csm.speaker: Worden
a15_1084300csm.text: Yes, just keep waiting.

a15_1084300csm.speaker: Fullerton
a15_1084300csm.text: ...and your cleared to turn it off.

a15_1084300csm.speaker: Worden
a15_1084300csm.text: Okay, and the Gamma-ray boom is going out now.

a15_1085437csm.speaker: Fullerton
a15_1085437csm.text: Endeavour, this is Houston. 30 seconds to T-stop on the Mapping Camera. Over.

a15_1085824csm.speaker: Fullerton
a15_1085824csm.text: Endeavour, Houston. I have the TEI-26 PAD for you. Over.

a15_1085824csm.speaker: Worden
a15_1085824csm.text: Okay, Houston. Stand by just one.

a15_1085824csm.speaker: Worden
a15_1085824csm.text: Okay, Gordon. I'm ready to copy.

a15_1085824csm.speaker: Fullerton
a15_1085824csm.text: Okay. TEI-26: SPS/G&N; Noun 47 is 37354; plus 0.60, plus 0.97; T IG is 129:22:25.54; Noun 81 is plus 3031.2, minus 1327.1, minus 0308.7; attitude is 180, 092, 339; ullage is four jets for 12 seconds. And other remarks: Lambda at T IG equal plus 172.93. Go ahead.

a15a1085936.speaker: Scott
a15a1085936.text: I'd like to confirm that, on the LMP camera for EVA-1, we use Mag Lima. Is that correct?

a15a1085936.speaker: Allen
a15a1085936.text: That's correct, Dave. Mag Lima on the LMP camera. And we copied all the frame counts.

a15a1085936.speaker: Allen
a15a1085936.text: And, Dave, this is Houston. Did you copy from me that your water separator number 1 looks good again?

a15a1085936.speaker: Worden
a15a1085936.text: Okay. TEI-26: SPS/G&N; 37354; plus 0.60, plus 0.97; 129:22:25.54; plus 3031.2, minus 1327.1, minus 0308.7; 180, 092, 339. That's four jets for 12 seconds and Lambda at T IG is plus 172.93.

a15a1085936.speaker: Scott
a15a1085936.text: Rog; I thought we called you back on that, Joe. We got it. Thank you. [Long Comm Break]

a15a1085936.speaker: Fullerton
a15a1085936.text: Okay, Al. Your readback is correct, and another comment. I think earlier we led you to believe that you shouldn't use the systems test meter. We retract that. We think the system - systems text - test meter is okay, and use it anytime you feel the desire to. Over.

a15a1085936.speaker: Fullerton
a15a1085936.text: And we're still missing the deploy time on the booms there back earlier. If you've got them written down and you want to get on, just give them to us anytime you have time.

a15a1085936.speaker: Worden
a15a1085936.text: Okay. I'll - Let me dig for them. Gordo, on these boom deploy times and retract times, I don't have all of those times each time I do it, precisely, because sometimes it happens that I'm off busy doing something else, and I - you know, I miss the barber pole, so I - I don't have all of them.

a15a1085936.speaker: Fullerton
a15a1085936.text: Okay. I'm sure it's not a matter of life or death.

a15_1090710csm.speaker: Worden
a15_1090710csm.text: Okay. Did you get the gyro torquing angles on that P52, Gordo?

a15_1090710csm.speaker: Worden
a15_1090710csm.text: Okay. I torqued them out at 109:07.

a15_1090710csm.speaker: Fullerton
a15_1090710csm.text: Roger; 109:07; and, for your information, there's one minute now until all those items on the SIM bay there is coming up.

a15_1091054csm.speaker: Fullerton
a15_1091054csm.text: A couple of requests - for you here. We would, first of all, like the Mass Spectrometer Discriminator switch to Low. Over.

a15_1091054csm.speaker: Worden
a15_1091054csm.text: Okay. The Mass Spec. Discriminator's in Low.

a15_1091054csm.speaker: Fullerton
a15_1091054csm.text: And we're ready for an E-Mod, and we'd also like to ask you for a crew status report. Over.

a15_1091054csm.speaker: Worden
a15_1091054csm.text: Okay. The E-Mod's coming your way, and stand by a minute and I'll give you all the status.

a15_1091054csm.speaker: Worden
a15_1091054csm.text: I guess just - if you want just crew status report - doing just fine. I don't know what else you can say.

a15_1091054csm.speaker: Fullerton
a15_1091054csm.text: Can you give us how much sleep you got last night, and also your PRD read-out.

a15_1091054csm.speaker: Worden
a15_1091054csm.text: Okay. I've got apparently a bad PRD, so I haven't been keeping track, but I will if you want. But I've got Dave's PRD. And, let's see, I guess you didn't get a status report this morning. I got - I think all three of us got seven and a half hours of sleep last night, and I got mine all in one segment. And I've taken no medication today.

a15_1091054csm.speaker: Fullerton
a15_1091054csm.text: Okay, Al. Fine. That - that was the problem; we didn't get this morning's report. One other quickie. If you'll comment if we're throwing too many reminders up from the ground here or not enough. We're just trying to get a feel for whether we're harassing you or helping you - on the timing callouts.

a15_1091054csm.speaker: Worden
a15_1091054csm.text: Gordo, I think - Yeah, yeah. I think if you don't expect me to answer, it's a great help to me, because I do find that I'm trying to be three places at once in here; and, if I'm doing a P52, I can't be over working the - the SIM bay at the same time. So the reminder is good. I can always break into a P52 to go turn something off, but bearing in mind that I don't have a mission timer in - in the Lower Equipment Bay, it's a little difficult for me to keep track of the time sometimes, so I do appreciate it.

a15_1091054csm.speaker: Allen
a15_1091054csm.text: Hadley Base, this is Houston. Requesting telemetry switch (to) Low bit rate (in order to conserve power). Please.

a15_1091054csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1091054csm.text: Rog. Low bit rate. [Long Comm Break]

a15_1091054csm.speaker: Fullerton
a15_1091054csm.text: Okay. We'll keep them coming. If they, at any time, become too much, just shut us up.

a15_1091513csm.speaker: Fullerton
a15_1091513csm.text: Endeavour, Houston. We got about 2 minutes until LOS. We still need the onboard readings, but if they were all nominal, just say so, and we'll get them some time later. And that's about all we have for you until tomorrow morning. Over.

a15_1091513csm.speaker: Worden
a15_1091513csm.text: Okay. Onboard read-outs: Bat[tery] C was 37 [volts]; Pyro Bat A was 37; Pyro Bat B, 37; RCS Alpha was 73 [percent]; Bravo, 71; Charlie, 72; and Delta, 73.

a15_1091513csm.speaker: Fullerton
a15_1091513csm.text: Okay. We copy all that. [Long pause.]

a15a1094339.speaker: Allen
a15a1094339.text: Hello, Hadley Base; this is Houston. Over.

a15a1094339.speaker: Irwin
a15a1094339.text: What can I do for you? 109:43:52 Allen: (Making a mis-identification) Roger, Dave. We've got two goodnight questions for you here. The first, we're trying to unravel some water-pressure data, and we just need to know if you charged the PLSSs using your checklist or using the decal instructions on the PLSSs. Over.

a15a1094339.speaker: Irwin
a15a1094339.text: No, we used the checklist. We used the checklist for the water recharge. [Having gone to low power transmissions, these transmissions from Hadley are relatively faint and noisy. Dave and I are convinced that this is Jim is talking, but only because of clues from cadence and word choices.]

a15a1094339.speaker: Allen
a15a1094339.text: Roger; understand you used the checklist and charged it with water for the specified 5 minutes then. Over.

a15a1094339.speaker: Allen
a15a1094339.text: Okay; copy that. (Still thinking he's talking to Dave) And, Dave, we've got a major discrepancy in your radiation dosimeter reading. It's either gone belly-up on us or we miscopied the number which you read. We'll have to ask you to read it again, please.

a15a1094339.speaker: Scott
a15a1094339.text: You know that we switched them?

a15a1094339.speaker: Scott
a15a1094339.text: You know that CDR and CMP's PRD's were interchanged.

a15a1094339.speaker: Allen
a15a1094339.text: That's affirm, Dave; and the last reading we got from Al was considerably higher than the one we got from you. The device is either broken or you're being un-irradiated, which seems unreasonable. Over. 109:45:38 Scott: Well, all I can do is look in this very tiny window and look at these very tiny numbers and they say 2501...I guess I can give you a seven on that one (that is, 25017, rather than the 25011 he read earlier).

a15a1094339.speaker: Allen
a15a1094339.text: Roger. Everybody's happy. Thank you, Dave. And we have no questions from Houston. We'll say a pleasant good night to the two of you and look forward to tomorrow. Over.

a15a1094339.speaker: Scott
a15a1094339.text: Okay, Joe. I guess we don't have any alarm clock, so if somebody'll give us the word, we'll be standing by.

a15a1094339.speaker: Allen
a15a1094339.text: I wouldn't be at all surprised. You're liable to get the word from down here. (Pause) And it's been an outstanding day.

a15a1094339.speaker: Scott
a15a1094339.text: Yeah, we've enjoyed it. [Very Long Comm Break]

a15a1094339.speaker: Scott
a15a1094339.text: Houston, Hadley Base. We're all tucked in. We'll see you in the morning. [Astronaut Bob Parker takes over as CapCom for the rest period.]

a15_1120611.speaker: Parker
a15_1120611.text: Roger, Al. Sorry to wake you up again, but we need Reacquire and Narrow with angles of Pitch, plus 25; Yaw, 185. Over.

a15_1120611.speaker: Worden
a15_1120611.text: Okay, Houston. You've got Reacq, Narrow; Pitch, plus 25; and a Yaw of minus 185. How do you read?

a15_1120611.speaker: Parker
a15_1120611.text: Roger. Read you much better now, Al. Sorry about that. Good night, again.

a15_1120611.speaker: Worden
a15_1120611.text: That's okay. I wasn't asleep yet. I was waiting for you to call.

a15_1120611.speaker: Parker
a15_1120611.text: Oh, okay. Anything else you want to tell us?

a15_1120611.speaker: Worden
a15_1120611.text: No. I was just wondering what you wanted setting on the - on the High Gain is all.

a15a1154022.speaker: Parker
a15a1154022.text: Okay, Jim. We'd like you to leave it in the configuration you found it in for a few minutes, because that will allow us to verify that that's where the leak was. Over.

a15a1154022.speaker: Irwin
a15a1154022.text: Okay. I'm going to open the (urine) valve again. [In Houston, there is some uncertainty as to whether Jim opened the urine valve or the Descent O2 valve. At 115:42:02 , he confirms that it is the urine valve.]

a15a1154022.speaker: Parker
a15a1154022.text: Roger. Thank you. (Pause) I'll tell you, that's good news if that's what it is, man.

a15a1154022.speaker: Irwin
a15a1154022.text: Understand on your first...(stops to listen to Parker) Okay, on that first step that you read, it said, if leak stops, to close both dump valves .

a15a1154022.speaker: Parker
a15a1154022.text: Roger. That's affirm. In other words, if we see that the leak has stopped here on the ground, we will then ask you to close both dump valves and also verifying the urine QD. And, if the leak in the cabin - now, if the cabin is completely isolated - continues to hold, we will then ask you to open the hatch valves one at a time to verify that the hatch valves are not going to leak or which hatch valve is leaking in the open position. Some of that will be not indicated (that is, not performed) if, indeed, it is the urine QD that's capped. Do you copy, Jim?

a15a1154022.speaker: Irwin
a15a1154022.text: Okay. Yes. We understand.

a15a1154022.speaker: Parker
a15a1154022.text: Rog. And we'd like to verify right now, just quickly, that the Descent O2 is Closed; that the urine receptacle is back in its original configuration. Over. 115:42:02 Irwin: That's verified.

a15a1154022.speaker: Parker
a15a1154022.text: Roger. Let's just stand by here for a couple of minutes and we'll see what the ground has to tell us. (Pause)

a15a1154022.speaker: Irwin
a15a1154022.text: Roger. (Long Pause) Bob, as long as we're talking about consumables, what are you showing down there for water? Because we are reading, oh, about 60 percent on descent 1 and 2 now. (Long Pause) [In Houston, the experts tell Flight, "We'll, have to convert that one for him; but we're okay." See the discussion below.]

a15a1154022.speaker: Parker
a15a1154022.text: Stand by, Jim. We've got to read our decals down here, too. (Pause)

a15a1154022.speaker: Irwin
a15a1154022.text: Bob, you did copy my question about the water quantity?

a15a1154022.speaker: Parker
a15a1154022.text: Roger, Jim. And we're having to read our decals down here, too. It will take us a minute. We'll be right back with you.

a15a1154022.speaker: Irwin
a15a1154022.text: Understand. [Comm Break] [Jones - "I understand the word decal in the sense of the decal I saw on the top of the PLSS that you've got in your office, outlining the steps for refill. Was decal a generic term for a list of instructions, a list of steps?"] [Irwin - "I didn't know what he was talking about. I think he's probably talking about, maybe, a conversion chart from a transmitted value to the real, corrected value. Kind of a matrix form. I think that's probably what he's talking about."] [Scott - "A 'decal' was sometimes used on a meter or gauge as a conversion scale from one unit of measu

a15a1154022.speaker: Parker
a15a1154022.text: Jim, we have an answer for you on your water gauge problem. The 60 that you're seeing indeed corresponds to a true 70 percent; which, indeed, is the number that we were expecting to see. Over. 115:47:09 Irwin: Okay. Fine, Bob. Thank you. [Comm Break] [In Houston, Flight is told that the Descent O2 tank pressure is holding steady and the cabin pressure is dropping. Both indicate that the open urine valve is, indeed, the source of the problem.]

a15a1154022.speaker: Parker
a15a1154022.text: And, Hadley Base; Houston. Over.

a15a1154022.speaker: Irwin
a15a1154022.text: Go ahead, Bob. 115:49:O2 Parker: Rog. It looks like your descent tanks are holding up very nicely; your cabin is falling slightly, as you may have noticed already on your meters. We'd like you to take the urine receptacle off the hose and then put the QD cap on after you remove the urine receptacle. Over. And then, after you have done this, we will watch the cabin for a little bit longer to see that it stops also. Over.

a15a1154022.speaker: Irwin
a15a1154022.text: Okay. That's in work. (Long Pause) Okay. The urine receptacle is off; and the other QD is installed.

a15a1154022.speaker: Parker
a15a1154022.text: Roger. We're standby to watch what comes off down here on the ground. (Long Pause) And, Jim, we'll be sitting here in this configuration for about 5 minutes to watch the cabin again.

a15a1154022.speaker: Irwin
a15a1154022.text: Roger.

a15a1154022.speaker: Parker
a15a1154022.text: It looked like you were getting pretty good sleep there for a while, Jim.

a15a1154022.speaker: Irwin
a15a1154022.text: Say again, Bob.

a15a1154022.speaker: Parker
a15a1154022.text: Rog. It looked like you were getting a pretty good sleep there.

a15a1154022.speaker: Irwin
a15a1154022.text: Yes, sir. That's the best sleep I've had on the flight.

a15a1154022.speaker: Parker
a15a1154022.text: Roger. [Jones - "You just said that, listening to this, you still sound a little sleepy."] [Irwin - "Maybe I was snoring. I don't know. I wonder if there's ever been a reported snoring in space?"] [Jones - "I take it Dave wasn't a snorer?"] [Irwin - "I never heard him. He might have heard me. I don't know. I don't recall he ever commented on it."]

a15a1154022.speaker: Parker
a15a1154022.text: How was Dave doing? (Pause)

a15a1154022.speaker: Scott
a15a1154022.text: Just fine, Bob. I was way down in sleep when you gave us a call.

a15a1154022.speaker: Parker
a15a1154022.text: Sorry about that, Dave.

a15a1154022.speaker: Scott
a15a1154022.text: Oh, no. That's okay! Let's get the problem squared away.

a15a1154022.speaker: Parker
a15a1154022.text: Yeah, I figured we lost a little bit of sleep down here on the ground tonight. I couldn't even fall asleep at my console. 115:51:47 Irwin: That is amazing. [Comm Break] [Jones - "I take it that Bob occasionally fell asleep during the..."] [Scott - "Anywhere. As I recall. Bob could sleep about anywhere."] [Irwin, from the 1971 Technical Debrief - "The temperature in the cabin was very comfortable (for sleeping). I slept in my constant Wear Garment in the sleeping bag and did not use the coveralls."] [Scott, from the 1971 Technical Debrief - "I slept in my coveralls without a sleeping bag; so I

a15a1154022.speaker: Irwin
a15a1154022.text: Houston, this is Hadley. If you're not too busy, I could copy the lift-off data for (Command Module orbits number) 21 to 27. [Jim wants to get as many checklist items out of the way as possible so that they can get out on time. He is on Surface 2-9 . He and Dave may have already stowed the hammocks and replaced the ECS Primary LiOH cartridge. See a detail from an Apollo 16 LM-close-out picture, showing the location of the replacment unit. Early in the EVA, Jim will load another ECS Primary cartridge in a transfer pallet. They will put that cartrige to use at EVA-2 wake-up.]

a15a1154022.speaker: Parker
a15a1154022.text: Roger, Jim. If you're ready to copy, then: T-21 is 188:30:48. (Pause as his error is pointed out to him) Negative; that should be a 118. I guess you'd gather that. T-22 is 120:29:00; T-23, 122:27:10; T-24, 124:25:21; T-25, 126:23:32; T-26, 128:21:44; T-27, 130:19:54. Over

a15a1161913.speaker: Parker
a15a1161913.text: Hadley Base, Houston. Over.

a15a1161913.speaker: Scott
a15a1161913.text: Go ahead.

a15a1161913.speaker: Parker
a15a1161913.text: Roger, Dave. It looks like we can tell you that, at the present time, our extrapolations indicate we'll have sufficient oxygen for a completely nominal mission, including the PLSS recharge on EVA-3. Having high enough pressure (in the descent stage oxygen tank) for the PLSS recharge was our hardest constraint, and it looks like we meet it, although rather closely. Over.

a15a1161913.speaker: Scott
a15a1161913.text: Okay. Well, we'll breathe slowly and save as much as we can.

a15a1161913.speaker: Parker
a15a1161913.text: Copy. [Comm Break]

a15a1161913.speaker: Scott
a15a1161913.text: Houston, Hadley. We've got another question for you since we're sitting here eating and looking around. Did you all, by chance, get any figures on our descent rate at touchdown? We're just taking a look out here, and it looks like we may have stroked a gear some (that is, compressed the shock absorber on the forward landing strut, the only one of the four that they can see); and, as near as we can recall, we were coming down about a foot per second when we got the contact, and we just wondered if you had any data on that yet. (Long Pause)

a15a1161913.speaker: Parker
a15a1161913.text: Stand by, Dave. We're getting that.

a15a1161913.speaker: Scott
a15a1161913.text: Okay. (Long Pause)

a15a1161913.speaker: Parker
a15a1161913.text: Okay, Dave. We have an answer for you; which is that we were showing 0.7 feet per second up to touchdown (means contact). And then at touchdown, it appears that, at the same point we got the roll and pitch, we picked up to something like 3.7 feet per second at that point. Over.

a15a1161913.speaker: Scott
a15a1161913.text: So we went from 0.7 to 3.7 from contact to touchdown. Is that right? (Long Pause) [As mentioned previously, the figures given in the Apollo 15 Mission Report are 0.5 fps at contact and 6.8 fps at touchdown. Readers should note that these figures imply a 1.18 second free-fall from about 12 feet. As Parker suggests at 116:23:54, someone did a quick calculation from a quick look at the telemetry and, probably, made an error.] [The following is taken from the Apollo 15 Mission Report. "Computer simulations (using telemetry data and the known, final tilt of the spacecraft, and the known shape of th

a15a1161913.speaker: Parker
a15a1161913.text: Dave, we're having to look at these based upon times. We don't see the contact light, and we don't really know when touchdown occurred; but we're looking at things like the times. You were coming down at 0.7 there, all the way to the very end; and, then, at the same time that we see the pitchup and the rollover, we see an increase suddenly to 3.7. Over.

a15a1161913.speaker: Scott
a15a1161913.text: Oh, I see. Like we might have stuck our rear paw [sic] in a crater back there somewhere, huh?

a15a1161913.speaker: Parker
a15a1161913.text: Say again, Dave?

a15a1161913.speaker: Scott
a15a1161913.text: Looks like we might have stuck the rear pad in a crater back there somewhere, huh?

a15a1161913.speaker: Parker
a15a1161913.text: Either that, or you touched down on something and fell through.

a15a1161913.speaker: Scott
a15a1161913.text: That's an interesting thought. (Long Pause) Well, that says the landing radar is pretty good data then. [Comm Break] [I asked Jim if Bob Parker's "touched down on something and fell through" might have been a reference to Tommy Gold 's theory of deep-dust layers, a theory that wasn't widely accepted in the lunar science community even before the successful and solid landings of the Russian Luna and U.S. Surveyor spacecraft blew it away.] [Irwin - "We had every confidence we'd hit a solid surface. We didn't have any fear of going through it. There wasn't any fear of any accumulation of dust, ei

a15a1161913.speaker: Scott
a15a1161913.text: Okay, Houston. Hadley Base, here. We're ready to talk over the EVA plan with you, if you'd like.

a15a1161913.speaker: Parker
a15a1161913.text: Roger, Dave. We're ready, too. First of all, we'll talk about the changes in the traverse plan, which are very minimal. But for your planning, we're now showing a LM location on the grid map in the coordinates of Bravo-Romeo 3 and 75.5. Over. [This spot is about 250 meters south and 500 meters east of the actual LM location.]

a15a1161913.speaker: Scott
a15a1161913.text: Okay, Bob. We're going to have to get in the ETB and pull the maps out. Just a second.

a15a1161913.speaker: Parker
a15a1161913.text: Okay, Rog. I'll wait, then. (Long Pause) [Bob Parker is a member of the support team and has participated in EVA planning, as illustrated by training photo 71-H-490 which shows him wearing EVA gloves while installing the DAC on the LRV qualification unit at Boeing on 29 January 1971. Bob served as EVA CapCom for Apollo 17.]

a15a1161913.speaker: Irwin
a15a1161913.text: Bob, will you give me the coordinates again?

a15a1161913.speaker: Parker
a15a1161913.text: Roger. Bravo-Romeo 3, 75.5. Over. (Pause)

a15a1161913.speaker: Irwin
a15a1161913.text: Roger. Copy. Bravo-Romeo 3, 75.5.

a15a1161913.speaker: Parker
a15a1161913.text: Roger. And that over there near November (Crater). Okay, to write down, the rest of this - for a while, anyway - is kind of just advisory. This new location adds approximately 0.6 kilometers to the EVA-1 traverse and, therefore, about six minutes driving time. However, that's only provisionary, of course; and our indications of a beautiful flat plain out there (from Dave's SEVA description, primarily the lack of rocks) may mean that we'll make up some of that time just in being able to drive faster than we were, perhaps, anticipating. (Pause) If this is not the case...

a15a1161913.speaker: Scott
a15a1161913.text: Say, let...

a15a1161913.speaker: Parker
a15a1161913.text: Go ahead.

a15a1161913.speaker: Scott
a15a1161913.text: Bob, before you get too far into that "broad flat plain" out there, I hope we made it clear that there is a fairly good population of craters which we're going to probably have to drive around. Even though there are no boulders, we're still going to have somewhat of a "wander factor" in avoiding, oh, the three- to four-meter craters. [Because they will not be able to drive in a straight line, they will actually travel about ten percent further than would be indicated by the straight-line distances between sites. This is the 'wander factor'.] 116:29:23 Parker: Okay, we realize that, Dave. And,

a15a1161913.speaker: Scott
a15a1161913.text: Okay. Very good. [Scott - "When you consider the planning that went into the mission, and then we get there and we're not exactly where we're supposed to be, and all the things that go on. And over a seven-hour EVA, all you change are six minutes at the end. Not bad. Pretty good planning. We didn't discover anything that would change, geologically, what we were doing. But at least it's a verification that the guys who put all this planning stuff were pretty good. And there's not a lot of waffling back there in Houston; and they leave us on the plan that we had, which I think is good from an ef

a15a1161913.speaker: Parker
a15a1161913.text: Okay. Extra activities we'd like you to include: We'd like the big glass ball you saw in the vicinity of the LM (after the SEVA at 108:30:36 , and, perhaps, it) could be picked up, hopefully, with the contingency sample, if it's convenient; if not, it should be retrieved as part of the LRV (Lunar Roving Vehicle: the Rover) preparation before the EVA traverse. The geology people, for obvious reasons, are rather interested in the large black rocks you described in the SEVA (debrief) - at 40 meters and 300 meters (west of the LM). And we'd like to pick those up before you leave (the Moon) sometim

a15a1161913.speaker: Scott
a15a1161913.text: Okay...(Stops to listen to Parker) Bob, give us a couple of minutes after each of those comments to come back at you.

a15a1161913.speaker: Parker
a15a1161913.text: Roger. Waiting. [The Backroom tells Flight that the "selected samples" are the black rocks. Flight points out that they should have said " black rocks".] [Jones - "Had you done much work in the field with Bob?"] [Scott - "Yeah, he'd done a fair amount of work in the field with us as CapCom. Not nearly as much as Joe Allen. And it is interesting that you see this overlap in pausing, because it's part of developing the capability to talk back and forth when, on Earth, you don't have the delay problem. We'd spent so much time with Joe, you don't really notice any problems due to the delay. It's t

a15a1161913.speaker: Scott
a15a1161913.text: Okay, we were just discussing the frags around the LM. We can see a number of interesting rocks out here, and we thought it might be better to wait until we got back to the LM (at the end of the EVA) to pick them up; and make sure we didn't disturb the surface around it. Although, we can pick them up fairly quickly in the beginning. I guess it's your choice: if you want to spend the time in the beginning or wait until we get back.

a15a1161913.speaker: Parker
a15a1161913.text: Roger, Dave. My first flip comment there was "before you leave the Moon". The second comment, on the selected samples, "should be taken at the crew's convenience at the end of EVA" was apparently intended by the geologists to mean selected samples of these black rocks and other interesting frags. Over.

a15a1161913.speaker: Scott
a15a1161913.text: Well, do you specifically want us to pick up the glass ball and the black rocks before we start (the) EVA-1 (traverse)?

a15a1161913.speaker: Parker
a15a1161913.text: Stand by, Dave. (Long Pause) [Scott - "He hadn't worked with us. 'What are you saying? Do you want us to do it or not?' And it's pretty trivial in the overall scheme of things. We know we're going to go get that rock, but we're also thinking in terms of not messing up the area, and we're also trying to think of getting on the road. That rock is a nice rock but, having seen all the other stuff out there, we know there are lots of those. And, perhaps in the Backroom, they've only heard a description of a couple, and they're all excited about the couple. I remember Jim and I talking that night (a

a15a1161913.speaker: Parker
a15a1161913.text: Okay, Dave. We'll put the glass ball at a higher priority, apparently, because they're worried that the glass ball might get lost once the area gets mucked up a little bit, whereas the black rocks will probably still be there. Over.

a15a1161913.speaker: Scott
a15a1161913.text: Okay. Understand. And...I guess our understanding of the contingency sample is that it's supposed to be typical of the surface around, rather than an exotic. (Pause) [The contingency sample is just that, a typical sample that Jim will collect and bag shortly after he gets out so that, if they have to leave quickly, they will at least have one sample of the soil and small rocks at Hadley. An 'exotic' is an unusual, atypical piece of rock, likely one thrown in by an impact somewhere else on the Moon.]

a15a1161913.speaker: Parker
a15a1161913.text: I guess that's basically true...I guess that's basically true, Dave; however, they would like this little glass ball. You could also put it separately in a bag before you leave with the Rover, or I guess they really wouldn't mind, since they know particularly what it is, if it was part of the contingency sample. [The Backroom tells Flight that they agree with this statement.]

a15a1161913.speaker: Scott
a15a1161913.text: Okay. We'll take care of that.

a15a1161913.speaker: Parker
a15a1161913.text: Okay. Let me talk to you about Rover status. The additional distance - this 0.6 (km) - and your new position will not affect the electrical power profile. It's really a very small and almost trivial distance (compared with the battery-supported potential of over 100 kilometers of driving). And, secondly, the LM slope (means the tilt), the 9 degrees by 9 (means 6) degrees, is within the angles for which the (Rover) deployment is specified - which is 15 degrees - and also within the angles for which it's been tested. And I guess a couple of days ago they did tests 15 degrees of pitch and 5 degre

a15a1161913.speaker: Scott
a15a1161913.text: Okay. That's nice to hear, and it sounds like those fellows are planning ahead as usual.

a15a1161913.speaker: Parker
a15a1161913.text: Hope so. And as far as checklist changes, we have none. As far as TV plan updates, we have none. (Pause)

a15a1161913.speaker: Scott
a15a1161913.text: Okay. Understand.

a15a1161913.speaker: Parker
a15a1161913.text: And, sometime, Dave, the medics would like a status report, post sleep.

a15a1161913.speaker: Scott
a15a1161913.text: Okay. Stand by. (Long Pause) [Jones - "Are there any comments you'd like to make about how that pitch and roll influenced your ability to move around inside. I realize that you don't hardly have room to swing a cat inside the spacecraft but, was the tilt enough to be bothersome?"] [Irwin - "No. I guess it was maybe a little distracting, the fact that we weren't level. But the only time we're in there, really, was the sleep and to get rest. And, when we were awake and taking data or checking systems, the angle didn't bother us at all. It is interesting to find out that they'd done the simulatio

a15a1161913.speaker: Parker
a15a1161913.text: And, when you're ready, Falcon, we've got some consumables (update) for you. 116:35:51 Scott: Okay. On the crew status, I guess we both got about 5 hours sleep, based on the time we went to bed and the time we got up; no medication; and we're in good shape. And I guess you can go ahead with the consumables.

a15a1161913.speaker: Parker
a15a1161913.text: Roger. And how about a PDR or PRD (Personnel Radiation Dosimeter) - or whatever they are - readout.

a15a1161913.speaker: Scott
a15a1161913.text: Okay. I'll tell you, it would help us out if we could do that once a day. You know they're stowed down in the suit pocket, and we've got to do some digging to get them. We'll give them to you twice a day if you really need them, but it takes a little time.

a15a1161913.speaker: Parker
a15a1161913.text: Roger, Dave. I think they're only called out for once a day, we agree; and somehow, I guess, TransEarth - (correcting himself) or Translunar - we got in the habit of getting them from you at the time when we didn't really need them, like at sleep. We got them from you at sleep last night; it's just that, in the checklist, it calls them out for right now. But you're right, it is only a requirement once a day, and we did get it last night.

a15a1161913.speaker: Scott
a15a1161913.text: Okay. Our crew status report has them in the evening before bed. Do you want them then, or do you want them in the morning?

a15a1161913.speaker: Parker
a15a1161913.text: Say again, Dave. When does your crew status report have them?

a15a1161913.speaker: Scott
a15a1161913.text: Prior to the rest periods.

a15a1161913.speaker: Parker
a15a1161913.text: Okay; the Flight Plan shows it in the post-sleep. (Pause) We'd like one this morning.

a15a1161913.speaker: Scott
a15a1161913.text: Well, make a decision. [Scott - "Does it really matter? Whatever you want to do. If there's a conflict between the status report and the checklist, that's because somebody in the medical world didn't check it. And it's their job to check it. If it's a conflict, okay, that's fine. You can probably hear the tone (of voice) here - we don't care. 'Just decide what you want to do and let's get on with it, rather than all this discussion.' The system didn't work, here. We were taking time with some relatively trivial procedural activities."] [Jones - "And the fact that this doesn't happen very often

a15a1161913.speaker: Parker
a15a1161913.text: Rog. We'd like one this morning before the EVA, and the surgeons promise they'll look at it (that is, the requirement) today.

a15a1161913.speaker: Scott
a15a1161913.text: (With a touch of sarcasm) That's encouraging. 116:37:50 Irwin: Okay, Bob, I'm ready to copy the consumables.

a15a1161913.speaker: Parker
a15a1161913.text: Okay. This is for GET of 116:40. RCS A, 85 (percent); B, 85. [These are fuel quantities remaining in the Reaction Control System, the small jets that control LM attitude in flight. There are two such systems: A and B.]

a15a1161913.speaker: Parker
a15a1161913.text: O2 descent (tank)1, 78.5; tank 2, 78; O2 ascent 1, 99; tank 2, 99; H2O descent 1, 58; tank 2, 58. H2O ascent 1, 100 percent; tank 2, 100 percent. Descent amp-hours (remaining), 1538; ascent amp-hours, 572. Over.

a15a1161913.speaker: Irwin
a15a1161913.text: Okay; I copy, Bob. (Long Pause) Bob, I'm just looking at the descent water. It looks like we're off about 12 percent. Is that any concern down there?

a15a1161913.speaker: Parker
a15a1161913.text: Roger, Jim. We didn't just suddenly lose that. That was TELMU's understanding of how we wanted the consumables updated. We're having a discussion about that right now. That was meant to be what your reading on board should be. I guess, saying that if you're reading 58 percent, you're in good shape. Whereas, there's a separate figure, which is a figure down here, which I guess is something like the 70 percent that I gave you a few minutes ago. (Pause) That seems to be a...

a15a1161913.speaker: Irwin
a15a1161913.text: Okay; understand.

a15a1161913.speaker: Parker
a15a1161913.text: That seems to be a question of how TELMU interprets what the consumables update should be. We may change that around and let you know later. (Pause)

a15a1161913.speaker: Irwin
a15a1161913.text: Roger. We copy. [Comm Break] [The water tank percentages that Parker read up were the gauge readings, rather than the actual values. Jim is implying that he expected a read-up of the actual values.] [Scott- "On board, the reading is from a dial or a gauge. The gauge was probably put in a couple of years before the flight. And there are some divergences in those kinds of systems, so they have to be calibrated. And what you try to do is get it so that your apples and oranges are all apples and mean the same thing."]

a15a1161913.speaker: Parker
a15a1161913.text: Okay, Hadley; this is Houston. The actual on-board figures - not the gauge figures that you'll read, but the actual onboard figures for water - are, descent 1, 70.7 and tank 2, 68.5. Over.

a15a1161913.speaker: Scott
a15a1161913.text: Rog; we copy that. Thank you. [Very Long Comm Break] [The Backroom asks Flight if he had a specific task in mind when he had Bob tell the crew at 116:29:23 that the six minutes of extra driving time has "already been deleted from the activities at the LM at the end of the traverse." Flight responds "No, we didn't designate anything specific. We took six minutes out of the traverse at the LM to make our bookkeeping come out and add up to seven hours. But (for only) six minutes, we didn't think it was worth picking a task and going through all the checklist changes that far into the EVA because,

a15a1172236.speaker: Scott
a15a1172236.text: Morning, Joe. We're about due to wake the computer up for a little while; and, if you're ready, we'll bring it out of its sleep period for a minute and then put it back to sleep - if you want to take a look at it. (Pause)

a15a1172236.speaker: Allen
a15a1172236.text: Roger, Dave; that sounds good to us. We'll be watching.

a15a1172236.speaker: Scott
a15a1172236.text: Okay, Houston. It looks like it's still with us.

a15a1172236.speaker: Allen
a15a1172236.text: Roger, Dave. That's good news. [Very Long Comm Break. They are about to start suit donning .] [Scott - "The donning and doffing of the PLSSs and the suits was the hardest work, by far, in the whole mission. And in training, too. That was hard work. We did this over and over, 'cause you have to do it and you've got to do it carefully. But, in the confinement of the LM, it takes a long time, it's very boring, and you have to pay precise attention to everything you do, because you can't afford to screw it up. It's not the fun part of getting out, but it's a necessity. It's real hard work. Boy, wh

a15_1184816csm.speaker: Henize
a15_1184816csm.text: Alfredo, Houston is calling. How are you doing up there? [Pause.]

a15_1184816csm.speaker: Worden
a15_1184816csm.text: Good morning, Houston; this is Endeavour. Doing - doing fine. Reading you loud and clear.

a15_1184816csm.speaker: Henize
a15_1184816csm.text: Glad to hear from you, Endeavour. We'd like to have Accept, when you have a chance to reach up that direction.

a15_1184816csm.speaker: Henize
a15_1184816csm.text: Roger. And down on panel 230, Mass Spectrometer, Multiplier, High, at your convenience. [Pause.]

a15_1184816csm.speaker: Henize
a15_1184816csm.text: Thank you. And, I've got that batch of updates there, whenever you can copy.

a15_1184816csm.speaker: Henize
a15_1184816csm.text: Al, on that mass spectrograph, we want the Multiplier, High and the Discriminator, Low.

a15_1184816csm.speaker: Worden
a15_1184816csm.text: Okay; understand. Multiplier, High, and Discriminator, Low.

a15_1184816csm.speaker: Henize
a15_1184816csm.text: That's - that's the right way, yeah. [Long pause.]

a15_1185456csm.speaker: Worden
a15_1185456csm.text: Okay, Houston. This is Endeavour. I'm ready to copy some updates there, Karl. [Long pause.]

a15_1185456csm.speaker: Henize
a15_1185456csm.text: Endeavour, this is Houston. The first thing we'd like get through to you are the Mapping Camera photo PADs over on the next page at 119:30.

a15_1185456csm.speaker: Henize
a15_1185456csm.text: "Start: 119:34:33; stop: 121:33:02." And a note to that is that the - the - the extend/retract times on the Mapping Camera seem to be getting longer with time, and, until further notice, we'd like for you to record and send down the Delta-T on each extend and retract.

a15_1185456csm.speaker: Worden
a15_1185456csm.text: Okay; understand. Yes, those times do seem to be getting longer, and I'll record the Delta-T and tell you what they are.

a15_1185456csm.speaker: Henize
a15_1185456csm.text: Roger. And, over there at 119:20, on the mass spectrometer boom retract, it says "record the retract time Delta-T." Instead of "in barber pole," we want all of these in the future "from switch on to gray." That corresponds to what we can monitor here on the ground, and we - we need to - we need to calibrate - comparison of your data and ours. I'm sorry; that's not what we monitor, but this is - this is - this is...

a15_1185456csm.speaker: Worden
a15_1185456csm.text: Roger. Instead you want that "switch on to gray."

a15_1185456csm.speaker: Henize
a15_1185456csm.text: Right. That compares with our test calibration data, that's what I should say. And while I'm reading up...

a15_1185456csm.speaker: Henize
a15_1185456csm.text: ...while I'm reading up to you, I'd also like to get something in on the ECS [Environmental Control System] radiators, the outlet temperature is running high 10 to 15 degrees [Fahrenheit], primary radiator outlet temperature. And we like for you to verify, first of all, that Flow Control on the ECS Radiators is Auto and Power. Is that the way they're setting?

a15_1185456csm.speaker: Henize
a15_1185456csm.text: Okay. And three circuit breakers over on panel 5, ECS Radiators, Controller, AC1 and AC2 should be closed, and, also Controller Heaters, Main A should be closed. All three closed.

a15_1185456csm.speaker: Worden
a15_1185456csm.text: Yes, that's verified. They're all closed.

a15_1185456csm.speaker: Henize
a15_1185456csm.text: Okay; thank you. You got a status report to send down to us?

a15_1185456csm.speaker: Worden
a15_1185456csm.text: Okay. Got about 5 and a half to 6 hours of sleep in 2 segments. My PRD [Personal Radiation Dosimeter] is reading 23105, but I'm not sure that's any good. And no medication, and standing by for a consumables update, and the rest of it.

a15_1185456csm.speaker: Henize
a15_1185456csm.text: Roger. Consumables update. Are you ready?

a15_1185456csm.speaker: Henize
a15_1185456csm.text: The time is 118:00; RCS total is sixty - is 63 [percent]; quad A, 63; 64; 61; 64; H 2 tank 1, 76.9; 75.6; 51.9; O 2 tank 1, 79.3; 87 - 82.5; 61.7.

a15_1190320csm.speaker: Henize
a15_1190320csm.text: Al, if you can listen while you work, I got a couple of short goodies for you before you go round the corner. First of all, the experimenters on the SIM bay are as happy as can be. I think on the Gamma-ray experiment, they say on that first rev data, they have enough to justify the whole flight; they're so happy with it. I have a more complete science report for you, which I will send up on the next rev. And just bringing you up to date on the news, the egress down on the surface will be beginning on schedule in just about one hour.

a15_1190320csm.speaker: Worden
a15_1190320csm.text: Hey, that all sounds real good, Karl. And, as you can see, I'm right in the middle of a P52 here. I'll have the second star and the gyro torquing angles in just a second.

a15_1190320csm.speaker: Worden
a15_1190320csm.text: And if you've got those torquing angles, I'll get them on the minute. [Pause.]

a15_1190320csm.speaker: Henize
a15_1190320csm.text: We don't have any CMC data at the present time. You'll have to read them down to us, Al.

a15_1190320csm.speaker: Worden
a15_1190320csm.text: Okay, Karl. I'll read them to you. P52: the stars were 01 and 36. The torquing angles were minus 3 balls 28; minus 3 balls 58; plus 3 balls 12; and they were torqued out at 119:05 on the minute.

a15_1190320csm.speaker: Henize
a15_1190320csm.text: We copy all of that. Loud and clear. Thank you. [Long pause.]

a15a1190546.speaker: Scott
a15a1190546.text: (Burst of static) Okay, Houston; Hadley Base. We're ready to go into a PLSS comm check, if you're ready. (Static clears)

a15a1190546.speaker: Henize
a15a1190546.text: And as you go around the corner Al, all your systems are looking good.

a15a1190546.speaker: Allen
a15a1190546.text: Roger, Dave. We read you about 3 by. [Scott - "Five-by-five means 'loud and clear'."] [Jones - "So Joe is saying it's a little faint and muddy."] [The fact that they are using aviation terminology generated the following discussion.] [Scott - "A lot of what we did, as you can see, was based on aircraft operations - which is one of the keys to the success of Apollo. When they started it, they brought in a lot of people who had aircraft operations and hardware experience. The group from Langley that formed NASA from NACA and the group from Langley that moved to Houston were all from the airplane

a15a1190546.speaker: Allen
a15a1190546.text: Stand by until I get a go-ahead from INCO here.

a15a1190546.speaker: Worden
a15a1190546.text: Roger, Karl. Thank you. See you on the other side.

a15a1190546.speaker: Henize
a15a1190546.text: Roger.

a15a1190546.speaker: Scott
a15a1190546.text: (Clear comm) Okay. (Pause)

a15a1190546.speaker: Allen
a15a1190546.text: Okay, Dave. We're go on the FM and high power. We've got it down here.

a15a1190546.speaker: Scott
a15a1190546.text: Okay. We'll be talking to you. [Comm Break]

a15a1190546.speaker: Scott
a15a1190546.text: (Reading Surface 3-7 at the bottom of the left-hand column) (sensitivity) VOX Max. VHF A to T/R; B to Receive. Okay. CB(16) Comm: SE Audio, open, and you connect to the PLSS comm. (Long Pause) [In this section of the audio tape, there are definite instances of words and/or parts of words not picked up due to slow VOX activation, also called clipping. This is a sensitivity problem that plagued Buzz Aldrin throughout the Apollo 11 EVA. Here, the problem will disappear shortly and, on the whole, the comm will be the best received from any crew while suited in the LM.]

a15a1190546.speaker: Scott
a15a1190546.text: Okay, CB(16) Comm: SE Audio, close. PLSS PTT (Push-to-Talk) ... Maintain right, verify. Okay, PLSS mode, A, wheel counter-clockwise.

a15a1190546.speaker: Irwin
a15a1190546.text: (Some interference) ... mode A. And wheel is full counter-clockwise.

a15a1190546.speaker: Scott
a15a1190546.text: Okay. Tone-on, vent flag P, Press flag O, O2 momentary.

a15a1190546.speaker: Irwin
a15a1190546.text: Okay; they're on.

a15a1190546.speaker: Scott
a15a1190546.text: Okay. PLSS O2 pressure gauge greater than 85 (percent).

a15a1190546.speaker: Irwin
a15a1190546.text: Verified.

a15a1190546.speaker: Scott
a15a1190546.text: Okay. You've made your comm check with me. Give Houston a call.

a15a1190546.speaker: Irwin
a15a1190546.text: Houston, how do you read the LMP?

a15a1190546.speaker: Allen
a15a1190546.text: Jim, you're loud and clear. There's a squeal in the background.

a15a1190546.speaker: Irwin
a15a1190546.text: Roger. I have that squeal, also. (Pause)

a15a1190546.speaker: Allen
a15a1190546.text: Jim, stand by; we'll...(Stops to listen)

a15a1190546.speaker: Irwin
a15a1190546.text: I'll turn the squelch down a little bit to see if that...

a15a1190546.speaker: Allen
a15a1190546.text: Roger. And, Jim, stand by; we're thinking about that tone a minute here...(correcting himself) about the squeal in the background.

a15a1190546.speaker: Irwin
a15a1190546.text: Okay. I'm standing by. (Long Pause)

a15a1190546.speaker: Allen
a15a1190546.text: Jim, this is Houston. Could you turn your volume down a little bit for us, please? (Pause) And that's volume on the wheel.

a15a1190546.speaker: Irwin
a15a1190546.text: Okay. The volume's down now.

a15a1190546.speaker: Allen
a15a1190546.text: That's...

a15a1190546.speaker: Irwin
a15a1190546.text: Okay. It's down about three quarters of the way. How do you read now?

a15a1190546.speaker: Allen
a15a1190546.text: Jim, that's beautiful. The squeal's gone and you're 5 by. (Pause) And we're ready to go to the next step.

a15a1190546.speaker: Irwin
a15a1190546.text: Okay; very good.

a15a1190546.speaker: Allen
a15a1190546.text: Rog. We're ready to go to the next step.

a15a1190546.speaker: Scott
a15a1190546.text: Okay. CB(11) Comm: CDR Audio, open. [Comm Break, as they get Dave off of LM comm and on to PLSS comm.]

a15a1190546.speaker: Scott
a15a1190546.text: Okay. I have a tone-on, vent flag P and pressure flag O. O2 pressure gauge is reading about 94 percent. And, how do you read me, Jim?

a15a1190546.speaker: Irwin
a15a1190546.text: I read you loud and clear.

a15_1203101csm.text: Okay, go ahead.

a15_1203101csm.text: And, this is one of those general things. On reporting the Delta-T, it should be from switch on to talkback gray.

a15_1203101csm.speaker: Worden
a15_1203101csm.text: Okay.

a15_1203101csm.speaker: Henize
a15_1203101csm.text: And, we have exactly the same thing at 129 hours and 20 minutes.

a15_1203101csm.speaker: Worden
a15_1203101csm.text: What was that again? What time was that?

a15_1203101csm.speaker: Henize
a15_1203101csm.text: At 129:20, the same thing, the switch - the Delta-T that you read back to us is switch on to talkback gray. And really, I suppose, we should make this a generality - that we don't have to put it in the Flight Plan every time.

a15_1203101csm.speaker: Allen
a15_1203101csm.text: Roger. Copy. [Scott, from the 1971 Technical Debrief - "I noticed that the battery voltage and amp readout on battery 2 were zero. That subsequently turned out to be an indicator problem; and we did have both batteries available."] [Each of the batteries is supposed to have a charge of 121 amp-hours and the cause of the initial readings of 105 amp-hours on both was never determined. At 121:30:18, just prior to leaving the LM, Dave will give readouts of 110 amp-hours on battery 1 and 115 on battery 2. Subsequent readings will decrease from those readings in a reasonable manner. See, also, the d

a15_1203101csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1203101csm.text: And the only discrepancy so far...I don't have any volts on number 2. (Pause) PWM Select is Both; Drive Enable, 2 in forward, PWM 1, (and) reverse, PWM 2. And Houston, I'll stand by for any comments you might have on that (zero voltage) readout.

a15_1203101csm.speaker: Worden
a15_1203101csm.text: Rog. I'd agree to that.

a15_1203101csm.speaker: Henize
a15_1203101csm.text: Incidentally, I have a question in that connection - [It] says verify that times previous to 118 hours were from switch on, beginning time. Do you recollect that?

a15_1203101csm.speaker: Allen
a15_1203101csm.text: Roger, Dave. I know you've rechecked your circuit breakers there.

a15_1203101csm.speaker: Worden
a15_1203101csm.text: Karl, the way we time it onboard here, is you have to hit the switch, and then look at the mission timer. Now, the - the Gamma-ray is taking about 6 seconds to go from switch on to barber pole, the Mass Spec. was going on immediately to barber pole, so it didn't make any difference in the case of the Mass Spec. And in the Gamma-ray, the most it could be off is 6 seconds.

a15_1203101csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1203101csm.text: That's correct. The circuit breakers are all in.

a15_1203101csm.speaker: Irwin
a15_1203101csm.text: Dave, just let me know before you drive.

a15_1203101csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1203101csm.text: Yeah. (Pause) [Jim doesn't want to miss filming the initial drive.]

a15_1203101csm.speaker: Allen
a15_1203101csm.text: Dave, we're standing by for you to drive away and monitor the amp...The amps on battery 2, please.

a15_1203101csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1203101csm.text: Okay, will do. Okay, 15 Volt DC is going to Secondary. Steering: Forward, Bus A; and Rear to Bus D. Drive Power: forward to Drive Power, forward to Bus A

a15_1203101csm.speaker: Henize
a15_1203101csm.text: Right. And, - I guess on the Gamma-ray when you reported the time - do you recall which it was that you were giving us, switch on or talkback barber pole?

a15_1203101csm.speaker: Worden
a15_1203101csm.text: Talkback barber pole.

a15_1203101csm.speaker: Henize
a15_1203101csm.text: Okay, fine. That's the way the instructions were, originally.

a15_1203101csm.speaker: Allen
a15_1203101csm.text: Roger, Dave...

a15_1203101csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1203101csm.text: And to Bus D.

a15_1203101csm.speaker: Allen
a15_1203101csm.text: ...and if battery 2 is out on us, we'll have no rear steering or no rear drive. Just be advised. [The four Rover wheels are each powered by a separate electric motor. In addition, with everything operational both the front and rear wheel-pairs can provide steering and, therefore, the Rover is capable of a very small turning radius. This type of steering was called "double Ackerman" steering.] [Jim carries the 16-mm camera across the TV field-of-view and off to the right.]

a15_1203101csm.speaker: Henize
a15_1203101csm.text: We have a comm change. It's simply an error in our Flight Plan at 128:10. [Pause.]

a15_1203101csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1203101csm.text: Okay. (Pause) out of detent; we're moving. 120:35:31 Allen: Extraordinary. (Pause) [The handcontroller has a detent at the neutral position so that it will sit there when Dave isn't applying forward or reverse power. Dave moves off slowly and out of view to the right.] [Scott - "Once it starts moving, the people in the backroom were breathing again."] [Jones - "Not only the people who designed and built the Rover, but all the geologists, too. Let's talk about that a little. I assume that there were contingency plans for walking EVAs."] [Scott - "Oh, yeah."] [The planned walking traverses as sh

a15_1203101csm.speaker: Henize
a15_1203101csm.text: And, at 128...

a15_1203101csm.speaker: Worden
a15_1203101csm.text: Okay, go ahead.

a15_1203101csm.speaker: Henize
a15_1203101csm.text: ...at 128:10, the first step in that configuration is "VHF AM A, Simplex." The second step is to change "VHF AM B," delete "Duplex," and make that "Off."

a15_1203101csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1203101csm.text: Hey, Jim, you can probably tell me if I've got any rear steering.

a15_1203101csm.speaker: Irwin
a15_1203101csm.text: Yeah, you have rear steering.

a15_1203101csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1203101csm.text: Okay.

a15_1203101csm.speaker: Allen
a15_1203101csm.text: Do you have...

a15_1203101csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1203101csm.text: But I don't have any front steering.

a15_1203101csm.speaker: Allen
a15_1203101csm.text: ...amps on Batt 2, Dave?

a15_1203101csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1203101csm.text: (Under Joe) Joe, you sure about that battery bit? (Answering Joe) Negative. But I don't have any front steering, Joe.

a15_1203101csm.speaker: Irwin
a15_1203101csm.text: Got just rear steering, Dave.

a15_1203101csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1203101csm.text: Yeah. (Long Pause) [Dave crosses the field-of-view from right to left, more or less in a direction perpendicular to the line-of-sight. He moves a Rover length in 3.75 seconds. That distance is 122 inches and the implied speed is 3.0 kilometers per hour. During the traverses, his top speed on reasonably level ground will be about 12 km/hr.] Video Clip 2 min 55 sec ( 0.7 Mb RealVideo or 26 Mb MPG )

a15_1203101csm.speaker: Worden
a15_1203101csm.text: Okay. Understand you want Simplex A in, B - and B, Off.

a15_1203101csm.speaker: Henize
a15_1203101csm.text: That's correct, and at 149 hours and 37 minutes, we do the same thing. [Pause.]

a15_1203101csm.speaker: Allen
a15_1203101csm.text: And, Dave, while you're rolling there, requesting Forward Steering to Bus C, Bus Charlie.

a15_1203101csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1203101csm.text: Okay. Steering, Forward, to Bus Charlie. (Pause) Still no forward steering, Joe.

a15_1203101csm.speaker: Worden
a15_1203101csm.text: Okay, gotcha.

a15_1203101csm.speaker: Henize
a15_1203101csm.text: And at 149:37, we also want to add "mode Vox." [Pause.]

a15a1203940.speaker: Allen
a15a1203940.text: And, Dave and Jim, you're both off the TV camera now. We're standing by for description of your progress.

a15a1203940.speaker: Scott
a15a1203940.text: We'll be back on occasionally as we get to the MESA. Back with you now?

a15a1203940.speaker: Allen
a15a1203940.text: Don't worry about it, Dave. We see you starting to come into view now.

a15a1203940.speaker: Scott
a15a1203940.text: Here. I tell you what I'm going to do, Joe. (Pause) I'm going to move the TV camera because it'll save us time if we don't have to tell you what we're doing. [Dave comes toward the TV camera. By now, he is using a skipping stride that was used by many of the astronauts. He has his right foot forward as he floats between steps. He lands first with his trailing left and pushes off, and then lands with his right and pushes off with the main power step to generate the next glide. It is an efficient stride that allows him to float in between steps. It is relatively difficult to do on Earth. Others

a15a1203940.speaker: Allen
a15a1203940.text: Okay, fine. Don't...Never...(Pause as Dave goes to the re-aim the TV at the Rover) Roger, Dave. Perfect. (Long Pause)

a15a1203940.speaker: Irwin
a15a1203940.text: I have the 16 millimeter on the Rover.

a15a1203940.speaker: Allen
a15a1203940.text: Roger. [Details of equipment stowage on the Rover are available in the Stowae Document ] [Dave goes to the MESA. Jim is at the Rover, which is pointing in toward the LM. The Swann Range is in the background, with Mt. Hadley at the left edge of the picture.] [Scott - "At this point in the program, I don't think anybody had ever seen a mountain, had they? 14 didn't have a mountain, did they?"] [Jones - "14 had a hill (Cone Ridge), but it was up under the Sun so you couldn't see much of it. It wasn't much of a hill."] [Scott - "For the geologists in the Backroom, this would have been pretty inter

a15a1203940.speaker: Irwin
a15a1203940.text: This is really tricky working on this slope in this soft material.

a15a1203940.speaker: Scott
a15a1203940.text: Sure is.

a15a1203940.speaker: Allen
a15a1203940.text: We copy, Dave and Jim, and we're standing by for an EMU (Extravehicular Mobility Unit, meaning the suit and backpack and related gear) status check when convenient.

a15a1203940.speaker: Irwin
a15a1203940.text: (To Dave) Let me know when you're finished...(Stops to listen to Joe) Okay, I'm reading 3.8 (psi) on my gauge. Flags are clear, and I'm reading 75 percent (oxygen remaining).

a15a1203940.speaker: Allen
a15a1203940.text: Roger.

a15a1203940.speaker: Scott
a15a1203940.text: Okay, I'm reading 3.85 (psi), flags are clear, and I'm reading 75 percent. (Long Pause) [A request for an EMU check is sometimes a veiled suggestion from Houston that they slow down. Here, Dave's heart rate is only about 100 beats per minute while Jim's is over 130. Jim has had a heart rate in that range since the start of the EVA at about 119:55.] [Dave turns to his right and faces southeast, apparently so that he can get some light on his checklist so he can read it. He then faces the front of the Rover again.] Video Clip 2 min 38 sec ( 0.7 Mb RealVideo or 24 Mb MPG )

a15a1203940.speaker: Irwin
a15a1203940.text: Trying to...Like walk up out of a crater each time. Uh! Boy!

a15a1203940.speaker: Scott
a15a1203940.text: Can you make it?

a15a1203940.speaker: Irwin
a15a1203940.text: Yeah, I'll make it. I don't know how it's going to work when I get that geology pallet. Might need a little help there.

a15a1203940.speaker: Scott
a15a1203940.text: Give a call (if you need help). [The LCRU is just above knee height on the front of the Rover, and, as Dave leans to his right, he starts to lose his balance and hops sideways on his right foot, trying to keep from falling, and finally gets his right hand on the left-front Rover wheel. Figure 4-1 from the Rover Handbook shows the relative positions and attachment points for the LCRU, the Television Control Unit (TCU), the TV camera, and the high-gain antenna.]

a15a1203940.speaker: Irwin
a15a1203940.text: Okay, I have a flag...(correcting himself) I have a tone, rather. [This warning tone is a signal of a possible problem with Jim's PLSS.]

a15a1203940.speaker: Scott
a15a1203940.text: I got one (meaning that he, too, heard a tone). I guess I heard yours.

a15a1203940.speaker: Allen
a15a1203940.text: (Sounding a little concerned) Roger.

a15a1203940.speaker: Scott
a15a1203940.text: Got any flags, Jim? [Another indication of a problem would be the appearance of a warning flag in one of the small windows on the top in Jim's chest-mounted Remote Control Unit ( RCU ). The windows are small and, unless the lighting is just right, the flags are difficult to see.] [In a 1996 draft review, Dave commented that "The flags were hard to see because the shadows on the Moon are 'deeper'. In daylight, the flags were fine on Earth, even in shadows."] [The reason for this, of course, is that dust and other particles in the Earth's atmosphere scatter a considerable amount of light and, co

a15a1203940.speaker: Irwin
a15a1203940.text: I can't quite see it. No, I don't have any flags.

a15a1203940.speaker: Allen
a15a1203940.text: We concur, Jim. No flags. (Pause)

a15a1203940.speaker: Irwin
a15a1203940.text: Are you finished at the MESA for a little bit, Dave?

a15a1203940.speaker: Scott
a15a1203940.text: Oh, no. (Finishing with the LCRU) This...

a15a1203940.speaker: Irwin
a15a1203940.text: Okay, I'm going to...

a15a1203940.speaker: Scott
a15a1203940.text: ...beauty (pause) beauty is really tight. (Pause) [Dave heads to the MESA to get the TCU. He pulls up quite hard on the TCU, failing to dislodge it and, in the process, jerks the entire MESA up by a few inches.]

a15a1203940.speaker: Allen
a15a1203940.text: And, Dave, this is Houston. Be advised Jim's got a flap hanging from the lower right-hand corner of his PLSS which perhaps you could button up the next time you're close to him. [Dave moves a few steps to his left so he can get a good look at Jim's PLSS.]

a15a1203940.speaker: Scott
a15a1203940.text: Yeah, okay. It's his water flap.

a15a1203940.speaker: Irwin
a15a1203940.text: Yeah, I can see that in the shadow. [Jones - "Was the flap part of the thermal-and-dust cover on the PLSS?"] [Irwin - "Yes; but it also protected it (meaning the innards of the PLSS) from manipulation or movement - if you bumped up against something."] 120:44:01 Scott: (Back at the MESA) Yeah, we're going to have to do some cleaning of him and get that dirt off so we don't have thermal problems. (Pause) [The suits absorb more sunlight as they get dirty and force the cooling system to work harder. Jim is particularly dirty because of his fall. However, the 16 and 17 crews got plenty dirty but d

a15a1203940.speaker: Scott
a15a1203940.text: Take this (entire TCU pallet) out. (Pause) [Scott, from the 1971 Technical Debrief - "The TCU was stuck in its mount in the MESA and I had to take the pallet out and then take the TCU off the pallet. But, once I got the pallet out, it was no problem to remove it."]

a15a1203940.speaker: Irwin
a15a1203940.text: Okay, I've got a tone again. I guess it's...I'm just...(Pause)

a15a1203940.speaker: Scott
a15a1203940.text: What, Jim?

a15a1203940.speaker: Irwin
a15a1203940.text: Flags are clear. (Pause)

a15a1203940.speaker: Scott
a15a1203940.text: (Taking the TCU off the pallet with his left hand, without much difficulty) This TCU was wedged in very tightly. [Dave will mount the Television Control Unit on the right front of the Rover and then will install the TV camera on top of it.]

a15a1203940.speaker: Allen
a15a1203940.text: Jim, all our numbers on you look good down here. Video Clip 3 min 04 sec ( 0.8 Mb RealVideo or 27 Mb MPG )

a15_1204444csm.speaker: Henize
a15_1204444csm.text: Incidentally, Al, we'd like to have the Gamma-ray Gin - Gain Step go through its usual procedures here, even though we don't have the boom extended.

a15_1204444csm.speaker: Irwin
a15_1204444csm.text: Okay. I keep getting a tone. (Long Pause) [Dave tosses a small object - perhaps a piece of packing material or a dust cap - off screen to the right. The throw appears to be made underhanded, mostly with motion of his left forearm and perhaps a little wrist action.] [Jones - "This shows how flat the trajectories are, how different they are from what we're used to."] [Scott - "Really, yeah. That's a good picture. I'd never seen that before."] [Right after Dave's throw, Jim comes into view carrying the geopallet, which he takes to the back of the Rover. He was supposed to have loaded the EVA-1 pa

a15_1205352csm.speaker: Henize
a15_1205352csm.text: Al, we'd like to have the Gamma-ray Gain Step back to the center position, please. [Long pause.]

a15_1205352csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1205352csm.text: Okay, Joe, I'm going to put the TV on the Rover now, if you're ready. And so far the LCRU is on, locked, cable's connected; the high-gain antenna bootie (that is, the dust cover on the connector) is on. I'll get the antenna (aimed at Earth) as soon as we get the TV on.

a15_1205352csm.speaker: Allen
a15_1205352csm.text: Roger, Dave. Have at it. (Long Pause) [Dave heads past the MESA toward the TV. He starts with three kangaroo hops, switches to the loping, foot-to-foot stride, and finishes with the skipping motion.]

a15a1205747.speaker: Scott
a15a1205747.text: There goes the old TV (on the TCU). Trouble getting it to fit today. (Long Pause) And the TV handle is stowed in the side so you get your thermal. (Pause) [By stowing the handle, Dave is reducing the surface area of the camera and, thereby, the amount of sunlight it will absorb and transmit by conduction to the TCU and other temperature sensitive equipment such as the Rover batteries.]

a15_1205803csm.speaker: Henize
a15_1205803csm.text: Endeavour, this is Houston. Surface activities are coming along swimmingly at the present time. The - the rover has already been driven - made one circle around the LM so far, and they're about ready to take off on traverse number 1.

a15_1205803csm.speaker: Irwin
a15_1205803csm.text: And I'm configuring the geopallet now, Joe, (as per the steps at 0+56 on LMP-6).

a15_1205803csm.speaker: Allen
a15_1205803csm.text: Okay, Jim. (Long Pause) [Pre-flight photo KSC-71-P222 shows Jim (second from the left), Dave, and Bob Parker examining geopallet and related gear at the back of the flight Rover.]

a15_1205803csm.speaker: Worden
a15_1205803csm.text: Oh, very good. Got the rover going, huh?

a15_1205803csm.speaker: Henize
a15_1205803csm.text: That's good news. And a time reminder here. Over at 21:03 is the time to configure the DSE, as you go around the corner.

a15_1205803csm.speaker: Allen
a15_1205803csm.text: Rog. 120:58:47 Scott: Okay, LCRU 's circuit breaker is closed. And the LCRU Power is going to Internal. CTV Power switch to On. (LCRU) whip antenna coming up. Okay; LCRU is going PM1/Narrow Band.

a15_1210447csm.speaker: Henize
a15_1210447csm.text: Al, this is Houston. As spacecraft Endeavour swings majestically around the eastern limb of the Moon, all systems are Go.

a15_1210447csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1210447csm.text: Okay, we are in TV Remote; high gain is looking right at that very pretty, blue ball up there - at least half of a blue ball (being sunlit). I did turn the CTV, On, I will...It's a spring-loaded switch; I'll do it again.

a15_1210447csm.speaker: Worden
a15_1210447csm.text: Hey, I'm suppose to say that.

a15_1210447csm.speaker: Worden
a15_1210447csm.text: See you on the other side, Karl.

a15_1210447csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1210447csm.text: And, it's spring loaded to neutral. It moves! I think. Maybe that's just Jim wiggling the rear end.

a15a1211227.speaker: Scott
a15a1211227.text: Good. Hey, Jim, before you go back (in the cabin), get the dustbrush out...

a15a1211227.speaker: Irwin
a15a1211227.text: Yeah.

a15a1211227.speaker: Scott
a15a1211227.text: ...and, I want to get you dusted off.

a15a1211227.speaker: Irwin
a15a1211227.text: Yeah, I don't want to take all that dirt into the LM. (Pause)

a15a1211227.speaker: Scott
a15a1211227.text: Boy, is it dirty. (Long Pause) [In a moment, Jim will climb up to the cabin to change some switch settings and stow the contingency sample.] [ Fendell pans to the left but then reverses direction and we get a brief view of Jim holding the dustbrush. It is about six inches across and an inch or so wide, rather like a large house-painting brush.]

a15a1211227.speaker: Irwin
a15a1211227.text: Where are you on your timeline, Dave?

a15a1211227.speaker: Scott
a15a1211227.text: Anytime you want to ingress, I'm ready for you.

a15a1211227.speaker: Irwin
a15a1211227.text: Okay, you brush me off; I'll go in.

a15a1211227.speaker: Scott
a15a1211227.text: Okay. (Long Pause) [Scott, from the 1971 Technical Debrief - "I would like to say that we had divided the tasks up - and had spent time cross-training - because there just wasn't the time available. We each had our particular thing to do on the Rover. I guess one man could have done it all with coaching from the other, but we had divided the tasks, and the timeline worked out well. I thought we were both finished almost right on the money together, didn't you?"] [Irwin, from the 1971 Technical Debrief - "It did, and we kind of swapped some of the tasks there during the early part of EVA-1 beca

a15a1211227.speaker: Scott
a15a1211227.text: (You) really are dirty.

a15a1211227.speaker: Irwin
a15a1211227.text: I want you to get my antenna, too, before I go in. (Pause) [Dave will stow Jim's PLSS/OPS antenna so that there is no chance of breaking it off while he's crawling through the narrow hatch opening.]

a15a1211227.speaker: Irwin
a15a1211227.text: My harness is still secure, isn't it?

a15a1211227.speaker: Scott
a15a1211227.text: Yeah, harness is fine, except for the dirt.

a15a1211227.speaker: Allen
a15a1211227.text: And, Dave, this might be a good time to button up the corner of Jim's PLSS there.

a15a1211227.speaker: Scott
a15a1211227.text: It's all buttoned; I got that a little while ago, Joe, (at 120:46:11 ).

a15a1211227.speaker: Allen
a15a1211227.text: Roger. Sorry, I missed it. And, for your thinking, we're down about 25 minutes, but no problem.

a15a1211227.speaker: Scott
a15a1211227.text: Okay; I guess we expected that.

a15a1211227.speaker: Allen
a15a1211227.text: Roger. [Dave and Jim are now in view but, because of the contrast between the lighted and shadowed portions of their suits, it is difficult to see exactly what Dave is doing as he examines and then, during his next transmission, readjusts the tool harness on the right side of Jim's PLSS.]

a15a1211227.speaker: Scott
a15a1211227.text: Hold the brush a minute and stand there. (Pause) It (Jim's tool harness) did come off. Okay; give me the brush. Try and get as much (dust off) as we can. (Pause) It'll help if you kick your feet when you go in, because a lot of the stuff will come off.

a15a1211227.speaker: Irwin
a15a1211227.text: Yeah. [This lesson was first learned on Apollo 11. Stomping your feet on the ladder doesn't get all the dirt off, but it helps a great deal.]

a15a1211227.speaker: Scott
a15a1211227.text: Can you bend over a tad? (Pause)

a15a1211227.speaker: Irwin
a15a1211227.text: How's that?

a15a1211227.speaker: Scott
a15a1211227.text: Yeah, that's good. Okay; I think I got the major portion of it, Jim. [Fendell has continued his pan and we are now looking at the north LM strut.]

a15a1211227.speaker: Irwin
a15a1211227.text: Okay, you want to stow my antenna?

a15a1211227.speaker: Scott
a15a1211227.text: Yeah...Oh, let me get your front here. (Pause) Okay. (Pause) Boy, working on this slope is another game, isn't it? (Long Pause as Dave stows Jim's OPS antenna)

a15a1211227.speaker: Scott
a15a1211227.text: Okay. It's stowed. [Fendell has reversed direction and is panning clockwise past the MESA. We get a quick look at Dave as he finishes stowing Jim's antenna, reaching up about as far as possible in the suit. Note the Velcro strips on the back of Dave's PLSS.]

a15a1211227.speaker: Irwin
a15a1211227.text: Okay, you'll stow the brush while I get in? [As can be seen on page 9 in the Apollo 15 LRV Stowage document , the large dustbush is stowed in a pouch on the aft-facing surface of the geopallet.]

a15a1211227.speaker: Scott
a15a1211227.text: Yeah, I'll get the brush.

a15a1211227.speaker: Irwin
a15a1211227.text: Okay.

a15a1211227.speaker: Scott
a15a1211227.text: Be careful.

a15a1211227.speaker: Irwin
a15a1211227.text: Yeah. [Fendell pans to the left just in time to miss Jim's jump up on to the ladder.]

a15a1211227.speaker: Allen
a15a1211227.text: And, Dave, this is Houston. While you're stowing the brush there, just thinking ahead; we've got a couple of checks to carry out on the Rover before you drive off from this site.

a15a1211227.speaker: Scott
a15a1211227.text: Yeah, that's good, Joe. Go ahead.
