a15a1254905.text: I'll do it.

a15a1254905.speaker: Irwin
a15a1254905.text: Okay, Dave; I'm ready to clean you.

a15a1254905.speaker: Allen
a15a1254905.text: Dave, I guess we don't have anything else for you right now. It's been a(n) outstanding EVA here; why don't you go ahead and get in at your leisure. Might want to pick up that glass rock (the Aggie) on your way in.

a15a1254905.speaker: Scott
a15a1254905.text: Okay. Hey, Jim, can you see me out the window? (Pause) Hey, Jim?

a15a1254905.speaker: Irwin
a15a1254905.text: Yeah, I'm looking for you. You weren't in the left window; are you in the right window?

a15a1254905.speaker: Scott
a15a1254905.text: Yeah. Talk me through the solar wind; let's get it up, they really need lots of data; we can give them lots of data. [If the SWC deployment had been deferred to early in EVA-2, it wouldn't have been done before about 142:33:52 . By deploying the experiment now, Dave is giving the experimenters an extra 16 hours of valuable exposure time.]

a15_1255118csm.speaker: Henize
a15_1255118csm.text: 15, this is Houston. We'd like to have you go Wide Beam on the High Gain Antenna, and then to Narrow. [Pause.]

a15_1255118csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1255118csm.text: Oh, okay. (Pause) You think that's possible? Use the brush. [They are now on LMP-30 and CDR-29 .]

a15_1255118csm.speaker: Worden
a15_1255118csm.text: Okay, Houston. This is Endeavour. Going Wide Beam, going back to Narrow.

a15_1255118csm.speaker: Allen
a15_1255118csm.text: Jim, while you're brushing there, did you get the seal made on the SRC?

a15_1255118csm.speaker: Henize
a15_1255118csm.text: Roger. [Long pause.]

a15_1255118csm.speaker: Irwin
a15_1255118csm.text: Yes, I did, Joe.

a15_1255118csm.speaker: Allen
a15_1255118csm.text: Good show.

a15_1255118csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1255118csm.text: Okay, Joe, there's quite a bit of dust on the mirror on the LCRU . As a matter of fact, there's quite a bit of dust all over the Rover. It's a very fine kind of dust. Do you want us to, maybe, brush that off? (Pause)

a15_1255118csm.speaker: Henize
a15_1255118csm.text: That's sounding better, Al. How are things going up there?

a15_1255118csm.speaker: Worden
a15_1255118csm.text: Ah, going okay, Karl. Looks like I've caught up a little bit. Got all the dumps out of the way, and got the libration photography. Looks like I'm going to be handicapped a little bit because of the mission timer, but we'll press on.

a15_1255118csm.speaker: Allen
a15_1255118csm.text: Dave, maybe a token effort, but don't take too long; it doesn't sound too serious to us.

a15_1255118csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1255118csm.text: Okay. (Pause) (To Jim) Okay, that's...Whoa! Right there. (Pause) If we can get it off out here, the less we're going to have to put up with in there (in the LM cabin). (Pause) (Laughing) That's really dirty stuff. (Pause)

a15_1255118csm.speaker: Henize
a15_1255118csm.text: All right. Our understanding on the mission timer is, that even though you tried to reset it, it still refused to count up. Is that correct?

a15_1255118csm.speaker: Worden
a15_1255118csm.text: That's correct. And I thought what I'd do now is reset to zero and start.

a15_1255118csm.speaker: Henize
a15_1255118csm.text: Roger. And for future reference, we'd like...

a15_1255118csm.speaker: Worden
a15_1255118csm.text: It counts from zero, Karl. I...

a15_1255118csm.speaker: Henize
a15_1255118csm.text: Roger - you say it is counting, but it had - it had - to start from zero to start counting again?

a15_1255118csm.speaker: Irwin
a15_1255118csm.text: Well, you dirty yourself (lost under Joe)

a15_1255118csm.speaker: Allen
a15_1255118csm.text: Okay, Dave. Go back to whatever cooling you want.

a15_1255118csm.speaker: Worden
a15_1255118csm.text: Yeah. Well, let me pick a random number and see if it'll count from there. I just tried to set it to the correct times... [Long pause.]

a15_1255118csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1255118csm.text: Okay, stand by. (Pause) Okay.

a15_1255118csm.speaker: Irwin
a15_1255118csm.text: (Shall I) put that brush away?

a15_1255118csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1255118csm.text: Huh?

a15_1255118csm.speaker: Irwin
a15_1255118csm.text: I'll put it away.

a15_1255118csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1255118csm.text: I'm going to dust off the mirror, there. Go ahead...Get your (PLSS/OPS) antenna ?

a15_1255118csm.speaker: Irwin
a15_1255118csm.text: Yeah. (Pause)

a15_1255118csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1255118csm.text: What's left of it. (Pause) [During the mission review, Dave and I interpreted this statement to mean that Jim's antenna had broken off by this time. However, I also noted that, before Jim climbed the ladder at 121:15:38 with the contingency sample, we saw Dave stow the antenna. Subsequently, I re-reviewed portions of the ALSEP deployment video tape and noted that the antenna was still intact - or, at least, was still vertical and of normal length - at about 125:16:27 . The mystery remains.]

a15_1255118csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1255118csm.text: Remember when you go in that my ACA...

a15_1255118csm.speaker: Irwin
a15_1255118csm.text: Yep.

a15_1255118csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1255118csm.text: ...controller mount is the thing that you're hanging up on. You sort of have to go easy and get down past that.

a15_1255118csm.speaker: Irwin
a15_1255118csm.text: Okay.

a15_1255118csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1255118csm.text: See you inside.

a15_1255118csm.speaker: Irwin
a15_1255118csm.text: Okay. (Pause) [Scott - "ACA is the Attitude Control Assembly (which is) right above the hatch. My handcontroller is mounted on a block, essentially, which is the electronics unit. So, why didn't we experience that in a simulated environment? Probably because we're in one-sixth g, now, and he doesn't compress. In training, you've got the backpack on, which will push the suit down, which helps you get in. Even in the one-sixth-g airplane, you probably get the residual effects of going up and down from one-sixth g to 2 g's to one-sixth g. So I can imagine that, running this in the airplane, when

a15_1255118csm.speaker: Worden
a15_1255118csm.text: Okay, Houston; Endeavour. Looks like we must have just run across a little funny there, Karl, because it started okay now and is running.

a15_1255118csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1255118csm.text: And back to intermediate (cooling), Joe.

a15_1255118csm.speaker: Allen
a15_1255118csm.text: Roger, Dave. (Long Pause)

a15_1255118csm.speaker: Henize
a15_1255118csm.text: Roger. Do you have a time source, or would you like a hack down here to get it started again, on the right number?

a15_1255118csm.speaker: Worden
a15_1255118csm.text: I used the CMC time.

a15_1255118csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1255118csm.text: You want both LRV battery covers open, is that correct?

a15_1255118csm.speaker: Allen
a15_1255118csm.text: That's affirm. (Pause)

a15_1255118csm.speaker: Henize
a15_1255118csm.text: Roger. [Long pause.]

a15_1255118csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1255118csm.text: Okay. (Long Pause) There's one open. (Long Pause) (Won't) stay open! Hmmm. (Long Pause) There. Oooh, me! They're open. (Pause) [Jones - "Am I right in assuming that this flight Rover had never been exercised."] [Scott - "Other than to check it out and make sure it worked."] [Jones - "So that cover hadn't been opened and closed numerous times like the one on the one-g trainer."] [Scott - "And we're in one-sixth g, so the weight of the cover wouldn't hold it as well."]

a15_1255118csm.speaker: Henize
a15_1255118csm.text: And now for a future reference, we'd like to know whether you found the quick disconnect? [Pause.]

a15_1255118csm.speaker: Worden
a15_1255118csm.text: Negative.

a15_1255118csm.speaker: Henize
a15_1255118csm.text: We copy. [Long pause.]

a15_1255118csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1255118csm.text: How you doing, Jim?

a15_1255118csm.speaker: Irwin
a15_1255118csm.text: Getting it. (Long Pause) I'm in, Dave.

a15_1255118csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1255118csm.text: Good boy. (Pause) [Scott, from the 1971 Technical Debrief - "I guess you had the same problem getting in (at 121:17:52 , when Jim entered the LM to set the comm switches) because of the same reasons. I think once we got everything in and you discovered that the hatch wasn't fully open, why, that made it a lot easier from then on. I guess I didn't have any problems getting back in because, again, you were able to guide me as I came in through the door."]

a15_1255118csm.speaker: Irwin
a15_1255118csm.text: Where are you out there?

a15_1255118csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1255118csm.text: (Garbled) the Rover (tasks at the bottom of CDR-29).

a15_1255118csm.speaker: Irwin
a15_1255118csm.text: (Breathing heavily) Okay, because I've got a pallet here that should come out; I'll put it on the porch.

a15_1255118csm.speaker: Henize
a15_1255118csm.text: Al, they want me to ask you once more about - tell - tell you once more where - where the location was. The waste management bag in A-8, but I think you know that already. Incidentally, it's a rather short thing, 2 or 3 inches long. It's got a thread on one end and a quick - quick disconnect on the other.

a15_1255118csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1255118csm.text: Okay, I can dump it when I get here. [As indicated in Figure 10-3b from the Apollo 15 Mission Report, Jim's heart rate is above 160 beats per minute.]

a15_1255118csm.speaker: Allen
a15_1255118csm.text: Okay, Dave. Jim, take a breather, if you would, please; and, Dave, you're getting (the) LCRU blankets at 35 percent open at the same time, I'm sure.

a15_1255118csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1255118csm.text: Yeah, let me just check on down the checklist, will you, Joe? 125:56:04 Allen: Rog. Rog. No problem. (Long Pause)

a15_1255118csm.speaker: Worden
a15_1255118csm.text: Yeah, Karl, that's exactly what I was looking for. And, problem is, the waste - the small waste management bag is not in A-8 right now. I'm going to have to - have to look around. Maybe Dave or Jim got it out on the way out. I'll look around and see if I can find it.

a15_1255118csm.speaker: Henize
a15_1255118csm.text: Okay, fine.

a15_1255118csm.speaker: Worden
a15_1255118csm.text: I just haven't had - haven't had the free minutes since they came up to do that.

a15_1255118csm.speaker: Henize
a15_1255118csm.text: Right. And there's no reason now to be troubled by it at all. We were just asking that for future reference. Sounds like it's only a matter of it being dis - misplaced somewhere, so let's forget it. [Long pause.]

a15_1255118csm.speaker: Allen
a15_1255118csm.text: Jim, did you carry the SRC up into the LM with you?

a15_1255118csm.speaker: Irwin
a15_1255118csm.text: Yes, I did, Joe.

a15_1255118csm.speaker: Allen
a15_1255118csm.text: Good show.

a15_1255118csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1255118csm.text: Hey, Jim.

a15_1255118csm.speaker: Irwin
a15_1255118csm.text: Yeah.

a15_1255118csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1255118csm.text: I've got something for you. (Pause)

a15a1260008.speaker: Allen
a15a1260008.text: Dave, I guess we don't have anything else for you right now. It's been a(n) outstanding EVA here; why don't you go ahead and get in at your leisure. Might want to pick up that glass rock (the Aggie) on your way in.

a15a1260008.speaker: Scott
a15a1260008.text: Okay. Hey, Jim, can you see me out the window? (Pause) Hey, Jim?

a15a1260008.speaker: Irwin
a15a1260008.text: Yeah, I'm looking for you. You weren't in the left window; are you in the right window?

a15a1260008.speaker: Scott
a15a1260008.text: Yeah. Talk me through the solar wind; let's get it up, they really need lots of data; we can give them lots of data. [If the SWC deployment had been deferred to early in EVA-2, it wouldn't have been done before about 142:33:52 . By deploying the experiment now, Dave is giving the experimenters an extra 16 hours of valuable exposure time.]

a15a1260008.speaker: Irwin
a15a1260008.text: Okay. Just take it out there about 50 feet.

a15a1260008.speaker: Scott
a15a1260008.text: Okay. Right about here, huh?

a15a1260008.speaker: Irwin
a15a1260008.text: Farther, if you want. Yeah. And just pull the tube out to full extension. Careful when you get to the end...

a15a1260008.speaker: Scott
a15a1260008.text: The little thing popped off the end.

a15a1260008.speaker: Irwin
a15a1260008.text: That's okay. Just pull it on out.

a15a1260008.speaker: Scott
a15a1260008.text: Okay.

a15a1260008.speaker: Irwin
a15a1260008.text: And, careful when you rotate the screen that you rotate in the right direction, so it doesn't pop off.

a15a1260008.speaker: Scott
a15a1260008.text: Did the...

a15a1260008.speaker: Irwin
a15a1260008.text: Just extend the tube several sections. Make sure they're in the red, indicating it's locked.

a15a1260008.speaker: Scott
a15a1260008.text: Okay, red, red, red. Red.

a15a1260008.speaker: Irwin
a15a1260008.text: Keep pulling.

a15a1260008.speaker: Scott
a15a1260008.text: Okay.

a15a1260008.speaker: Irwin
a15a1260008.text: And pull that...Yeah, pull that out.

a15a1260008.speaker: Scott
a15a1260008.text: Oh, yeah. Window shade...

a15a1260008.speaker: Irwin
a15a1260008.text: Just be careful you rotate in the right direction so it doesn't drop off.

a15a1260008.speaker: Scott
a15a1260008.text: Want to rotate it against the opening, right?

a15a1260008.speaker: Irwin
a15a1260008.text: Yeah.

a15a1260008.speaker: Scott
a15a1260008.text: Like that. Okay; that's easy enough to do.

a15a1260008.speaker: Irwin
a15a1260008.text: Okay, and then...

a15a1260008.speaker: Scott
a15a1260008.text: Yeah.

a15a1260008.speaker: Irwin
a15a1260008.text: ...grab that there, and...

a15a1260008.speaker: LM Crew
a15a1260008.text: Pull it down.

a15a1260008.speaker: Irwin
a15a1260008.text: And make sure you get the - not the wire, but the bottom of the screen - over the loop.

a15a1260008.speaker: Scott
a15a1260008.text: Okay, I see that. (Long Pause) Okay the bottom of the screen is over the loop. It says "Sun," I guess that means that's...

a15a1260008.speaker: Irwin
a15a1260008.text: Yeah.

a15a1260008.speaker: Scott
a15a1260008.text: ...what you face to the Sun, doesn't it?

a15a1260008.speaker: Irwin
a15a1260008.text: Isn't that a neat experiment?

a15a1260008.speaker: Scott
a15a1260008.text: Yeah, that's the kind of experiment I like.

a15a1260008.speaker: Irwin
a15a1260008.text: Yeah. 126:02:08 Scott: Okay, we're out here at good distance where it won't get any dust on it from the Rover. And I'll turn it into the Sun here; stick it into the ground. It's core tube. (Pause) There. Okay, Joe, solar wind is deployed. (Pause) And I'm going to...

a15a1260008.speaker: Allen
a15a1260008.text: Beautiful!

a15a1260008.speaker: Scott
a15a1260008.text: ...pick up a...

a15a1260008.speaker: Allen
a15a1260008.text: Ingress the Falcon, please.

a15a1260008.speaker: Scott
a15a1260008.text: ...a couple of rocks. (Responding to Joe) Yes, sir. (Long Pause) Oh, my! (Pause) I couldn't resist this one, Jim.

a15_1260305csm.speaker: Henize
a15_1260305csm.text: Endeavour, this is Houston. You can turn Pan Camera Power, Off, now.

a15_1260305csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1260305csm.text: Oh, look at what I got! You wouldn't believe it! (Pause) Okay, pick up the ETB. [This is sample 15015 , a 4.7 kilogram, glass-coated, regolith breccia, the third largest rock collected during the mission. This is the 'black rock' Dave described after the SEVA at 107:33:34 .] [Scott, from the 1971 Technical Debrief - "Through the windows, prior to leaving the LM, we had seen a large black fragment on my side. And you had seen a black frag on your side, as you looked out the front window. These were unique to the local surroundings. I don't think we'd seen other fragments that black and prominen

a15_1260600csm.speaker: Irwin
a15_1260600csm.text: Yeah. (Pause) (Garbled). (Pause) Just a minute; I'm... (Pause) Okay, I'm kind of hung up on you, Dave. Let me move back.

a15_1260600csm.speaker: Henize
a15_1260600csm.text: Endeavour, this is Houston. Go ahead.

a15_1260600csm.speaker: Worden
a15_1260600csm.text: Okay, Karl. Just for your information, I finally dug all the way through A-8 and got a hold of the quick disconnect. And it's - it's as I expected it. But, it was there, and we're squared away now.

a15_1260600csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1260600csm.text: There you are! (Pause) [Dave probably has just gotten to his feet and has turned enough that he sees Jim.]

a15_1260600csm.speaker: Henize
a15_1260600csm.text: Very good. That makes people feel better down here. We did stow it, after all.

a15_1260600csm.speaker: Irwin
a15_1260600csm.text: (Reading checklist page Surface 5-1) Prim(ary) Water, Close.

a15_1260600csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1260600csm.text: Oh, wait a minute. I'm not ready to do anything yet. Let me turn around. (Pause) [They need to turn off the primary feedwater valves on their PLSSs. Dave needs to get his right arm free so that he can reach back.]

a15_1260600csm.speaker: Worden
a15_1260600csm.text: Yeah, well, one of my problems is that I've got the center couch underneath the right-hand couch, and I've also got the L-shaped bag and a few other things stowed on top of A-8. So, it's not quite so easy to get to.

a15_1260600csm.speaker: Allen
a15_1260600csm.text: Loud and clear. Loud and clear.

a15_1260600csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1260600csm.text: Okay. Prime Water, Close, huh? (Pause) If I can find it.

a15_1261230csm.speaker: Henize
a15_1261230csm.text: Al, the boys are in the LM, and they're repressurizing the cabin now.

a15_1261230csm.speaker: Worden
a15_1261230csm.text: Roger, Karl. Sounds like they had a pretty good day.

a15_1261230csm.speaker: Henize
a15_1261230csm.text: Yes, sir. They had a terrific day. I think they're going to sleep well tonight.

a15_1261230csm.speaker: Irwin
a15_1261230csm.text: Suit Fan 2 coming - I didn't read...Where are we, Dave? I can't read you.

a15_1261230csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1261230csm.text: Right here; "CB(16) ECS: Suit Fan number 2, closed."

a15a1261602.speaker: Scott
a15a1261602.text: Okay, put up the old helmet bag. (Pause) [Some of the crews hung the helmet bag over the forward instrument panel and this may be what Dave and Jim are doing.]

a15a1261602.speaker: Irwin
a15a1261602.text: There's a funny smell in here.

a15a1261602.speaker: Scott
a15a1261602.text: Yeah, I think that's a lunar dirt smell. (Pause) Never smelled lunar dirt before, but we got most of it right here with us. [Jones - "How would you describe the smell of lunar dirt?"] [Scott - "Like gunpowder."] [Jones - "That's what most people say."] [Scott - "I hadn't heard that before we went. I don't think."] [Jones - "Here, you don't actually describe it as gunpowder."] [Scott, from a 1996 letter - "I actually whispered it to Jim so that nobody would become alarmed."]

a15a1261602.speaker: Scott
a15a1261602.text: Okay. "Doff helmets with visors, lower shades, stow in helmet bags. Verify safety on the dump valve ."

a15_1261633csm.speaker: Henize
a15_1261633csm.text: Endeavour, this is Houston. You getting a good look at Littrow up there?

a15_1261633csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1261633csm.text: Can you get that? (Pause) [They are talking about getting down to verify that the safety is on the dump valve.]

a15_1261633csm.speaker: Worden
a15_1261633csm.text: Yes, sir. Just went by Littrow. And right over Serenitatis now, coming up on the landing site.

a15_1261633csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1261633csm.text: Okay. Where are we here? Okay, "Descent Water valve, Open". (Pause)

a15_1261633csm.speaker: Henize
a15_1261633csm.text: Very good. Hey, you been looking the Littrow for a couple of days now. Are you forming any opinions whether that dark area is lava flow or ash flow?

a15_1261633csm.speaker: Irwin
a15_1261633csm.text: Descent Water, Open. 126:17:06 Scott: Okay. Now "remove purge valves, stow in the purse." Uh, oh; the purse fell down. [The purse is a bag that normally attached to the front of Panel 5 on the CDR's side of the cabin. Putting the purge valves in the purse keeps them handy at waist height, keeps them clean, and reduces the chances of dropping them.]

a15_1261633csm.speaker: Worden
a15_1261633csm.text: Well, Karl, if I had to give you the opinion right now, I'd say it was all some - some kind of ash. I don't - I'm not sure it's flow. But it certainly is - it looks like a deposit over the entire surface. You can see it - mostly in the upland areas and down in the mare areas and mostly in - in valleys - in depressions, this stuff seems to have collected almost like it was - there was some mass wasting down the hills making the - making the valleys darker in color and maybe a little thicker with that kind of material. But there are - there are still at least three different distinctive colorati

a15_1261633csm.speaker: Irwin
a15_1261633csm.text: I took it down, Dave. I thought that was one of the things that I was hanging up on.

a15_1261633csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1261633csm.text: Yeah; okay. (Pause) Where did you put it, Jim?

a15_1261633csm.speaker: Irwin
a15_1261633csm.text: I put it right behind you. (Pause) 126:17:33 Scott: Whew! (Garbled; Pause) Oh, yeah. Okay. Mag bags all fell out. [These are probably transfer bags for the film magazines, listed in the Stowage list ( ) for transfer from the CM to LM on page 75, for LM Lunar Launch on pages 97-98, and for LM to CM transfer on pages 111 and 112. Dave and Jim apparently stowed them in the purse .] 126:17:50 Irwin: Now that purge valve is really dirty!

a15_1261633csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1261633csm.text: Yeah, I bet it is. (Pause) Okay; I'll show you what you were hanging up on. Thing right here.

a15_1261633csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1261633csm.text: I'll show you later. (Pause) [Irwin, from the 1971 Technical Debrief - "I'm trying to think of when we noticed the break in the bacteria filter."] [Scott, from the 1971 Technical Debrief - "I think it was right after we got our helmets and our gloves off. I think you looked down and saw it. The water was in and out of there, the hose right at the connection where the bacteria filter joins the water hose. The bacteria filter has some plastic attachments to it. There were two little nicks about, probably, a quarter of an inch long and about a quarter of an inch wide out of the side of the plasti

a15_1261633csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1261633csm.text: Okay; purge is up. (Correcting himself) Purse .

a15_1261633csm.speaker: Irwin
a15_1261633csm.text: Mine is up. [Jim may mean that he has removed his purge valve.]

a15_1261633csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1261633csm.text: Yeah. I guess what we ought to do is not get this clean stuff dirty. (Pause) They really ought to have another neat bag for the dirty stuff.

a15_1261633csm.speaker: Henize
a15_1261633csm.text: Okay. I guess we better let you go back to work on Hadley, which is coming up any minute now.

a15_1262304csm.speaker: Worden
a15_1262304csm.text: Okay, Karl. I'm over the Hadley area now. I've gone by it. And nothing more to report on the Hadley, except one observation that I meant to make on the last pass and didn't. I'll make it now. That is that the landmark, 15 dash 40, is readily visible, even with the naked eye. You don't need a sextant to see it.

a15_1262304csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1262304csm.text: Yeah. Let's cool off. Got a ways to go. (Pause) Oh, that's okay; let her run. (Pause) Okay, "PLSS mode, both, to O. Audio circuit breaker open and connect to LM comm." (Long Pause)

a15_1262304csm.speaker: Henize
a15_1262304csm.text: Does that secondary crater complex stand out in any special way that gives you some idea as to its origin?

a15_1262304csm.speaker: Worden
a15_1262304csm.text: Well, I didn't look at it from that standpoint when I was going over it before, but - I guess I'll have to take a special look at that to answer your question.

a15_1263405csm.speaker: Henize
a15_1263405csm.text: Hey, Al, how's that sunset look down below you?

a15_1263405csm.speaker: Worden
a15_1263405csm.text: Well, I can't see it from here Karl.

a15_1263405csm.speaker: Henize
a15_1263405csm.text: Any - any chance - you got light - in the Aristarchus area yet? Seeing anything down there?

a15_1263405csm.speaker: Henize
a15_1263405csm.text: That's a very interesting observation. You still see some of it out there now, do you?

a15_1263405csm.speaker: Worden
a15_1263405csm.text: Yeah, that's affirmative. I do, and - Now, I dimmed the lights down; and I have a pretty nice view of the Moon in Earthshine.

a15_1263405csm.speaker: Henize
a15_1263405csm.text: Ah, hah. Any chance you see Aristarchus? Are you, - maybe you're not looking that way, I guess. Are you looking down on Aristarchus by any chance?

a15_1263405csm.speaker: Worden
a15_1263405csm.text: Well, just a second, and I'll turn the lights down and let you know.

a15_1263405csm.speaker: Henize
a15_1263405csm.text: Good. That's Schröter's Valley, you know, and was once known to glow red.

a15_1263753csm.speaker: Worden
a15_1263753csm.text: Rog, Karl. I've been sitting here looking at Aristarchus, and I finally had to check the map to make sure; because it's - it's so bright in Earthshine, it's almost as bright, it seems like, as it is in sunshine. Very, very bright crater. It looks very much like Copernicus at night.

a15_1263753csm.speaker: Henize
a15_1263753csm.text: I'll be darned. Sounds real interesting.

a15_1263753csm.speaker: Worden
a15_1263753csm.text: Yeah. And I can quite clearly trace out Schröter's Valley going off toward the northwest. I can't see it. It's a little bit out of range; it's north of [my] track, and so it's somewhat out of range for me to see.

a15_1263753csm.speaker: Henize
a15_1263753csm.text: Very good. Hey. Spence [Spencer Gardner] is asking me to remind you about the film magazine update if you have any time yet this rev.

a15_1263753csm.speaker: Worden
a15_1263753csm.text: Okay. I'm going to have to go back through the Flight Plan and get the numbers out. But I will do that.

a15_1263753csm.speaker: Henize
a15_1263753csm.text: Okay. I'm not sure we want you to do that at the expense of anything else here, like to P52. Hang on.

a15_1263753csm.speaker: Worden
a15_1263753csm.text: So, I'll go ahead and do the P52, Karl.

a15_1263753csm.speaker: Henize
a15_1263753csm.text: Right. We'd rather have you do the P52 if there is any either/or there.

a15_1264232csm.speaker: Henize
a15_1264232csm.text: We've got your torquing angles, Al.

a15a1264238.speaker: Worden
a15a1264238.text: Okay, Karl. Get them [torqued] out in a minute.

a15a1264238.speaker: Allen
a15a1264238.text: Hello, Hadley Base; this is Houston.

a15a1264238.speaker: Scott
a15a1264238.text: Rog. How is everything down there?

a15a1264238.speaker: Allen
a15a1264238.text: Dave, the dust may have settled up there; I'm not sure if it's settled down here. We've got more data than we know what to do with at the moment. What can we help you with?

a15a1264238.speaker: Scott
a15a1264238.text: Oh, just wanted to tell you, we've got two PLSSs charged with O2: one at 95 (percent oxygen) and one at 93.

a15a1264238.speaker: Allen
a15a1264238.text: Roger. We copy that. [Deke Slayton joins the conversation. Slayton was a Mercury Astronaut who became head of Flight Crew Operations and was responsible for crew selection.]

a15a1264238.speaker: Slayton
a15a1264238.text: Real fine day's work up there, guys. Why don't you take the rest of the day off?

a15a1264238.speaker: Allen
a15a1264238.text: Dave, on that PLSS reading, could you tell us which number belongs to which PLSS, please?

a15a1264238.speaker: Scott
a15a1264238.text: We should have done that. Jim's got a 95, and I've got a 93.

a15a1264238.speaker: Scott
a15a1264238.text: Give us about 30 minutes to get a bite to eat, and we'll press on for the next one. Then we won't have to doff the PLSSs.

a15a1264238.speaker: Allen
a15a1264238.text: Dave, Deke says okay, but I'm not sure if the question was understood.

a15a1264238.speaker: Slayton
a15a1264238.text: I thought you added one more word there, like "eat and rest".

a15a1264238.speaker: Scott
a15a1264238.text: Roger. [Scott - "This was just banter. 'Hey, we've got the PLSSs charged, give us 30 minutes to get something to eat, and we'll press on and do the next EVA!' And that's why Slayton comes in and adds, 'Eat and Rest'. It's all light-hearted stuff. But he does want us to rest!"] [Very Long Comm Break] [During this Comm Break, they remove the PLSSs, disconnect the OPSs, and, as per checklist page 5-3, replace the PLSS batteries and LiOH canisters.] [Scott - "It was hard work to suit and unsuit ! There was no room in there."] [Jones - "But it was also true, was it not, that you could not have func

a15_1264506csm.speaker: Henize
a15_1264506csm.text: Hey, Al. You've got a couple of people interested down here in particle clouds now. And, first of all, we'd like to have you verify that you saw particles all the way until you went into the shadow. I certainly believe you did. You were telling me about them just as you were in that position. And likewise, if you have a chance at sunrise tomorrow where you are in that same position, with the Sun illuminating you, but not the background, could you see if you - there is any remaining signs of those particles?

a15_1264506csm.speaker: Worden
a15_1264506csm.text: Okay, be glad to. Now, as far as how long I saw them; I saw them as long as the spacecraft was still in sunlight. However, I was beyond the terminator - surface terminator. And, - right now, looking out the window I don't see any of them.

a15_1264506csm.speaker: Henize
a15_1264506csm.text: Okay, fair enough. And I got some words for you on that bad attitude that we had on the oblique mapping camera photography this morning. If...

a15_1264506csm.speaker: Henize
a15_1264506csm.text: Evidently, we - sent you up the right attitude angles, but somehow or other we had a - slightly erroneous omicron. And, the actual photograph - I think we were something like 10 or 15 degrees off attitude - were perfectly good. No problem there. But, we have gone through the Flight Plan and made sure in the future that we will have the proper omicron and everything will be right on the nose.

a15_1264506csm.speaker: Henize
a15_1264506csm.text: Just in case you was wondering what in the heck went wrong that time. [Changing subject.] And, I have a TEI-37 any time you have time to copy it.

a15_1264506csm.speaker: Worden
a15_1264506csm.text: Okay, Karl. Go ahead with the TEI-37.

a15_1264506csm.speaker: Worden
a15_1264506csm.text: Go ahead with your TEI-37 PAD.

a15_1264506csm.speaker: Henize
a15_1264506csm.text: Roger. TEI-37, SPS/G&N; 37350; plus 0.60, plus 1.01; 151:00:17.43; plus 2979.1, minus 0745.2, minus 0243.3; 180, 109, 349; the rest is NA. Ullage, 2 jets for 17 seconds - 17 seconds - and the longitude at T IG is minus 179.52. That's all.

a15_1265302csm.speaker: Henize
a15_1265302csm.text: Al, how's your exercise machine going up there. Getting - getting all you need for the - for the big day in the future.

a15_1265302csm.speaker: Worden
a15_1265302csm.text: Right now I'm trying to figure out your film usage.

a15_1265302csm.speaker: Worden
a15_1265302csm.text: But yes, the exerciser is working fine. The rope's getting a little frayed right now.

a15_1265302csm.speaker: Henize
a15_1265302csm.text: You're really putting in all your hours on it, are you? Glad to hear that.

a15_1265302csm.speaker: Worden
a15_1265302csm.text: You might also be interested to know that, at least up to this point, we've eaten every morsel of food that was allotted for us at that time.

a15_1265302csm.speaker: Henize
a15_1265302csm.text: Sounds like you're really living it up, up there. Chuck Berry says he's delighted.

a15_1265516csm.speaker: Worden
a15_1265516csm.text: Okay, [I've] got a quick rundown on the film for you. The DAC magazine, Hotel, is - has 65 percent left; and for the Hasselblad, mag Metro is - I've used 155 frames, November: used 56 frames; Romeo's used 40 frames; Sugar used 80 frames, and Nikon, I've used 16 frames. And let me reverse the first one just to make it consistent. I've used 35 percent out of magazine Hotel for the 16 millimeter. That makes it all consistent.

a15_1265516csm.speaker: Henize
a15_1265516csm.text: Very good, Al. That came through loud and clear. [Long pause.]

a15_1274744csm.speaker: Henize
a15_1274744csm.text: Endeavour. We'd like to have narrow beam, please. [Pause.]

a15_1274744csm.speaker: Henize
a15_1274744csm.text: And what's new on the west limb of the Moon?

a15_1274744csm.speaker: Worden
a15_1274744csm.text: Well, I must confess, I wasn't watching. I was eating.

a15_1274744csm.speaker: Henize
a15_1274744csm.text: Enjoy it. Looks like, looking at the Flight Plan, looks like you finally had a restful sort of eat period.

a15_1274744csm.speaker: Worden
a15_1274744csm.text: That's true, and it certainly was good. Incidentally, I did look for the - the particle cloud that was around me at sunrise, and it looked like it had diminished somewhat from the sunrise - or from the sunset terminator. But it may have been - it may have been the angle of the sunlight also.

a15_1274744csm.speaker: Henize
a15_1274744csm.text: But you definitely did see some particles yet?

a15_1274744csm.speaker: Henize
a15_1274744csm.text: Fewer particles, but still - still some were there, were they?

a15_1274744csm.speaker: Henize
a15_1274744csm.text: And how do you enjoy that coquina soup?

a15_1274744csm.speaker: Allen
a15_1274744csm.text: Falcon, you can go Power Amp(lifier), Off; Low bit rate.

a15_1274744csm.speaker: Worden
a15_1274744csm.text: Almost as good as the parsley soup.

a15_1275752csm.speaker: Henize
a15_1275752csm.text: Okay, If you'll give us Accept, we'd like to up - update your state vector.

a15_1275752csm.speaker: Henize
a15_1275752csm.text: Roger. And we've got a comm check coming up with the LM and the - the time - the earliest time at which you've got a contact with them is 128:14:14.

a15_1275752csm.speaker: Henize
a15_1275752csm.text: Roger. And Bob [Parker] is onboard now. So I'll be signing off and seeing you in the morning.

a15_1275752csm.speaker: Worden
a15_1275752csm.text: Okay, Karl. Go home and have a nice dinner and I'll talk to you in the morning.

a15_1280337csm.text: Roger; copy, Al. That sounds like a pretty complete description.

a15_1280337csm.speaker: Worden

a15_1280712csm.speaker: Worden
a15_1280712csm.text: And, in addition to that, I didn't see - I didn't see a great deal of difference in the - in the terrain or in the structure of the terrain across the excluded zone.

a15_1281237csm.text: Go ahead.

I see the whole area around Littrow, particularly - particularly in the area of Littrow where we've noticed the darker deposits, there are a whole series of small, almost irregular shaped cones, and they have a very distinct dark mantling just around those cones. It looks like a whole field of small cinder cones down there. And they look - well, I say - I say cinder cones, because they're somewhat irregular in shape. They're not all - they're not all round - they're positive features - and they have a very dark halo, wh

a15_1281237csm.text: Beautiful, Al. [Long pause.]

a15_1281656.text: And save us some food!

a15_1281656.speaker: Worden
a15_1281656.text: Save you some food?

a15_1281656.speaker: Irwin
a15_1281656.text: Yeah.

a15_1281656.speaker: Irwin
a15_1281656.text: Yeah. [Worden has hot-water to use in preparing his meals, a luxury the LM crews have to do without.]

a15_1281656.speaker: Worden
a15_1281656.text: I'm not sure there'll be any left. I have a well-stocked pantry here. [Long pause.]

a15_1281656.speaker: Worden
a15_1281656.text: I'm not sure there'll be any left. I have a well-stocked pantry here. (Long Pause) Well, Davy, I think I got you on the monocular.

a15_1281656.text: Well, Davy, I think I got you on the monocular.

a15_1281656.text: No, I can't see any tracks, Jim, but I can see discoloration, rather circular, that looks like it's around the LM.

a15_1281656.speaker: Irwin
a15_1281656.text: That's good. Maybe - maybe you can see the ALSEP.

a15_1281656.speaker: Irwin
a15_1281656.text: That's good. Maybe you can see the ALSEP.

a15_1281656.text: Is it over east of you?

a15_1281656.speaker: Irwin
a15_1281656.text: No, it's west about 300 feet. [Pause.]

a15_1281656.speaker: Irwin
a15_1281656.text: No, it's west about 300 feet. (Pause)

a15_1281656.speaker: Worden
a15_1281656.text: No, I don't have it.

a15_1281656.text: No, it's not very big. You're looking at best at something that's 2 to 3 feet.

a15_1281656.speaker: Worden
a15_1281656.text: Yeah. All I've got's the monocular.

a15_1281656.speaker: Worden
a15_1281656.text: Yes, all I've got's the monocular.

a15_1281656.speaker: Scott
a15_1281656.text: Oh, well. [Long pause.]

a15_1281656.speaker: Scott
a15_1281656.text: Oh, well. (Long Pause)

a15_1281656.speaker: Scott
a15_1281656.text: Well, have a nice time. We're going to go back to work. We'll talk to you later.

a15_1281656.speaker: Worden
a15_1281656.text: Okay; get to work, and I'll talk to you tomorrow.

a15_1281656.speaker: Worden
a15_1281656.text: Okay; get to work, and I'll talk to you tomorrow. 128:21:38 Scott: Okay. [Very Long Comm Break] [Jones - "Is there an operational purpose to checking out the VHF at this point?"] [Scott - "Well, there's an operational purpose to check and make sure we're all still there. If you're asking if this is just a chit-chat or if this is an operational procedure, it's an operational procedure."] [Jones - "There is a social, team-building, 'hi, we're still here, we haven't forgotten you, everything's okay' aspect to it."] [Scott - "Sure. It's just like keeping the loop closed, and it's also verifying th

a15_1282833csm.speaker: Parker
a15_1282833csm.text: Okay. T-start; 129:26:52; T-stop; 130:26:30. And it says note: at T-start, Map Camera Image Motion, Increase; talkback barber pole, plus 4. And at - at 130:08, Mapping Camera Image Motion, Increase, talkback barber pole. Over.

a15_1282833csm.speaker: Worden
a15_1282833csm.text: Roger; understand. Mapping Camera photo PAD. T-start, 129:26:52; T-stop, 130:26:30; and at T-start you want the Image Motion Increased to barber pole, plus 4; and at 130:08, you want the Image Motion Increased to barber pole.

a15a1284901.speaker: Allen
a15a1284901.text: Go ahead, Hadley Base; this is Houston.

a15a1284901.speaker: Scott
a15a1284901.text: Okay, we're all settled down now with some good beefsteak, and all cleaned up and ready to talk.

a15a1284901.speaker: Allen
a15a1284901.text: Sounds very good, Dave. [Jones - "I know that the food you had on the surface was cold. You could add cold water to the food packs, but that was about it."] [Scott - "Yeah, but I think we had some bite-sized items. Either in orbit or...I'd have to look at a menu. But I remember that, when we got back from Apollo 9, one of the things we pointed out that we missed was chewing. When we got back after ten days, part of the debriefing was 'What did you miss?' And we, all three, agreed we missed chewing things. And they said, 'You had chewing gum,' and we said 'It's just not the same.' And I remembe

a15a1284901.speaker: Allen
a15a1284901.text: We've got a list of questions here; some fairly general geology questions at the last, and, depending upon your answers, we'll build a good part of EVA-2 on it. Stand by a second; I've lost a lock-on. (Pause) Okay, we'd like to begin, though, with some fairly simple mechanical questions that'll require a ja/nein answer to most of them, I think. And they involve ALSEP and Rover. [Jones - "This isn't the only use of German on the flight. (In Spanish)Por que? "] [Scott - "Well, I think Joe lived over there for a while. Didn't Joe go to school in Heidelberg or somewhere? And in the months that we

a15a1284901.speaker: Allen
a15a1284901.text: And I'll just start off at the top of the list here. Dave, which ALSEP photos did you get out of the way?

a15a1284901.speaker: Scott
a15a1284901.text: I got them all but the heat flow, Joe.

a15a1284901.speaker: Allen
a15a1284901.text: Roger. Copy all but the heat flow. And, Jim, when the LSM (magnetometer) sunshield was deployed, do you think the instrument stayed more or less steady? Or do you think it may have moved a little bit?

a15a1284901.speaker: Irwin
a15a1284901.text: (Faint) It might have moved a little, Joe.

a15a1284901.speaker: Allen
a15a1284901.text: (Making a mis-identification) Dave, say again. I didn't copy that.

a15a1284901.speaker: Irwin
a15a1284901.text: Is there a problem with the...(Stops to listen to Joe) Hey, Joe, this is Jim. It might very well have moved. In other words, it's not level any longer?

a15a1284901.speaker: Allen
a15a1284901.text: Negative, Jim. We don't necessarily know that. As far as we know, the data looks pretty as a picture. We just want your own feel for it. (Pause) In other words, we have no reason to believe it moved. We just wanted to get some words from you on that. (Pause)

a15a1284901.speaker: Irwin
a15a1284901.text: This is Jim. I didn't notice any meter motion or anomalies, Joe.

a15a1284901.speaker: Allen
a15a1284901.text: Okay, Jim, thank you. And we're assuming that the Rover is now parked facing north. Is that correct?

a15a1284901.speaker: Allen
a15a1284901.text: I could have guessed as much. And a question about the suspension, which sounds kind of exciting. Did you ever notice it hitting bottom?

a15_1285137csm.text: And, Endeavour, Houston. We can terminate Batt B charge at this time, please.

[Jones - "The ALSEP deployment site was out west, so it would have been right out the window."] [Scott - "But quite a ways."] [Jones - "300 feet. Far enough that you couldn't see the details?"] [Scott - "Good heavens, you wouldn't be able to see details."] [Jones - "The impression I get from looking at the TV is that the ground right around the LM was fairly flat. Or is that just a down-Sun effect?"] [Scott - "Pretty level."] [Jones - "It doesn't look like it has the general rigosity that you describe

a15_1285501csm.speaker: Parker
a15_1285501csm.text: And, Endeavour; Houston. We're 4 minutes to LOS. A couple of comments before you go around the corner. First, the Surgeon thinks you may have loosened part of your EKG harness while you were exercising. Would like you to check that at your convenience. Second, we have a new Gamma-ray [boom] retract time on the back side of 129:20. Over.

a15_1285501csm.speaker: Allen
a15_1285501csm.text: Okay, Dave, that's a clear description. We know that the stem is loose in the hole as far as the rotational motion goes. We're wondering if it's loose in the up and down direction. Do you think you could pull it out?

a15_1285501csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1285501csm.text: I don't know, Joe. I don't really know. (Pause)

a15_1285501csm.speaker: Allen
a15_1285501csm.text: Okay, Dave, copy that. Is the drill thermal shroud off the drill unit?

a15_1285501csm.speaker: Worden
a15_1285501csm.text: Roger, Houston. Understand going around the back side. I'll check out my biomed harness. I may have loosened it exercising. And understand you want the gamma-ray boom retracted at 129:20.

a15_1285501csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1285501csm.text: Oh, yes. You mean the small aluminum-colored shroud that goes over the battery?

a15_1285501csm.speaker: Allen
a15_1285501csm.text: Okay, and were the Boyd-bolt guide cups removed from the heat flow experiment?

a15_1285501csm.speaker: Parker
a15_1285501csm.text: Roger. We won't be able to see it to keep track of [retraction] times, remember, Al. And, also I guess the Mass Spec. people would appreciate any more comments you can think of, next time you take a look at those particles at sunrise. Over.

a15_1285501csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1285501csm.text: Gee, I guess I have to think about what you mean. All the Boyd bolts are off of the box (meaning the Heat flow Electronics package), as far as I know.

a15_1285501csm.speaker: Allen
a15_1285501csm.text: Okay, Dave. Our question concerns the covers (also know as 'sleeves')for the Boyd bolts. They're calling them "the guide cups" down here.

a15_1285501csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1285501csm.text: Do you mean are they off now or were they off when we started?

a15_1285501csm.speaker: Worden
a15_1285501csm.text: Okay. When I took the battery B off charge and checked the systems test meter for battery pressure - battery compartment pressure - and it was - systems test meter read 1.4, which is - looks like it's getting pretty close. Is that test - test meter still working all right?

a15_1285501csm.speaker: Allen
a15_1285501csm.text: Dave, we mean are they off now. Did they fall away from the unit when you picked the unit up. It's of relative unimportance, really, but it would be an interesting data point.

a15_1285501csm.speaker: Scott
a15_1285501csm.text: I didn't pay much attention, Joe, but I think all the Boyd bolts came off the heat flow, finally, I think. (Pause)

a15a1290038.speaker: Irwin
a15a1290038.text: This is Jim. I didn't notice any meter motion or anomalies, Joe.

a15a1290038.speaker: Allen
a15a1290038.text: Okay, Jim, thank you. And we're assuming that the Rover is now parked facing north. Is that correct?

a15a1290038.speaker: Scott
a15a1290038.text: That's correct.

a15a1290038.speaker: Allen
a15a1290038.text: I could have guessed as much. And a question about the suspension, which sounds kind of exciting. Did you ever notice it hitting bottom?

a15a1290038.speaker: Scott
a15a1290038.text: Yes, we hit bottom a couple of times when we hit a rock, and it seemed to respond fairly well. I mean you could just feel that it had bottomed out. I might add something else, too, on your battery problem, Joe. I'm sure you're right about that because I noticed, in backing up a couple of times, that the front wheels did drive.

a15a1290038.speaker: Allen
a15a1290038.text: Okay, interesting comment, Dave. Thank you. Now we're getting on to the toughies here, and coming up to a very interesting one. We'd like to know what your best estimation of the LM's position is. Over.

a15a1290038.speaker: Scott
a15a1290038.text: Stand by.

a15a1290038.speaker: Allen
a15a1290038.text: And, Dave and Jim, let me give you some background on that. We've got several points that are in a very tight cluster around the first location we gave you. We think, however, because of bootstrapping a location from Elbow Crater backwards using the Rover navigation system, we think that you may be mistaking Last Crater for Index Crater. And I want you to consider this as you look at your map and think about your present position. Over.

a15a1290038.speaker: Scott
a15a1290038.text: My! [Comm Break] [Scott - "I remember all this discussion. In retrospect, it wasn't really significant - especially with the beauty of the Rover. You could be sort of anywhere in the area. If you're trying to make a pinpoint landing and walk to Surveyor, as Pete did, that's one thing. But if you're exploring a region with a Rover, you don't really care. And I think we all spent far too much time discussing where we were. In retrospect, we could have been forward or aft a kilometer and, for the purpose of what we did, there wouldn't be much effect. I mean, you wouldn't want to be too far east o

a15a1290038.speaker: Scott
a15a1290038.text: Joe, you've stimulated an interesting discussion. Give us a couple of more minutes.

a15a1290038.speaker: Allen
a15a1290038.text: We thought we might, Dave. (Pause) And, Dave and Jim, as you well know, this question is pretty much academic because we're doing great guns, no matter where your exact location is; and it's something we'll construct later (from the Rover Navigation readouts and the photography); but we're interested nonetheless. 129:05:07 Scott: Roger. (Long Pause) Okay, Joe. How about 73.3 Bravo Sierra 4? And I guess that's because we are on the northeast side of the double crater.

a15a1290038.speaker: Allen
a15a1290038.text: Voila! We understand.

a15a1290038.speaker: Scott
a15a1290038.text: Sure nice that Rover will make 12, 13 clicks, isn't it?

a15a1290038.speaker: Allen
a15a1290038.text: That sure is. Richard (Gordon, the back-up commander)'s studying the maps here momentarily. In the meantime, could you give us just a rough guess - a quick rundown - as to where the samples at Station 1 were taken with respect to the rim of Elbow, and we're interested in distance and direction from the rim. Just a rough guess.

a15a1290038.speaker: Scott
a15a1290038.text: Stand by. (Long Pause as he studies EVA-1/2, Part B) [Jones - "Let's see. Dick was the CMP on 12, right?"] [Scott - "Yeah. He was my backup on (Apollo) 15. And he was my backup on (Gemini) 8. We rotated."] 129:06:38 Scott: Okay, Joe, 70.9, Bravo Echo 5, and we moved out about 200 feet to the east of that point in picking up the three radial samples.

a15a1290038.speaker: Allen
a15a1290038.text: Okay, Dave, copied that loud and clear. And, by the way, Rover Nav system gave us exactly the same coordinates as you just called down for your LM location. Interesting coincidence, or perhaps not a coincidence.

a15a1290038.speaker: Allen
a15a1290038.text: Moving on to the next question. Near Elbow Crater, Dave, you mentioned that your footprints exposed white soil. We wonder if this was a common occurrence. Did you observe similar white soil in footprints elsewhere? Over.

a15a1290038.speaker: Scott
a15a1290038.text: Joe, I sort of kicked through a rim of a small, l-meter, subdued crater; and, as I did that, I kicked up some white soil. And so I kicked a couple of more times and it spread out; and whether I was breaking up a very friable rock or not, I don't know. But there was a couple of kickfuls of dirt that were white, and as we came back past it on the return trip to the LM, why, I pointed it out to Jim and he saw it too. And I'm not sure whether that was just at that one small crater, which was an old crater, or whether that was typical of that particular area. We just didn't have time to look at it.

a15a1290038.speaker: Allen
a15a1290038.text: Roger, Dave. Copy that. And coming back to Station 1, Elbow Crater, could you give us a quick rundown on the changes in block distribution around Elbow Crater and, if possible, maybe even the changes in rock types there. Over.

a15a1290038.speaker: Scott
a15a1290038.text: Stand by one. (Long Pause) Joe, our clocks were running pretty fast when we were there, and I guess we didn't get a chance to look at the distribution very well. As I remember it, there were more blocks - not really blocks, but large fragments on the order of 6 inches to a foot (in size) - more on the southern rim, although it wasn't really heavily concentrated; I'd say 10 percent of the surface at most (was covered with pieces of rock). There was more on the southern rim than on the northern rim. And the ones we sampled all looked pretty much the same. As I remember, the radial sample didn't

a15a1290038.speaker: Allen
a15a1290038.text: Roger, Dave. We copy that, and answers that question very well. But, once again, regarding Elbow Crater; Jim, you called out to us a bench around the east side of Elbow and you were looking down into Elbow from higher up on the front. We wonder if you could compare that bench with breaks in the slope of the Rille wall. Over. (Long Pause) [That is, is there any evidence that both Elbow Crater and the rille wall are showing signs of near-surface structure in the underlying layers of bedrock.]

a15a1290038.speaker: Irwin
a15a1290038.text: Joe, when I commented on "bench", I would estimate there are two or three different levels that were very-subdued, possible benches in Elbow. And I did not see any immediate relation between those subdued benches in Elbow and the Rille.

a15a1290038.speaker: Allen
a15a1290038.text: Okay, Jim, copy that. That sounds very reasonable. We'd like to move on down towards Station 2 now, and have a series of questions about Station 2. The first one being, what rock samples did you get from Station 2, and we're more interested in the samples that did not come from the large boulder, but rather what other samples did you get there? Over.

a15a1290038.speaker: Scott
a15a1290038.text: Okay, stand by. (Long Pause) Okay, Joe, our sum total at Station 2 was two chips off the large rock, soil from the fillet, soil adjacent about a couple of feet away from the rock, soil from beneath the rock, and the double core, and the comprehensive.

a15a1290038.speaker: Allen
a15a1290038.text: Okay, Dave, you called it right on from memory. That's exactly the score sheet we had. (Pause) Stand by a second. Let me read over this second question. Okay...

a15a1290038.speaker: Scott
a15a1290038.text: Okay, Joe. ...

a15a1290038.speaker: Allen
a15a1290038.text: ...regarding the boulder, do you think, possibly, that the black part of the boulder might be a big clast in a coarse breccia? Over.

a15a1291348.speaker: Scott
a15a1291348.text: Okay; if you consider the boulder being divided in fifths, 1/5th of it was a different type, apparently, by this sort of topographic contact. We took one chip from that side and one chip from a corner on the other side.

a15a1291348.speaker: Allen
a15a1291348.text: We copy that; thank you. We'd like for you to summarize the relationships of mare and Apennine Front in the Elbow-St. George area. And, we're looking for any evidence whatever of a contact, an albedo change, or a change in coarse-frag abundance. Over.

a15a1291348.speaker: Scott
a15a1291348.text: Joe, we looked, and we discussed it before we went out, and we've discussed it since we came back, and we honestly didn't see anything.

a15a1291348.speaker: Allen
a15a1291348.text: Roger, Dave; and you discussed it, then, about the same way during the traverse. So it sounds very consistent to us. Do you think that you can drive to either Spur or to Window Crater (which are planned EVA-2 stops on the flank of Mt. Hadley Delta).

a15a1291348.speaker: Scott
a15a1291348.text: Let us take a look here, quick. (Long Pause) Well, there are a number of craters down there in the area of Spur and Window, and those are the only craters up on the Apennine Front. And there are several the same size as Spur and Window, which I think were not evident on the photography because of the (relatively high) albedo and the Sun. I think we could get to some of those craters, yes. I'm not sure it would be Spur or Window, but there are some craters up on the side of the Front I'm fairly sure we could get to.

a15a1291348.speaker: Allen
a15a1291348.text: Roger, Dave. Copy that. And that is exactly the answer we were after; not necessarily those particular craters, but craters similar to them; and we understand exactly what you're saying. [The geologic interest is in finding one or more relatively fresh craters which have penetrated through the soil layer and exposed fragments of rocks of which the mountain is made.]

a15a1291348.speaker: Allen
a15a1291348.text: We'd like to ask: "Was the abundance of white and light-gray rocks described in the vicinity of Falcon the same seen along the entire route to St. George, or did this abundance of white and light-gray rocks seem to vary?" Over.

a15a1291348.speaker: Scott
a15a1291348.text: Joe, I think we have a great variety of fragments out here. I...I wouldn't want to pin down any particular type in any area until we had more time to look. We've got a couple of surprises for you. We have one fragment (the Seatbelt Basalt) on the order of 6 inches which is a fairly well rounded, highly vesicular basalt with vesicles on the order of 3 millimeters all over it, apparently quite old and rounded, and it's a brownish gray. We also have a large piece of glass, just sheer glass, apparently, which is about a foot long and about 6 inches wide and very rough-textured surface; and that wa

a15a1291348.speaker: Allen
a15a1291348.text: Roger, Dave. Read you loud and clear on that, and that really brings us to our last question. We're in the process of starting to plan your traverse tomorrow. It's going to be a good one. We have no equipment problems that we're looking at right now and we'd like to ask you if there're any particular inputs you would like to make into the planning team regarding tomorrow's traverse. Over.

a15a1291348.speaker: Scott
a15a1291348.text: Okay, let us talk it over a minute, please. [Comm Break] [Scott - "Silver used to debrief us on field trips . It's too bad we didn't take this transcript and the photos, and sit down and spend a year going back through it. I wonder if that would have been scientifically useful. It would have been interesting, but would it have contributed much more to what they learned anyway?"] [Jones - "We've talked about it in the context of the Mars mission - that part of the job of the crew is to spend the voyage back going through the material and doing thorough debriefs."] [Scott - "Absolutely. Nine mon

a15a1291348.speaker: Scott
a15a1291348.text: Joe, we've talked it over, and we think the best thing to do is to stick exactly with the plan we have now. I think we understand what we're looking for, and even though we didn't find some of the things we were looking for today (crystalline rocks, in particular), that doesn't mean that we won't find them as we head down to Front Crater. And I guess about the only input we'd have would be that, if we can make as good a time on the Rover tomorrow as we did today, perhaps we'd have more time to sample a variety of stations along the Front and on the way back. But, in general, I think we'd do be

a15a1291348.speaker: Allen
a15a1291348.text: Right on, Dave. We copy that, and I think we're going that direction. Sounds good. We got a couple more general questions and then a comment about the 16-millimeter camera, and after that we're going to be closing up shop down here. One more geology question. Do you have any feel for whether the frags around the small fresh craters that you've called out to us are, in general, pieces of the projectile or do you think they're ejecta frags? Over.

a15a1291348.speaker: Scott
a15a1291348.text: Well, Joe, we're pretty sure they're projectile frags, and that's one (type of crater) we really need to stop and sample. 129:22:12 Allen: Agreed, Dave. We think the same thing here. A quick comment on your 16-millimeter film. We think that that camera, the DAC, is still in good shape. That Mag Charlie was a bad magazine, and we think you can help us out on the other magazines left, tomorrow, by advancing the film with your finger just to make sure it's moving freely in the magazine before you clip it onto the camera itself.

a15a1291348.speaker: Scott
a15a1291348.text: That's a grand analysis, Joe. We're ...

a15a1291348.speaker: Allen
a15a1291348.text: And that's something you can do while you're packing the ETB. Can do it tonight. Over.

a15a1291348.speaker: Scott
a15a1291348.text: Rog, Joe. That's a good analysis. We took Mag Charlie and tried to run it with our fingers and it won't run. It's absolutely jammed right in the beginning. And we'll run the others through tonight to make sure they'll work. [See the discussion following 120:36:40 .]

a15a1291348.speaker: Allen
a15a1291348.text: Sounds terrific. And, Dave and Jim, we'll be standing by for a crew status report. No hurry on that; and, as I say, we're going to close up shop down here. We've got more data, really, than we know what to do with. But we'll work hard on it and be back with you in the morning. I do have (a) lift-off time Pad to send to you, Jim, when you're ready to copy.

a15a1291348.speaker: Scott
a15a1291348.text: Okay, he's got his pencil out. Go ahead. [Jones - "There were, in fact, forms with blank spaces? And did you mean a literal 'pencil'."] [Scott - "And pens. I've still got my pencils. Most of the time I think we used Pentels, which were the first felt-tipped pens. In fact, we used those back on Gemini."] [Jones - "Capillary feed rather than gravity feed."] [Scott - "Every time that we need to write down something that the ground reads up to us, there is a block in the flight plan to record that data, or in the checklist or whatever is appropriate at that time. You don't just get a blank piece o

a15a1291348.speaker: Allen
a15a1291348.text: Readback's correct. Jim, you've been doing good work all day.

a15a1291348.speaker: Irwin
a15a1291348.text: Well, we're trying. (Pause)

a15a1291348.speaker: Allen
a15a1291348.text: Roger. And, Dave and Jim, one last comment, which we're pretty sure you're aware of. We think we're looking at an EVA tomorrow that'll run about six and a half hours, about the same thing we did today. And we do have a few miscellaneous (ALSEP) items to clean up, most likely at the end of the traverse, so it's liable to be a little shorter distancewise, but otherwise, other than that, it'll be more or less unchanged. Over.

a15a1291348.speaker: Scott
a15a1291348.text: Okay, very good, Joe. By the way, did you notice that I had a higher O2 usage all the way through, and is that why we're looking at six and a half instead of seven hours?

a15a1291348.speaker: Allen
a15a1291348.text: That's correct, Dave. We've got very good data points on you. It's a steady curve, and the O2 rate is just a little bit higher than we predicted. From the looks of it, you've really been doing some work up there.

a15a1291348.speaker: Scott
a15a1291348.text: Well, do you have any idea why there's a rate? Perhaps maybe a (suit) zipper could be lubricated or something like that?

a15a1291348.speaker: Allen
a15a1291348.text: Dave, this is a metabolic curve, plain and simple. It's not a leak rate at all. [Jones - "What does Joe mean by 'metabolic rate'? That, when you were working harder, the use rate went up more than expected?"] [Scott - "Yeah, I discussed that when I was down in Houston (being interviewed about the suits). Let me recall if I can...I don't know how they plan the metabolic rate but, obviously, the amount of "work" work that you do determines the amount of oxygen you consume. So they were looking at the consumption of the oxygen, I guess, relative to the heart rate and everything else. And that giv

a15a1291348.speaker: Scott
a15a1291348.text: Okay, well, I'll breathe a little less tomorrow.

a15a1291348.speaker: Allen
a15a1291348.text: We don't recommend that - (joking) although the Surgeon's working on it right now. The numbers though, actually that we're coming up with, Dave, is about...The two numbers are 1150 Btu's per hour, working; and about 700 Btu's, riding. Over.

a15a1293238.speaker: Parker
a15a1293238.text: And, Falcon, we'd like biomed, right, please. [Houston wants to look at telemetry from Jim's sensors. Biomed left would give them Dave's telemetry.]

a15a1293238.speaker: Scott
a15a1293238.text: Okay, biomed right. There's nothing there right now (that is, Jim does not have his sensors on), but we'll give it to you.

a15a1293238.speaker: Parker
a15a1293238.text: Roger. Yes. We understand. [Very Long Comm Break. During this half hour, Dave and Jim are probably finishing their meal.]

a15_1334613csm.speaker: Fullerton
a15_1334613csm.text: Hello, Endeavour; this is Houston. Over. [No answer.]

a15_1334613csm.text: Endeavour, this is Houston. Over. [No answer.]
