a15_2670833.text: Okay, Houston. Ready to go with the right-hand column. U-4 is as prescribed, and R-2 is as prescribed.

a15_2670833.speaker: Henize
a15_2670833.text: Roger.

a15_2670833.speaker: Scott
a15_2670833.text: Okay. The PGA bag is as prescribed with the following additions. First we have - in - in the bag where we'll put the lunar sample - we'll have R-12, with the CSM Malfunction Procedures and Systems Book. [Pause.]

a15_2670833.speaker: Henize
a15_2670833.text: We copy.

a15_2670833.speaker: Scott
a15_2670833.text: And the lunar sample is bag number 7, for 24 pounds. [Pause.]

a15_2670833.speaker: Henize
a15_2670833.text: Roger.

a15_2670833.speaker: Scott
a15_2670833.text: Okay. And then, everything else is as prescribed. And the CMP PGA will be in the sleep restraint under the right-hand couch with two TSBs, which are now acting as waste containers. [Pause.]

a15_2670833.speaker: Henize
a15_2670833.text: Roger. And that - that location was where again?

a15_2670833.speaker: Scott
a15_2670833.text: Underneath the right-hand couch, strapped down as - as it's prescribed. We just wanted to note that, within that sleep restraint with the PGA, will also be two TSBs.

a15_2670833.speaker: Henize
a15_2670833.text: Roger. We copy.

a15_2670833.speaker: Scott
a15_2670833.text: And that's just light waste material in those TSBs. And I guess that pretty much takes care of it, unless you have any questions. [Long pause.]

a15_2670833.speaker: Henize
a15_2670833.text: Thank you, Dave. We copy all of that.

a15_2670833.speaker: Scott
a15_2670833.text: Okay. And, as you go through it and look it over, if you have any questions or anything you would like us to shuffle around, why, let us know.

a15_2670833.speaker: Henize
a15_2670833.text: Okay. We sure will. Thanks.

a15_2675348.speaker: Henize
a15_2675348.text: 15, this is Houston. The next several attitudes are going to require us to use Omni Delta, and we suggest that you go Manual and Wide and stow the High Gain Antenna.

a15_2675348.speaker: Irwin
a15_2675348.text: Okay. We'll do that and go to Omni Delta.

a15_2681349.speaker: Henize
a15_2681349.text: Apollo 15, this is Houston. We'd like to have you retract the Mass Spectrometer boom for 85 seconds.

a15_2681349.speaker: Worden
a15_2681349.text: Understand. Retract the Mass Spec. Boom for 85 seconds. [Pause.]

a15_2681349.speaker: Irwin
a15_2681349.text: Yes, I will. Soon as I get the door closed here.

a15_2681349.speaker: Henize
a15_2681349.text: That's affirm, and then we'll leave it there for about 5 minutes. We'll cue you when to extend it again.

a15_2682025.speaker: Irwin
a15_2682025.text: Says we're supposed to use the PCM cable. How can we shoot - that PCM cable for the 250? The EL? It won't reach this window, will it? And we'll have the Nikon in the other window.

a15_2682402.speaker: Henize
a15_2682402.text: 15, this is Houston. Would you please extend the Mass Spec. boom all the way out again.

a15_2682402.speaker: Henize
a15_2682402.text: And I have a T-start for the lunar eclipse photo's when you're ready to copy.

a15_2682402.speaker: Worden
a15_2682402.text: Okay. [Pause.] Go ahead with the T-start.

a15_2682402.speaker: Irwin
a15_2682402.text: Yes, my camera's still up here, Dave.

a15_2682402.speaker: Worden
a15_2682402.text: Hey, we're going to have to rush.

a15_2682402.speaker: Scott
a15_2682402.text: Huh? I know it. Why - logical.

a15_2682402.speaker: Scott
a15_2682402.text: How long is that from now?

a15_2682402.speaker: Irwin
a15_2682402.text: Well, why don't we go ahead to U - Why don't you go...

a15_2682402.speaker: Henize
a15_2682402.text: Al, we had a question on the Mass Spectrometer and it may be too late. Was it possible to confirm by visual look through the window that it was retracted? [Pause.]

a15_2682402.speaker: Worden
a15_2682402.text: Negative, Karl. You can't determine that it's retracted. All you can determine is that it's full out.

a15_2682402.speaker: Henize
a15_2682402.text: Rog. Well, when it was retracted, you wouldn't be able to see it. That's what I'm asking. Is it possible for you to take a look now and see if it slowly comes into view. [Pause.]

a15_2682402.speaker: Scott
a15_2682402.text: Okay, he wants you to watch and see if it does come full out.

a15_2682402.speaker: Worden
a15_2682402.text: Roger. In other words, you're asking to a confirm that it does come full out.

a15_2682402.speaker: Scott
a15_2682402.text: ...and if you can't see it, it was retracted. If you can see - You can't see it then.

a15_2682402.speaker: Worden
a15_2682402.text: Sure I can. Okay, Jim, I'll go ahead maneuver you. You're the act again.

a15_2682402.speaker: Irwin
a15_2682402.text: Well, if we can't find that other mag, Al, we might have to use this one. Got the one MAG here of black and white from the LM. It has got to be...

a15_2682402.speaker: Henize
a15_2682402.text: ...our question, Al, the main question was just to confirm whether or not it did go out of your field of view. Did it actually move from the full - from the full-extended position? Since we saw no change in the data when we retracted it during the test yesterday, there is a suspicion that, even though you actuated the switch, that for some reason it didn't retract.

a15_2682402.speaker: Irwin
a15_2682402.text: I see - there's one boom extended.

a15_2682402.speaker: Worden
a15_2682402.text: Okay. It's fully extended now, Karl. But it may be too late. It may have already been out by the time we looked.

a15_2682402.speaker: Worden
a15_2682402.text: Is that talkback barber pole or gray?

a15_2683653.speaker: Henize
a15_2683653.text: 15, this is Houston. We have a rather extensive update to the Flight Plan. And also, a change to the procedure for the contamination photos, which we can read up to you at your convenience. [Pause.]

a15_2683653.speaker: Scott
a15_2683653.text: Okay. Does it involve the things going on here in the next couple of hours?

a15_2683653.speaker: Henize
a15_2683653.text: It's pertinent beginning at 271. [Pause.] We probably ought to get it in before the press conference at 270.

a15_2683653.speaker: Scott
a15_2683653.text: Okay. Stand by one. [Long pause.]

a15_2683653.speaker: Scott
a15_2683653.text: Okay. Go ahead, Karl

a15_2683653.speaker: Henize
a15_2683653.text: Okay. If you've got the Flight Plan out, we go over to 271 hours. And at 271:20, just under S-Band Aux TV Science, we add Verb 49, maneuver to contamination photo attitude. [Pause.] The attitude is 014, 195, 016; High Gain [Antenna]; pitch, minus 23; yaw, 252. [Pause.]

a15_2683653.speaker: Scott
a15_2683653.text: Okay. At 171:20 [means 271:20] just after S-band Aux TV Science, Verb 49 to 014, 195, 016; High Gain; pitch, minus 25 - 23; and the yaw, 252.

a15_2683653.speaker: Henize
a15_2683653.text: Roger. Just after that, we delete "Mass Spectrometer, Ion Source, Off", and in the space there, add "Configure for urine dump." [Pause.]

a15_2683653.speaker: Scott
a15_2683653.text: Rog. Delete the Mass Spec. and Ion Source, Off, and configure for urine dump. Go.

a15_2683653.speaker: Henize
a15_2683653.text: Okay. Delete the next one, two, three, four lines, but we - and that brings us to Gamma - Gamma-ray Gain Step, Shield, Off, which we leave in.

a15_2683653.speaker: Scott
a15_2683653.text: Rog. Delete four and leave in the Gamma-ray Gain Step, Shield, Off. Go.

a15_2683653.speaker: Henize
a15_2683653.text: Delete all of the rest of that page. And add at 271:40, Verb 48, 11101, 01111, and P52, option 3. [Pause.]

a15_2683653.speaker: Scott
a15_2683653.text: Okay. 271:40, Verb 48, 11101, 01111, and a P52, option 3.

a15_2683653.speaker: Henize
a15_2683653.text: Roger. And at 271:45, we add Gamma-ray Boom Deploy, 41 seconds, then Off. Gamma-ray Gain Step, Center, and start contamination photos. [Long pause.]

a15_2683653.speaker: Scott
a15_2683653.text: Okay. 271:45, Gamma-ray Boom Deploy, 41 seconds, then Off. Gamma-ray Gain Step to Center. Start the contamination photos.

a15_2683653.speaker: Henize
a15_2683653.text: And there's a note on the photos that you begin to dump according to the photo procedures, which are - I have an update to that I'll give you later. And that we dump the water to 40 percent, in order to have the right weight at entry. [Pause.] Roger. It's important that we don't go below 40 percent on the water dump. [Pause.]

a15_2683653.speaker: Scott
a15_2683653.text: Okay. Understand. Dump according to photo procedures and the water dump to no less than 40 percent for entry.

a15_2683653.speaker: Henize
a15_2683653.text: That's affirmative. On the next page, 272 hours and zero minutes, we - I - I presume you know that we're not doing the midcourse correction 6. We cancelled the P52 there. And we keep the H 2 purge line heater on, but we cancel the P30 external Delta-V. We cancel the Verb 49 maneuver, we cancel the next one, two, three, four, five, all the way down to the H 2 and O 2 fuel cell purge, which we keep.

a15_2683653.speaker: Scott
a15_2683653.text: Okay. Understand. Keep the H 2 purge line heater, cancel the P52, and the set of lines below H 2 line heater on, and keep the H 2 /O 2 fuel cell purge.

a15_2683653.speaker: Henize
a15_2683653.text: Roger. And at 272:28, a note that you should be ending the contamination photos at that point.

a15_2683653.speaker: Scott
a15_2683653.text: Say again.

a15_2683653.speaker: Henize
a15_2683653.text: 2 - 272:38. [Long pause.]

a15_2683653.speaker: Scott
a15_2683653.text: Okay. 272:38, end contamination photos. Go ahead.

a15_2683653.speaker: Henize
a15_2683653.text: Right. At 42 we cancel - we delete the waste water dump, since we've already done it. And at 42 we add: "Start the Mass Spec. boom test." and the procedures are to be read up in real time. At 58 we cancel the midcourse 6. [Long pause.]

a15_2683653.speaker: Worden
a15_2683653.text: Okay. At 272:47, that's the - hold on. Let me read it back. 272:42 the Mass Spec. boom test procedures in real time, and cancel MCC-6. Go ahead.

a15_2683653.speaker: Henize
a15_2683653.text: Roger. At 273:01, we cancel the burn status report and we add: "X-ray experiment, On. Alpha/X-ray Covers, Open, and record the GET." [Long pause.]

a15_2683653.speaker: Worden
a15_2683653.text: Okay. 273:01, X-ray experiment, On, Alpha/X-ray Covers, Open, and record the GET. Go ahead.

a15_2683653.speaker: Henize
a15_2683653.text: Roger. At 03, we delete the Gamma-ray, X-ray, alpha particle, MSO, On. And down at 273:47, we add Gamma-ray Boom, Deploy. [Long pause.]

a15_2683653.speaker: Worden
a15_2683653.text: Okay. A deletion at 273:00 - or 03, the four items there and then Gamma-ray Boom, Deploy, at 273:47. Go ahead.

a15_2683653.speaker: Henize
a15_2683653.text: Roger. And one final item on 274:05, in the Mass Spectrometer instructions there, the discriminator should be Low instead of High. [Pause.]

a15_2683653.speaker: Worden
a15_2683653.text: Okay. 274:04 Mass Spec. discriminator, Low vice High.

a15_2683653.speaker: Henize
a15_2683653.text: Roger. And if you have the time, I can give you the update on the contamination photography, which is on photo 25 and 26 in the back of volume 1 of the Flight Plan.

a15_2683653.speaker: Worden
a15_2683653.text: Stand by one, please. [Long pause.]

a15_2683653.speaker: Worden
a15_2683653.text: Okay, Houston. Let's hold off on the updates of those other photos, so we can get squared away for the eclipse photos.

a15_2683653.speaker: Henize
a15_2683653.text: Roger.

a15_2691308.speaker: Henize
a15_2691308.text: 15, this is Houston. Your astronomer CapCom is getting curious to know whether you're seeing anything of the lunar eclipse. Anything visible?

a15_2691308.speaker: Scott
a15_2691308.text: Oh, sure, we've seen it come down to about half to about one-fifth illumination at the present time, relative to the Sun's illumination.

a15_2691308.speaker: Henize
a15_2691308.text: Roger. And what percent of the disk is covered now? [Pause.]

a15_2691547.speaker: Scott
a15_2691547.text: Okay, Karl. Looks like about 9/10ths of the disk is covered at the present time, and we've been taking the pictures all along. It's a very pretty sight out there.

a15_2691547.speaker: Henize
a15_2691547.text: Roger. Sounds like you're getting close to total eclipse there. Hey, we note down here that in your Free mode you are drifting somewhat in pitch and you are about 5 degrees off now. The recommendation is to go Auto and stop the drift if you can and cycle back to Free before you take your next photo. If there is anything you can do to correct the pointing it might be a good idea.

a15_2691547.speaker: Scott
a15_2691547.text: Okay. Right now those photos are handheld, so we'll get to it when we get to the Nikon.

a15_2692204.speaker: Scott
a15_2692204.text: Houston, 15. The Moon's in the shadow now and we have a variation in color from a - almost a light gray to a burnt orange from one side of the Moon to the other. Almost like the old harvest Moon, except that I'm not sure there's any atmosphere up here yet.

a15_2692517.speaker: Scott
a15_2692517.text: Houston, 15. We've finished the photos, and Al had the Moon in the reflex part of the Nikon all the way, so I'm sure the pointing was okay.

a15_2692517.speaker: Scott
a15_2692517.text: Right now the Moon is sort of - varies from sort of a very pale orange to a good deep burnt orange on one side and a very gradual change. And I hope the - the photos come out because it sure - certainly be pretty.

a15_2692517.speaker: Henize
a15_2692517.text: Very good. It sounds like a beautiful view from up there. You've seen a lunar eclipse of the Moon twice as big as anyone else has ever seen such an eclipse.

a15_2692517.speaker: Scott
a15_2692517.text: That's very interesting, and it certainly is a - a pretty view. It'd be a - a great place for somebody like you to come up and use your trained eye to interpret all this and understand it.

a15_2692517.speaker: Henize
a15_2692517.text: Sounds like it would be fun, someday. [Long pause.]

a15_2692517.speaker: Henize
a15_2692517.text: I see you have your EMS entry check coming up. If there is any chance of my slipping in this change of procedure on contamination cloud photography I'd be pleased to - at this point.

a15_2692517.speaker: Scott
a15_2692517.text: Okay, give us a couple of minutes to reconfigure here. We'll have time to do that.

a15_2692517.speaker: Henize
a15_2692517.text: Okay, fine. I'll stand by for your word.

a15_2693108.speaker: Scott
a15_2693108.text: Okay, Houston. Go with the contamination cloud photography update.

a15_2693108.speaker: Henize
a15_2693108.text: Roger, Dave. Are we on photo 25?

a15_2693108.speaker: Scott
a15_2693108.text: Photo 25. Go.

a15_2693108.speaker: Henize
a15_2693108.text: Okay, the reason for this change is that we have to use the DAC, instead of the Nikon, since we've run out of Nikon film. The first change is under procedure - one, configure camera; we go down to the second line in the CM4, et cetera , we X that out, and we substitute - CM4...

a15_2693108.speaker: Scott
a15_2693108.text: Stand by one, Karl. We want to find out if we have any more Nikon film. We may have some.

a15_2693108.speaker: Henize
a15_2693108.text: Okay. [Long pause.]

a15_2693108.speaker: Henize
a15_2693108.text: 15, Houston. Our records show that you will be out of Nikon film when you finish the lunar eclipse photography, and we'd prefer that you use it for the lunar eclipse. [Pause.]

a15_2693108.speaker: Scott
a15_2693108.text: Does that include mag W.

a15_2693108.speaker: Henize
a15_2693108.text: Stand by. [Pause.]

a15_2693108.speaker: Scott
a15_2693108.text: Oh, disregard that. We just found a - a little note on mag W. It says "Do not load in camera." I guess that takes care of that. Go ahead with your update.

a15_2693108.speaker: Henize
a15_2693108.text: Okay, fine. The basic specs there in - are - We're using window 4/DAC - D-A-C/18 [-mm lens]/VHBW [Very High-speed Black and White film]-bracket, M-I-R for mirror, PCM pic cable. Parenthesis, T1, 1/1,000, infinity, 24 feet [frames?] per second.

a15_2693108.speaker: Scott
a15_2693108.text: Okay. DAC/18/VHBW-bracket, mirror, PCM cable, T1 1/1,000, infinity, and 24 frames per second. Go.

a15_2693108.speaker: Henize
a15_2693108.text: Correct. The next line, it's magazine H, magazine Hotel, and magazine - and instead of frame number, it's magazine per cent to be filled in there.

a15_2693108.speaker: Scott
a15_2693108.text: Roger. Hotel and per cent. Go.

a15_2693108.speaker: Henize
a15_2693108.text: Okay. Completely delete number 2, and substitute instead the following. "Utility Power, On, cover lens, DAC On, 2 seconds." [Pause.] Change shutter to "1/60;" change frame rate to "Time." [Pause.]

a15_2693108.speaker: Scott
a15_2693108.text: Okay. "Utility Power, On; cover lens; DAC, On, 2 seconds," change shutter to "1/60th," frame rate to "Time," in place of the number 2 you have. Go ahead.

a15_2693108.speaker: Henize
a15_2693108.text: Roger. In step 3, we delete "Inhibit all jets," and, at the end, we add "CMC Mode, Free."

a15_2693108.speaker: Scott
a15_2693108.text: Roger. Delete "Inhibit all jets," and add "CMC Mode, Free" at the end. Go ahead.

a15_2693108.speaker: Henize
a15_2693108.text: Roger. At the - at the end of step 4, before, "Repeat 4-frame sequence," we write "CMC Mode, Auto." And we delete "Repeat 4-frame"...

a15_2693108.speaker: Scott
a15_2693108.text: Okay. CM...

a15_2693108.speaker: Henize
a15_2693108.text: We - we - we - we delete the "Repeat 4-frame sequence."

a15_2693108.speaker: Scott
a15_2693108.text: Okay, step 4. Add "CMC Auto" and delete "Repeat 4-frame sequence." Go ahead.

a15_2693108.speaker: Henize
a15_2693108.text: Roger. Step 5. Instead of T plus 6 plus 6:30, we - it's T plus 3:30, 3 plus 30. Dump waste water...

a15_2693108.speaker: Scott
a15_2693108.text: Roger. T plus 3:30 vice T plus 6:30.

a15_2693108.speaker: Henize
a15_2693108.text: Roger. And it says "Waste water or urine," it's really "Waste water and urine." [Pause.] The - and we dump...

a15_2693108.speaker: Scott
a15_2693108.text: And vice or.

a15_2693108.speaker: Henize
a15_2693108.text: Go ahead, and - Okay, and we dump to 40 percent as you've been previously advised. Also a part of 5, add "Repeat step 4 (damp rates)." [Pause.]

a15_2693108.speaker: Scott
a15_2693108.text: Okay. In step 5, add "Repeat step 4 and damp rates, parenthesis." Go.

a15_2693108.speaker: Henize
a15_2693108.text: Step 6, the time there is not 26 plus 30, but it's 28 plus 30. Also...

a15_2693108.speaker: Scott
a15_2693108.text: Roger; 28 plus 30 vice 26 plus 30.

a15_2693108.speaker: Henize
a15_2693108.text: Roger. At the bottom, we delete "Repeat 4-frame sequence," and we add the following: "T plus 32 plus 0; CMC Mode, Auto," and below that "Repeat step 4 (damp rates)." [Long pause.]

a15_2693108.speaker: Scott
a15_2693108.text: Okay. At the end of step 6, can - cancel "Repeat 4-frame sequence," and add "T plus 32 plus 0, CMC, Auto," and then "Repeat step 4 and damp rates."

a15_2693108.speaker: Henize
a15_2693108.text: Roger. On step 7, it's "T plus 43" instead of 48; and, at the end, delete "Repeat 4-frame sequence," and add "CMC Mode, Auto." [Pause.]

a15_2693108.speaker: Scott
a15_2693108.text: Okay. Step 7 is "T plus 43" and delete the "Repeat 4-frame" and add "CMC, Auto." Go.

a15_2693108.speaker: Henize
a15_2693108.text: Roger. Step 8. We delete "Enable all jets," and what we record is the magazine percent. And that's the end of the correction.

a15_2693108.speaker: Scott
a15_2693108.text: Okay. Step 8, delete "Enable all jets," and add percent instead of frames.

a15_2693108.speaker: Henize
a15_2693108.text: Roger. That's got it.

a15_2693108.speaker: Scott
a15_2693108.text: Alrighty we'll do all those.

a15_2694035.speaker: Henize
a15_2694035.text: 15, this is Houston. Sorry to tell you, but I made a couple of errors in that read-up. Can we make it two corrections?

a15_2694035.speaker: Irwin
a15_2694035.text: Okay. Stand by one, please, Karl. [Long pause.]

a15_2694035.speaker: Irwin
a15_2694035.text: Okay, Karl; where are the corrections?

a15_2694035.speaker: Henize
a15_2694035.text: Right. At the end of step 5 and step 6, I put in a little statement saying "Repeat step 4, damp rates." That's really meant to say, "Repeat step 3," which is "damp rates," in both cases.

a15_2694543.speaker: Henize
a15_2694543.text: Guys, at the end of photo 26, when you get through with this sequence, requesting 2 seconds of protect frame, also. [Pause.]

a15_2694834.speaker: Gordon
a15_2694834.text: 15, Houston. [I] have a lunar eclipse photo PAD [as required] on your Flight Plan, page 384, when you're ready. [Pause.]

a15_2694834.speaker: Irwin
a15_2694834.text: Okay. I'm ready to copy the photo PAD on the lunar eclipse.

a15_2694834.speaker: Mission Control
a15_2694834.text: This is Apollo Control at 269 hours, 51 minutes. Those last couple of transmissions have been by the backup crew Commander, Dick Gordon, who has joined CapCom Karl Henize at the console. Apollo 15 now 111,271 nautical [206,073 km] miles from Earth. Velocity: 4,746 feet per second [1,447 m/s].

a15_2695837.speaker: Henize
a15_2695837.text: 15, we'd like to have Omni Charlie.

a15_2700909.speaker: Henize
a15_2700909.text: 15, Houston. We'd like to get the High Gain [Antenna] up. Pitch, 22; Yaw, 261. [Pause.]

a15_2700909.speaker: Scott
a15_2700909.text: Okay, Houston. Are your High Gain angles for the sextant photos or for the lunar eclipse photo attitudes?

a15_2700909.speaker: Henize
a15_2700909.text: Sorry about that, Dave. When you complete this maneuver, they're in your Flight Plan. Pitch, minus 22; Yaw, 227.

a15_2701218.speaker: Henize
a15_2701218.text: 15, we'd like to have Omni Bravo. [Pause.]

a15_2701218.speaker: Scott
a15_2701218.text: Can you get that for him, Jim? Omni Bravo?

a15_2701640.speaker: Henize
a15_2701640.text: 15, Houston. Give us Auto and Narrow on the High Gain, please.

a15_2701640.speaker: Worden
a15_2701640.text: You want the front end to come this way a little? You want the front end to come this way?

a15_2701640.speaker: Scott
a15_2701640.text: No, I guess it's all right, if I can - It - it - There.

a15_2701640.speaker: Mission Control
a15_2701640.text: This is Apollo Control at 270 hours, 17 minutes. We should be getting television in a few minutes now. Apollo 15's distance from Earth, 110,080 [nautical] miles [203,868 km]. Velocity: 4,790 feet per second [1,460 m/s].

a15_2702142.speaker: Irwin
a15_2702142.text: Well, it's in TV already. Who put it in TV?

a15_2702142.speaker: Henize
a15_2702142.text: We're close to ready. Are you ready for the big press conference?

a15_2702142.speaker: Scott
a15_2702142.text: Rog. We're ready. Anytime you want to go to transmit, let us know.

a15_2702142.speaker: Henize
a15_2702142.text: Okay. You can go ahead to transmit.

a15_2702142.speaker: Scott
a15_2702142.text: Roger. We are. I got 3 seconds, 2 seconds, 1 second. How's that? There.

a15_2702142.speaker: Worden
a15_2702142.text: Except for - move your wire, Jim.

a15_2702142.speaker: Scott
a15_2702142.text: That a boy, now. See? They get it all. Okay, Houston, talk to us. We're all here. Except how does it...

a15_2702142.speaker: Henize
a15_2702142.text: Hey, 15, we're getting a beautiful picture coming through.

a15_2702142.speaker: Scott
a15_2702142.text: Roger. Go ahead with your questions.

a15_2702142.speaker: Henize
a15_2702142.text: Roger. We'll - we'll admire the beautiful picture for - for a few minutes here.

a15_2702142.speaker: Henize
a15_2702142.text: Deke just passed out from the shock, incidentally.

a15_2702142.speaker: Scott
a15_2702142.text: Yes - yes. No, we look so good.

a15_2702142.speaker: Irwin
a15_2702142.text: It's just because we haven't shaved in 2 weeks.

a15_2702142.speaker: Henize
a15_2702142.text: Okay, fellas. I have a preliminary statement to make here. The questions you will be asked in this news conference have been submitted by newsmen here at the Manned Spacecraft Center who've been covering the flight. Some of the questions they raised have been answered in your communications with - with Mission Control, but the public-at-large has not necessarily heard them. The questions are being read to you exactly as submitted by the newsmen, and in an order of priority specified by them.

a15_2702142.speaker: Henize
a15_2702142.text: Question number 1. This last week, we have shared scores of exciting moments with you. Which single moment would you most like to live again, and is there any moment which you would never like to repeat?

a15_2702142.speaker: Scott
a15_2702142.text: Well, I guess we all probably have a different idea of which would be the single most exciting moment of the flight, and maybe we'll just run through it one at a time. I guess the most impressive moment I can remember is standing up on Hadley mountain - Hadley Delta, and looking back at the plain and seeing the LM and the rille and Mount Hadley, and the whole big picture in one - one swoop. And I think we've got some pictures for you from up there, and I believe the TV was running at the same time, and I think that was probably the most impressive sight that I've ever seen. Al?

a15_2702142.speaker: Worden
a15_2702142.text: I guess I'd have to say - sort of, two events occurred which were exciting, for different reasons, and I guess they were really kind of the highlights of - of the flight for me. One was, right after LOI, when we got our first look at the Moon, and it was a fantastic, spectacular sight. And the other, I guess, was when TEI burned so beautifully, and right after TEI, that was an awfully good feeling.

a15_2702142.speaker: Irwin
a15_2702142.text: Okay. Well, I guess there were a great many new thrills for me, and the one that was most impressive though, was the lift-off. It began the flight, and I knew that I was going into space after a few years of waiting and training. And then, as far as the event that I would not like to - to repeat again, was probably the time when I fell down in front of the TV, when we were deploying the Rover.

a15_2702545.speaker: Henize
a15_2702545.text: Question number 2. Near Spur crater, you found what may be "genesis" rock, the oldest yet collected on the Moon. Tell us more about it.

a15_2702545.speaker: Scott
a15_2702545.text: Well, I think the one you're referring to was what we felt was almost entirely plagioclase or perhaps anorthosite. And it was a small fragment sitting on top of a - a dark brown larger fragment, almost like on a pedestal. And Jim and I were both quite impressed with the fact that it was there, apparently waiting for us. And we had hoped to find more of it, and, I'm sure, had we more time at that site, we would have been able to find more. But I think this one rock, if it is, in fact, the beginning of the Moon, will tell us an awful lot. And we'll leave it up to the experts to analyse it when w

a15_2702545.speaker: Henize
a15_2702545.text: Question number 3. Apollo 15 is already being described as one of the great events in the history of science. Aside from the crystalline rock, what other findings at Hadley-Apennine seem most important to you?

a15_2702648.speaker: Henize
a15_2702648.text: Question number 3. Apollo 15 is already being described as one of the great events in the history of science. Aside from the crystalline rock, what other findings at Hadley-Apennine seem most important to you?

a15_2702648.speaker: Scott
a15_2702648.text: Jim? Why don't you answer that?

a15_2702648.speaker: Irwin
a15_2702648.text: I guess, immediately, I think of the orientation, or organization that was revealed in the side of Mount Hadley. There's 14,000 feet vertical relief of vast mountain face exposed to us. And there was layering in there that was most impressive for the total 14,000 feet, and we commented on the number of beds we could see. That really impressed me, that you could have that much organization in - on a large mountain on the Moon.

a15_2702648.speaker: Henize
a15_2702648.text: Question number 4. This was the toughest landing area we have attempted to - to reach on the Moon. Describe what it was like, flying into it.

a15_2702745.speaker: Henize
a15_2702745.text: Question number 4. This was the toughest landing area we have attempted to - to reach on the Moon. Describe what it was like, flying into it.

a15_2702745.speaker: Scott
a15_2702745.text: Well, I think, to begin with, we had every confidence that we could get to the landing site. The trajectory had been modified such that we had adequate clearance over the mountains. And the first sight I had out the window was somewhere around probably 9 or 10,000 feet, as we passed down below the upper elevations of Mount Hadley. And I could see Mount Hadley to my left before we pitch - pitched over and saw the plain at Hadley, and that was probably as impressive sight - a sight as I've seen. The landing itself, once we pitched over, was somewhat of a surprise in that the - the cratering was

a15_2702745.speaker: Henize
a15_2702745.text: Question number 5 for Al Worden. In lunar orbit, you too carried out geologic observations; for example, you reported cinder cones. Could you discuss this and other observations from 60 miles up?

a15_2702939.speaker: Henize
a15_2702939.text: Question number 5 for Al Worden. In lunar orbit, you too carried out geologic observations; for example, you reported cinder cones. Could you discuss this and other observations from 60 miles up?

a15_2702939.speaker: Worden
a15_2702939.text: Yes, the comment on the cinder cones was one of color, but we noticed particularly on - on some of the lighter part of the back side that many, many of the craters that we flew over were filled with what appeared to be lava. There seemed to be a great number of lava flows in the mare area, particularly Mare Imbrium. Mare Imbrium seems to be a - just a - countless numbers of - of lava flows, which were all apparently very thin and very fluid. And you can see - you can just count number - numbers of flow fronts covering Mare Imbrium. So, we got, I think, quite a distinct impression of a - of a -

a15_2703106.speaker: Henize
a15_2703106.text: Question number 6. Do you feel that the workload during your three lunar surface excursions was too demanding? You appeared at times to be reaching the limit of your endurance. Any recommendations for Apollo 16?

a15_2703106.speaker: Scott
a15_2703106.text: I think any time you set out on a task such as the one we had, you're bound to, at certain times, get a little tired, which I think we probably did. However, I think we came back and I don't think we ever reached anywhere near the limit of our physical endurance. I think Apollo 16 probably has everything in hand; it's just a matter of conditioning yourself. Jim and I have discussed it since we got back on board the Endeavour and concluded that our training is what really prepared us, and the many hours we spent during geology field trips and in simulations at the Cape in our suits, we feel was

a15_2703106.speaker: Henize
a15_2703106.text: Question number 7. You described the Lunar Rover as a bucking bronco on the Moon. Would you elaborate and assess the Rover's performance and tell us what changes you recommend for the 1972 model? [Pause.]

a15_2703250.speaker: Henize
a15_2703250.text: Question number 7. You described the Lunar Rover as a bucking bronco on the Moon. Would you elaborate and assess the Rover's performance and tell us what changes you recommend for the 1972 model? [Pause.]

a15_2703250.speaker: Scott
a15_2703250.text: [Laughter.] Jim, you want to talk about that? Why don't you go ahead? Not too hard, though [laughter].

a15_2703250.speaker: Irwin
a15_2703250.text: Well, there were several times there when we were riding along where we'd hit on a sizable bump and you could - you could see the - the wheels come off the ground and then float through the air and - but Dave should comment more as far as the - the driving. And it was really like a bucking bronco, that's true, because I was strapped in. As you know, Dave had to strap me in because I had some trouble with my seatbelt, but I - I really did feel like I was on a - a bucking bronco.

a15_2703250.speaker: Scott
a15_2703250.text: I think I might add that it's a - it's a very stable machine, but because of the - the one-sixth gravity, it tends to float. In - in the simulations we ran in Houston, we saw the same amplitude or same degree of bouncing but a different damping. In other words, the - the vehicle would come off the ground, or one wheel normally would come off the ground, and it would take somewhat longer to return to the ground than in one g. And I think it's just a matter of being - becoming accustomed to the - to driving. It's a very stable vehicle; the suspension system - system is excellent. We had to make

a15_2703502.speaker: Henize
a15_2703502.text: Question number 8 for Dave Scott. The drill seemed to drive you up the crater walls. What was the problem, and was it worth the time?

a15_2703502.speaker: Scott
a15_2703502.text: I guess I'd anticipated that question. I think the problem was a - a striking discovery. When we went to Hadley Rille, we expected to find a regolith, or the soil, about 5 meters thick. And with that in mind, like 25 feet, I expected to have no trouble putting the heat flow probes in or drilling the - the core stem because of the expected soft soil. After about 1 meter, I ran into hard rock, and my first thought was it was an isolated rock somewhere within the - the soil. But that was not the case. Apparently, what we have is a very thin regolith, or a thin soil layer above solid rock. And wit

a15_2703714.speaker: Scott
a15_2703714.text: Gee, I don't want them all.

a15_2703714.speaker: Scott
a15_2703714.text: Well, since I really have very little say-so as to which - which people get selected for which crews, I might sort of bypass it with a - with a one comment that the more qualified a man is on the Moon, the more results you're going to get. And I think that's one of the reasons that we put as much time as we did into the geological aspects, in hopes of - of learning enough to bring back some significant data. I think that in any situation such as this, in any scientific endeavor, that you want the most qualified people possible. You must also remember that this is a - a highly complex operation

a15_2703840.speaker: Henize
a15_2703840.text: Question number 10 for Al Worden. What runs through the mind of a man orbiting the Moon alone? [Pause.]

a15_2703840.speaker: Worden
a15_2703840.text: Well, I guess - I guess the - the thing foremost in my mind during those three days was how I was going to keep up with the time line and the Flight Plan, and how I was going to keep track of all the experiments we had going and where they were, and - and whether they were operating or not. And I guess that was a very, very fast three days for me. When I wasn't looking at the SIM bay experiments, I was looking out a window and taking pictures, and it was a pretty crammed three days. As a matter of fact, I - I guess I didn't really have - have much time to give any thoughts to being alone up th

a15_2703840.speaker: Henize
a15_2703840.text: Question number 11, again for Al. You said, after your spacewalk, you wish you'd stayed out longer. What was it like out there between the Earth and the Moon, and why did you come in so soon?

a15_2703930.speaker: Henize
a15_2703930.text: Question number 11, again for Al. You said, after your spacewalk, you wish you'd stayed out longer. What was it like out there between the Earth and the Moon, and why did you come in so soon?

a15_2703930.speaker: Worden
a15_2703930.text: Well, let me answer the last one first. I - I guess I didn't come in soon; I came in when the job was done. And, as a matter of fact, I made an extra trip back out to take a look at the Mapping Camera. Now as - as far as what I felt like when I was out there, we talked a little bit about it after - after the EVA and decided it was sort of like walking on stage at your high school - dinner dance or something. We opened the hatch and it was pitch black, and as soon as we got out, the Sun was beating down on everything, and it looked like a very large floodlight on a stage. And then putting the T

a15_2704055.speaker: Henize
a15_2704055.text: Question number 12 for Dave and Jim. You - you didn't have time to get to North Complex, craters which may have been formed volcanically and where you thought some surprises might be found. Was this a significant loss? [Pause.]

a15_2704055.speaker: Scott
a15_2704055.text: Well, I'll start out and - and throw an answer there. I think if you look back at the original requirements for the landing at the Hadley-Apennines, they were primarily to inspect the front and the rille. It was only after a - a considerable amount of study had been done and some rearrangement in the Flight Plan - the timing on the surface, that we found we had enough time to plan to go to the Northern Complex. So the Northern Complex was, in fact, an addition to the original requirement; it was a bonus. And I think because Jim and I have spent so much time with volcanics in our terrestrial ge

a15_2704055.speaker: Irwin
a15_2704055.text: No, I agree with everything you said. It was just a little personal disappointment that we couldn't get up there, because we - we thought we'd have another beautiful view of the - the plains there and the LM, a view almost...

a15_2704055.speaker: Irwin
a15_2704055.text: ...as beautiful as it - as it was from the side of Hadley Delta.

a15_2704055.speaker: Henize
a15_2704055.text: Question number 13 for each of you. Would you, please, in your own words, tell us what you gave the American taxpayers besides a few hours of good television? [Pause.]

a15_2704237.speaker: Henize
a15_2704237.text: Question number 13 for each of you. Would you, please, in your own words, tell us what you gave the American taxpayers besides a few hours of good television? [Pause.]

a15_2704237.speaker: Scott
a15_2704237.text: Oh, I think - the magnitude of the scientific data we return will speak for the taxpayers' money. The small amount of time they had for television, I think, is rather insignificant relative to the amount of return we've gathered in the SIM bay and in the lunar samples we have aboard right now. I think these data will not only en - enhance the progress of science, but it'll reach the common man on the street directly by the - the byproducts of what we learn. I think man must extend himself, the new frontiers must be open in order for us to - to propagate mankind, and I think this is one way in

a15_2704237.speaker: Worden
a15_2704237.text: Well, I really guess that there's not much to add to what Dave said. He - he expressed my sentiments exactly, and that the - the knowledge that, hopefully, we've - we've added to our store of information about the Moon and about ourselves will be increased in an extent which is greater than - than the - than the capital that was - spent on the flight itself. And, I would certainly think that - that the full theory adds significantly to - to man's knowledge about himself primarily and about himself in those areas where it will help future generations maybe.

a15_2704237.speaker: Irwin
a15_2704237.text: I can only add that we're bringing back just a lot of - lot of data and a lot of material, and it's going to take many years for people to really appreciate how much was gained from - from this flight.

a15_2704505.speaker: Henize
a15_2704505.text: Question number 14. It seemed this flight had as many problems as some of the old Gemini missions. Which of these gave you the most concern; and, for Dave, did you ever feel you were back on Gemini VIII?

a15_2704505.speaker: Scott
a15_2704505.text: Well, I guess we weren't aware we had that many problems. I thought this was a rather trouble-free flight, myself. We went a long way, we spent a long time doing the job, and I think, relative to the number of systems we have in all the spacecraft, that we had very few problems. I can think of none that were significant that would enable me to compare it with Gemini VIII at all. We had a - I guess the first little problem we had was a - a leak in our water system, which was cleared up rather rapidly by somebody having already done some investigation and having a procedure at hand. I believe ou

a15_2704505.speaker: Irwin
a15_2704505.text: You know really, we had very few problems. It seemed like a very tame simulation, as far as I was concerned.

a15_2704505.speaker: Worden
a15_2704505.text: Certainly, there were - there were - there were irritating things that happened like some circuit breakers in the spacecraft here that gave us some trouble, and some lights that aren't working exactly right. But certainly none of the important aspects of the flight or - or none of the essential pieces of equipment have malfunctioned, and I think it's been just great. [Pause.]

a15_2704505.speaker: Henize
a15_2704505.text: Gentlemen, we'd like to continue the press conference in a few minutes. But, in the meantime, we'd be anxious to get - start - get one of you started on the lunar eclipse photos. We have three more questions.

a15_2704505.speaker: Scott
a15_2704505.text: We got to try to do both?

a15_2704505.speaker: Irwin
a15_2704505.text: Why don't we show them the lunar eclipse?

a15_2704505.speaker: Irwin
a15_2704505.text: There's a lunar rock to show them.

a15_2704740.speaker: Scott
a15_2704740.text: Yeah, I guess I fell down twice, too, and as Jim said, it was never any real problem. It's a matter of if you start to go - and, of course, the terrain there, I guess you could see the television, was quite rough and irregular with occasionally rocks around, and we were pressing to try and get things done. And it was just a matter if you just start losing your balance, to go ahead and go easy, and accept somewhat of a - a light fall. Because of the one sixth gravity, there was never any impact when we hit. Take it easy and get up slow. And I don't think either one of us ever came anywhere near

a15_2704913.speaker: Henize
a15_2704913.text: Rog. We're going to skip down to the last question, Dave, which says your cabin must be jammed with Moon rocks, core samples, suits and assorted hardware. Can you show us what it's like in there? And, as you show us around, you can get set up for the Moon photos and dim the lights when you like.

a15_2704913.speaker: Henize
a15_2704913.text: O - okay, Dave. That's fine. And I guess one last request is when you get over to that window to - and before you take the photos, could you give us a quick picture of the Moon with the TV camera?

a15_2704913.speaker: Scott
a15_2704913.text: Have I got any pictures? I'll cut this thing down.

a15_2704913.speaker: Irwin
a15_2704913.text: Right here's some, Dave. I got Al's. You got some? Procedures, cameras...

a15_2704913.speaker: Worden
a15_2704913.text: You ought to get over here.

a15_2704913.speaker: Henize
a15_2704913.text: 15, the word here is to proceed; give your photography first priority there, and maybe we can see the - the Moon out of the other window.

a15_2704913.speaker: Scott
a15_2704913.text: Okay. We're working on it. [Long pause.]

a15_2704913.speaker: Irwin
a15_2704913.text: Hold it, Al. It's still going...

a15_2704913.speaker: Scott
a15_2704913.text: Monitor? Yes, I can get it from here. I think.

a15_2704913.speaker: Henize
a15_2704913.text: 15, Houston. We hear that your attitude is very good right now; there's no need to trim the maneuver.

a15_2704913.speaker: Irwin
a15_2704913.text: Okay, Al, you got the camera all set up over there, huh?

a15_2704913.speaker: Irwin
a15_2704913.text: Do you want me to read the settings to you, just in case?

a15_2704913.speaker: Irwin
a15_2704913.text: What do you want me to get, Dave? Get the lights? Yes, I can get them.

a15_2704913.speaker: Worden
a15_2704913.text: If you can get the lights -

a15_2704913.speaker: Irwin
a15_2704913.text: Turn this up a little bit. Okay, Al, when you're ready for me, I'll read to you.

a15_2704913.speaker: Scott
a15_2704913.text: No, I don't think so. See what it looks like.

a15_2704913.speaker: Irwin
a15_2704913.text: Well, it's completely dark now. Just the lower part is orange.

a15_2704913.speaker: Irwin
a15_2704913.text: The top part's almost a red, a dark red, and the bottom is an orange.

a15_2704913.speaker: Scott
a15_2704913.text: There you go. Yes, you got her.

a15_2704913.speaker: Scott
a15_2704913.text: Okay, Houston. I think you have a picture of her now. There she is.

a15_2704913.speaker: Irwin
a15_2704913.text: Take eight frames? Okay, I guess we'll give priority to you, huh, Al?

a15_2704913.speaker: Scott
a15_2704913.text: Okay, we - we got to get the...

a15_2704913.speaker: Henize
a15_2704913.text: 15, so far we have a blank screen down here.

a15_2704913.speaker: Scott
a15_2704913.text: Oh, really? I've got a good picture on the monitor.

a15_2704913.speaker: Henize
a15_2704913.text: Hang on for a moment, please. [Pause.]

a15_2704913.speaker: Irwin
a15_2704913.text: Okay, we're coming up on 6 minutes here at 55...

a15_2704913.speaker: Scott
a15_2704913.text: Boy, every time those - the jet fires [garble].

a15_2704913.speaker: Irwin
a15_2704913.text: Okay, stand by. Your first one'll be a 60-second exposure time and I'll - it'll be at 55:53.

a15_2704913.speaker: Henize
a15_2704913.text: That's a beautiful picture with just an edge of the Moon coming out of the eclipse.

a15_2704913.speaker: Henize
a15_2704913.text: 15, Houston. We'd like to ask if you got full zoom there?

a15_2704913.speaker: Scott
a15_2704913.text: Rog. It's all the way out.

a15_2704913.speaker: Henize
a15_2704913.text: Could you please give us ALC [Automatic Level Control] to Peak [to try and give the picture more contrast]?

a15_2704913.speaker: Scott
a15_2704913.text: Oh, I think we are - stand by one.

a15_2705951.speaker: Gordon
a15_2705951.text: Hello, Endeavour; this is Yankee Clipper. Over.

a15_2705951.speaker: Scott
a15_2705951.text: Hello, Yankee Clipper. How are you?

a15_2705951.speaker: Gordon
a15_2705951.text: Roger, I've got a naval tradition to pass on to you.

a15_2705951.speaker: Gordon
a15_2705951.text: Roger. When ships of the line have completed a mission such as yours and they return to home port, they always have a broom flying from the yardarm. Over.

a15_2705951.speaker: Scott
a15_2705951.text: We wouldn't want to break any traditions, Dickie. [Pause.]

a15_2705951.speaker: Gordon
a15_2705951.text: Dave, I'm watching you; I wouldn't let you.

a15_2705951.speaker: Scott
a15_2705951.text: Atta boy, and I'm glad. [Long pause.]

a15_2705951.speaker: Scott
a15_2705951.text: Okay, Houston. We're going to switch windows here with the TV camera, so we can switch windows with the camera cameras. [Pause.]

a15_2705951.speaker: Parker
a15_2705951.text: 15, Houston. When somebody gets a free hand up there, could we start the charge on battery A? [Pause.] We're afraid that might keep us from going to bed if we don't get it started soon.

a15_2705951.speaker: Scott
a15_2705951.text: Houston, the Moon is an orange ball, now - a dull orange ball with a sort of a gray area in the center on - on one side opposing the side that's slowly coming into illumination at the present time, and you'll probably get more and more of the lunar surface exposed to sunlight as we go along here. The picture you have is really pretty good for what we see, because there's very little illumination on the Moon. And only when we get the cockpit lights down reasonably low and get our face up in the window can we see the definition. So it's really not a bad picture.

a15_2705951.speaker: Parker
a15_2705951.text: Roger, 15. Thanks for the description, and the picture we're getting down here is quite good also.

a15_2705951.speaker: Scott
a15_2705951.text: Okay, I'm sure you'll have a much better one here in a few minutes.

a15_2711202.speaker: Parker
a15_2711202.text: Roger. It looks like you've had enough of the pho - [TV] photography for right now. It's beginning to get pretty bright on the tube. I guess we can go ahead and power it down.

a15_2711202.speaker: Scott
a15_2711202.text: That's interesting, Houston, because it looks like only about - oh, maybe 1/20th or so, maybe, of the Moon is illuminated at this time; just a thin sliver, but very bright.

a15_2711732.speaker: Parker
a15_2711732.text: Apollo 15, Houston. Request S-band Aux to Science, please.

a15_2713911.speaker: Scott
a15_2713911.text: In getting ready for contamination photography, we find that we've got a - a certain number of exposures left in the Nikon. Namely, we're on exposure number 29 in mag Victor, and we think we have 45 total, which would enable us to complete the contamination photography with the Nikon, if you desire, rather than with the DAC, as you changed. [Long pause.]

a15_2713911.speaker: Parker
a15_2713911.text: 15, they plan on using those last 15 frames or so on Victor for postmission calibration, so we still intend to press on with the DAC, please, Dave.

a15_2713911.speaker: Parker
a15_2713911.text: And, Dave, if you'll give us a start time on that, I'll give you a call at the end, because we want you to cycle some extra film through the DAC to give them a little leader there at the end to protect their film or something.

a15_2713911.speaker: Scott
a15_2713911.text: Okay, we'll do that. Stand by.

a15_2714314-cospb.speaker: Parker
a15_2714314-cospb.text: Rog. We were seeing the Optics drifting around against the hard stops. We'd like to have you bring them back and then zero them in, per the usual procedure. We kind of guess your getting ready for [a P]52 anyway, aren't you?

a15_2714314-cospb.speaker: Mission Control
a15_2714314-cospb.text: This is Apollo Control at 271 hours, 51 minutes. We accumulated less than a half a minute of tape during the change of shift briefing. We'll play back the tape conversations with the crew at this time and then I'll leave the lines up live.

a15_2714723.speaker: Parker
a15_2714723.text: Rog. We were seeing the Optics drifting around against the hard stops. We'd like to have you bring them back and then zero them in, per the usual procedure. We kind of guess your getting ready for [a P]52 anyway, aren't you?

a15_2715422.speaker: Parker
a15_2715422.text: And, 15, we have your torquing angles. You're Go to torque.

a15_2720749.speaker: Parker
a15_2720749.text: Apollo 15, Houston. If one of you guys is free, we've got some updates we could read to you. [Long pause.]

a15_2720749.speaker: Parker
a15_2720749.text: Okay, understand you're ready. What - the first thing is an Entry PAD. So you might whip out your Entry Checklist.

a15_2720749.speaker: Worden
a15_2720749.text: Okay, Houston; 15. Go ahead on the Entry PAD.

a15_2720749.speaker: Parker
a15_2720749.text: Roger. Would you believe it, we're going to land in mid-Pacific? And after that, it's 000, 153, 000; 294:41:37, 267, plus 26.12, minus 158.10; 06.2; 36097, 6.50; 1084.8, 36179; 294:58:37; 00:29; Noun 69s are NA; 4.00, 02:13; 00:18, 03:38, 07:44; 04, 140.3, 37.5; 213, down, 09.6, right, 4.7; lift vector, up. Comments: 1. Use nonexit EMS pattern, 2. RET of 90K, 6 plus 06, RET of mains, 8 plus 32; landing, 13 plus 29; constant g, roll right; Moon set time, 294:56:20. Over. [Pause.]

a15_2720749.speaker: Worden
a15_2720749.text: Okay, Houston. Understand. Entry PAD, mid-Pac; 000, 153, 000; 294:41:37, 267; plus 26.12, minus 158.10; 06.2; 36097, 6.50; 1084.8, 36179; 294:58:37; 00:29; 4.00, 02:13; 00:18, 03:38, 07:44; 04, 140.3, 37.5; 213, down, 09.6, right, 4.7; lift vector, up. Comments: nonex - use nonexit EMS pattern; RET 90K is 6 plus 06; RET mains, 8 plus 32; RET landing, 13 plus 29; constant g is roll right, Moon set at 294:56:20.

a15_2720749.speaker: Parker
a15_2720749.text: Roger, Al. Good readback. And we'd be interested in knowing the status of the EMS check you ran 2 or 3 hours ago, if you have it.

a15_2720749.speaker: Worden
a15_2720749.text: Yes, sir. The EMS check was just fine.

a15_2720749.speaker: Parker
a15_2720749.text: Okay, that's good to know. At the end of your contamination experiment here, we'll be going into this Mass Spec. boom test. And, if you guys let me know when you're ready, we've got a procedure to read up to you for that. We'll read up to you at that time. I assume you've been told that we aren't going to a midcourse 6, and right now mid-course 7 is looking like .09 [feet per second] which is - makes it kind of problematical as to whether we burn it or not. Weather in the recovery area is currently predicted to be, for your splashdown, 15-knot winds, 4-foot seas, 2,000 scattered, 10 miles - in

a15_2722656.speaker: Parker
a15_2722656.text: Apollo 15, Houston. If you'll give us Accept, we'll give you a very slight clock update to sync you for entry. And be advised we will not be sending a state vector uplink at this time; your vector is still just as good as the one on the ground.

a15_2722656.speaker: Scott
a15_2722656.text: Rog; understand, and you've got Accept. [Long pause.]

a15_2723733.speaker: Parker
a15_2723733.text: 15, Houston. Request you trim back to the original attitude now.

a15_2723733.speaker: Parker
a15_2723733.text: And again, if one of you has a couple of minutes, we can tell you a couple of other things.

a15_2723733.speaker: Scott
a15_2723733.text: Okay, in - in other words, you want us to maneuver back to the original attitude, rather than just damp rates, huh?

a15_2723733.speaker: Parker
a15_2723733.text: Rog; yeah. We'd like to use the same star backgrounds; so that means going back to the original attitude in the Flight Plan around 271:20 or so.

a15_2723733.speaker: Parker
a15_2723733.text: Which is what you got called up.

a15_2723733.speaker: Scott
a15_2723733.text: No, we don't have that called up. All we have is damp rates, but we'll do that. [Realises the Flight Plan has been updated.] Oh, what we have called up here? Yeah, okay.

a15_2724031.speaker: Parker
a15_2724031.text: And, 15; Houston. If one of you has some time, we'd like to talk about some stowage, please.

a15_2724031.speaker: Parker
a15_2724031.text: Okay, we've gone over the stowage which you read down this morning, and everything's shipshape, except we have one question on one item and that concerns the stowage of the core stems. The core stems should be stowed in the sleep restraint that has the CMP's PGA in it. We understand that it's now stowed in the bag on the side of A-8. I guess our first question is, how many - How long is the core stem at the present time? Did you break it down, or is it still three sections long, which we think it is on the ground.

a15_2724031.speaker: Scott
a15_2724031.text: No, it's still three sections long, and we could put it in the sleep restraint. It just seemed like a convenient place to stick it in the bag over there to keep it tied down well.

a15_2724031.speaker: Parker
a15_2724031.text: Okay. Next question is, how'd you get it in the A-8 bag, which according to our measurements on the ground is only 36 inches [92 cm] long and, therefore, apparently not long enough to hold the three lengths of core stem?

a15_2724031.speaker: Scott
a15_2724031.text: Well, it's sticking out a little bit, I guess we have to admit, but it's pretty well cinched down.

a15_2724031.speaker: Scott
a15_2724031.text: But it's no problem; we can put it any place you like. [Long pause.]

a15_2724031.speaker: Parker
a15_2724031.text: Okay, Dave, I guess we - I don't think it makes an awful lot of difference, but it'd probably make a lot of other people happy if we ended up putting it in the sleep restraint. They wouldn't worry about that loose end hanging out there - if it's not too much trouble.

a15_2724031.speaker: Scott
a15_2724031.text: Oh, it's no problem at all; be glad to do that.

a15_2724031.speaker: Scott
a15_2724031.text: You know, we know what number one priority on this spacecraft is. [Pause.]

a15_2724031.speaker: Scott
a15_2724031.text: We wouldn't - we wouldn't lose that or misplace it or get it rattled around for anything, Bob. [Pause.]

a15_2724031.speaker: Scott
a15_2724031.text: And you say everything else is okay, huh?

a15_2724621.speaker: Parker
a15_2724621.text: And, 15, reminder or a question. Did you guys get the word that they like a pad of about 2 seconds worth of 24 frames per second at the end of those photos to protect these things?

a15_2724621.speaker: Scott
a15_2724621.text: Roger; we got that, Bob. Thank you. [Long pause.]

a15_2724621.speaker: Parker
a15_2724621.text: And if you guys'll give me a call when you're ready to do the Mass Spec. boom test, I'll read it up to you.

a15_2724621.speaker: Scott
a15_2724621.text: All righty, Houston; stand by. [Long pause.]

a15_2724621.speaker: Worden
a15_2724621.text: Okay, you going to read up the procedures real time on the Mass Spec. boom?

a15_2724621.speaker: Worden
a15_2724621.text: Okay, why don't we go ahead and do that, then, while we're finishing up the contamination photos?

a15_2724621.speaker: Parker
a15_2724621.text: Okay, stand by. [Pause.] Okay, 15, first step is Mass Spec. boom to Retract, talkback barber pole for 4 minutes or until gray. If talkback fully gray within 4 minutes, deploy boom and return to Flight Plan. Over. [Pause.]

a15_2724621.speaker: Worden
a15_2724621.text: Roger. Understand you want retract on the Mass Spec. boom for 4 minutes, and, if it goes gray before then, go back to deploy and return to the Flight Plan.

a15_2724621.speaker: Parker
a15_2724621.text: That's affirm. And give - give us a call when you get done.

a15_2725238.speaker: Worden
a15_2725238.text: Okay, there's 4 minutes of Retract, and it's still barber pole.

a15_2725238.speaker: Parker
a15_2725238.text: Okay, if the talkback is not fully gray in 4 minutes, let's go to Mass Spec. Boom, Off, center, for one minute. That's just to let the motor cool down.

a15_2725238.speaker: Worden
a15_2725238.text: And what at the end of the one minute?

a15_2725238.speaker: Parker
a15_2725238.text: Okay, at the end of the one minute, we will deploy it for 20 seconds and then Off, center, and then we will retract for 40 seconds or until the talk back is one half barber pole [stalled] or fully gray [retracted] and then Off. Over.

a15_2725238.speaker: Worden
a15_2725238.text: And do you want to pause it off between extend and retract?

a15_2725238.speaker: Parker
a15_2725238.text: Stand by. Not necessary to pause between Deploy and Retract on this.

a15_2725238.speaker: Worden
a15_2725238.text: Okay, Houston, that's the 40 seconds of Retract, and it's at half barber pole, and I've turned it off.

a15_2725238.speaker: Parker
a15_2725238.text: Okay. In that case, we'd like you to repeat the 20-second Deploy, 40-second Retract sequence twice more and, if gray talkback is still not obtained, we'll turn it off and wait until 275 hours, at which point we'll give you a call and we'll replay - we'll repeat that. Over.

a15_2725238.speaker: Worden
a15_2725238.text: Okay, fine. We'll cycle that whole thing twice more.

a15_2725716.speaker: Parker
a15_2725716.text: 15, Houston. We'd like to proceed with the fuel cell purges now to get those out of the way before the P23s.

a15_2725716.speaker: Worden
a15_2725716.text: Houston, Mass Spec. boom has been cycled three times. All I can get out of it is a half barber pole, and I've got it turned off right now.

a15_2725716.speaker: Parker
a15_2725716.text: Roger; copy, Al. We'll call you at 275 hours to repeat that, the reason for that is that presently we are sort of sitting in a cold-soak attitude. We're going to repeat it at 275 hours when we're sort of in a hot-soak attitude.

a15_2730941.speaker: Parker
a15_2730941.text: Apollo 15, Houston. We'd like to go to Ion Source, Off, and Mass Spec. Experiment to Standby.

a15_2730941.speaker: Scott
a15_2730941.text: Ion Source, Off, and Mass Spec. to Standby.

a15_2730941.speaker: Mission Control
a15_2730941.text: This is Apollo Control. The crew has completed the program 23 midcourse navigation exercise, aboard the spacecraft, and should be beginning their eat period - or are already into it at this time. Before we put them to bed, they'll have one more set of navigation sightings to take on a series of stars. And we'll put the spacecraft in a Passive Thermal Control mode. The rest period is scheduled to begin at 277 hours, 30 minutes, or about 4 hours from now. Apollo 15 at the present time is 101,214 nautical miles [187,448 km] from the Earth, and traveling at a speed of almost 1 mile per second. We'

a15_2732848.speaker: Parker
a15_2732848.text: 15, Houston. Al, we missed your last Noun 49 [change in position and change in velocity]. [Long pause.]

a15_2732848.speaker: Worden
a15_2732848.text: Okay, I'll show you this one.

a15_2733930.speaker: Parker
a15_2733930.text: 15, Houston. Looks like a good set of P23s again, Al. And your gamma, right now, on your vector, is 6.5. [Pause.]

a15_2733930.speaker: Worden
a15_2733930.text: It sounds like, after a while, we might get along without you, huh, Bob.

a15_2733930.speaker: Scott
a15_2733930.text: As a matter of fact, if you guys keep working on your ground [calculated] vectors, they might even converge to the onboard vectors pretty soon.

a15_2740515.speaker: Parker
a15_2740515.text: Rog; 274:05, we'd like to delete the Mass Spec. line, where you turned on Multiplier, Low, et cetera . We'll delete that.

a15_2740515.speaker: Worden
a15_2740515.text: Okay. We'll delete that line, Robert. Thank you, sir.

a15_2740515.speaker: Worden
a15_2740515.text: Rog; want us to - delete the Logic Power, two, if we're going to do the Mass Spec. at 275? [Pause.]

a15_2740515.speaker: Parker
a15_2740515.text: And, 15; Houston. You got any more updates to our Flight Plan?

a15_2740515.speaker: Worden
a15_2740515.text: No, but I'll scan it over; and, if I find any, I'll let you know.

a15_2743729.speaker: Parker
a15_2743729.text: Roger; we have an update to the Flight Plan, if you guys are ready to copy.

a15_2743729.speaker: Parker
a15_2743729.text: Okay. The attitude that we maneuver to at 274:46 there, for the second set of X-rays should be changed - that Verb 49 maneuver, should be changed to 196, 346, 012. [Pause.] Over. [Pause.]

a15_2743729.speaker: Worden
a15_2743729.text: Roger. Understand the Verb 49 maneuver to the X-ray pointing attitude should be changed to 196, 346, 012.

a15_2743729.speaker: Parker
a15_2743729.text: Roger. And, before we start that Verb 49 maneuver at 274:45 or thereabouts, we'd like to cover the ex - We'd like to close the experiment covers, Alpha/X-ray, to Close. That's the one on panel 278. And then after we get to attitude at about 275:00, we'll go ahead and open those covers again, the Alpha/X-rays. [Long pause.]

a15_2743729.speaker: Worden
a15_2743729.text: Roger. Understand, you want the Alpha/X-ray covers closed before the maneuver and opened after the maneuver.

a15_2743729.speaker: Parker
a15_2743729.text: Roger. These - the new position I sent you up on that - Those two steps there in the procedure are to keep from getting sunlight right in on some of the stuff to protect it. And...

a15_2743729.speaker: Parker
a15_2743729.text: ...and, also at this time, you may terminate the battery A charge.

a15_2743729.speaker: Worden
a15_2743729.text: Okay, terminating the battery A charge. [Long pause.]

a15_2743729.speaker: Worden
a15_2743729.text: Roger, Bob. Do you want us to go to Standby on X-ray while the door is closed, or is it okay to leave it in 'On'?

a15_2743729.speaker: Parker
a15_2743729.text: Rog. You can leave it on - Dave.

a15_2744529.speaker: Parker
a15_2744529.text: Apollo 15, Houston. Request Omni Charlie, please.

a15_2751153.speaker: Parker
a15_2751153.text: Roger. Remember back aways, we were talking about doing some more Mass Spec. boom tests at 275 hours, which is gone by. We're right now talking about delaying that until 276 hours, approximately, or at least until before you start your Verb 49 maneuvers for the next set of P23s. Over.

a15_2751153.speaker: Parker
a15_2751153.text: We're just letting it [the Mass Spectrometer's boom] heat-soak a little bit longer. [Long pause.]

a15_2751153.speaker: Irwin
a15_2751153.text: Is that okay on 6-C, the fact that it's...

a15_2751153.speaker: Worden
a15_2751153.text: I don't know; we'll tell them.

a15_2751153.speaker: Worden
a15_2751153.text: And, Houston; 15. I have some Command Module RCS injector temperatures for you.

a15_2751153.speaker: Worden
a15_2751153.text: Okay, these are readings off the Systems Test Meter. 5-A is 4. - or 5-C is 4.2; 5-D is 3.9; 6-A is 4.1; B is 4.2; C is greater than 5; and D is 4.5.

a15_2755508.speaker: Parker
a15_2755508.text: Apollo 15, Houston. Over.

a15_2755508.speaker: Irwin
a15_2755508.text: Go ahead, Bob.

a15_2755508.speaker: Parker
a15_2755508.text: Rog. If one of you fellows has the time, we might like to continue on with the Mass Spec. boom retract test.

a15_2755508.speaker: Irwin
a15_2755508.text: Okay. Is it something I should write down, or can I just do it real time?

a15_2755508.speaker: Parker
a15_2755508.text: I'll give it to you real time. It's not that complicated, Jim.

a15_2755508.speaker: Irwin
a15_2755508.text: Okay. Go ahead.

a15_2755508.speaker: Parker
a15_2755508.text: Okay. We need the Experiment switch to On down there in the Alpha - Excuse me, the Mass Spec. Experiment switch to On; and the Ion Source, On. Over. [Pause.]

a15_2755508.speaker: Irwin
a15_2755508.text: David, can you get a couple of switches over there? The Mass Spec. Experiment, On; and the Ion Source, On.

a15_2755508.speaker: Irwin
a15_2755508.text: Okay. I understand Mass Spec. Experiment, On; and Ion Source, On. Stand by. [Long pause.]

a15_2755508.speaker: Irwin
a15_2755508.text: Okay, Bob. They're both On.

a15_2755508.speaker: Parker
a15_2755508.text: Okay. And then next, you go down to the other panel, and we go Deploy for 20 seconds on the Mass Spec. boom, and then Retract for 40 seconds, or until we get a gray indication. Over. [Pause.]

a15_2755508.speaker: Irwin
a15_2755508.text: Understand you want Deploy for 20 seconds and then - on the Mass Spec. boom, and then Retract, until we get gray, or 40 seconds.

a15_2755508.speaker: Parker
a15_2755508.text: Roger. Whichever occurs first.

a15_2755508.speaker: Irwin
a15_2755508.text: Okay.

a15_2755508.speaker: Irwin
a15_2755508.text: Okay, Dave. On that Mass Spec. Boom, we go Deploy for 20 seconds. If you want, I can give you a mark.

a15_2755508.speaker: Scott
a15_2755508.text: That's okay.

a15_2755508.speaker: Scott
a15_2755508.text: They're Off.

a15_2755508.speaker: Irwin
a15_2755508.text: Go to Off and then I'll have you - and then Re - and then Retract it for 40 seconds...

a15_2755508.speaker: Irwin
a15_2755508.text: Okay, Bob. It [the talkback] went gray after thirty seconds.

a15_2755508.speaker: Parker
a15_2755508.text: Roger; copy. Stand by. [Long pause.]

a15_2755508.speaker: Parker
a15_2755508.text: Okay, 15. Looks like it's a cold soak problem, then, Jim. We'll just deploy it all the way out and leave it there.

a15_2755508.speaker: Irwin
a15_2755508.text: Okay. You want us to deploy it all the way now, huh?

a15_2755508.speaker: Parker
a15_2755508.text: Right. After we did all that work and succeeded in retracting it, now we'll deploy it.

a15_2755508.speaker: Irwin
a15_2755508.text: Okay. We'll deploy it.

a15_2761304.speaker: Parker
a15_2761304.text: Roger, Al. Recommendation from the ground here. They'd like to see - maybe as many as five optics calibration marks the next time, instead of the two. It's just to give them some data.

a15_2761304.speaker: Irwin
a15_2761304.text: Okay, I'll relay that information to our navigator.

a15_2761304.speaker: Parker
a15_2761304.text: Sorry about that, Jim. You sound like Al these days.

a15_2761304.speaker: Irwin
a15_2761304.text: Oh, we're getting so we all sound alike up here.

a15_2762108.speaker: Parker
a15_2762108.text: Apollo 15, Houston. We're standing by ready to copy your Noun 49s.

a15_2762416.speaker: Parker
a15_2762416.text: 15, Houston. We'd like High Gain [Antenna], pitch at minus 30, yaw of 150.

a15_2762416.speaker: Worden
a15_2762416.text: Okay. Pitch, minus 30; and yaw, plus 5 - 150.

a15_2762416.speaker: Worden
a15_2762416.text: And do you want us to go ahead and try and lock it up?

a15_2764131.speaker: Parker
a15_2764131.text: Roger. Guidance says thank you to Al [for the P23s]. And if - a couple of other things here, if one of you guys has a chance, we'd like a mag sta - magazine status read-out tonight, and we're seeing some noise on Dave's biosensors. He might want to check them or push them down a little bit or something.

a15_2764131.speaker: Scott
a15_2764131.text: Okay, I'll do that. And you want a magazine status read-out. What do - What do you mean by that exactly.

a15_2764131.speaker: Parker
a15_2764131.text: Roger. That means how many picture's been taken in some of the magazines there. I think Al's been doing it. He probably knows what's going on, if he can tell you. [Long pause.]

a15_2764131.speaker: Scott
a15_2764131.text: Okay. I - I guess we don't have a good answer for you on that, Bob. They're all stowed away. And they've all been recorded as we've gone along. Is there any particular need for them before tomorrow sometime?

a15_2764131.speaker: Parker
a15_2764131.text: Negative, Dave. That's a good answer, it turns out.

a15_2764131.speaker: Scott
a15_2764131.text: Okay. I think you'll find them all neatly tucked away and recorded when - when you get them on the ship. [Long pause.]

a15_2764131.speaker: Scott
a15_2764131.text: If you're wondering how many pictures we took, at last count, night before last, it was something like 1,840 some.

a15_2764131.speaker: Scott
a15_2764131.text: Or somewhere around the ball park.

a15_2764811.speaker: Scott
a15_2764811.text: Well, I had - had the log out here, and I took a look at it, and at last count last night, we were 2,631 on Hasselblad pictures, total.

a15_2765106.speaker: Parker
a15_2765106.text: Roger, Dave. The interest in the mags was in reference to the UV - the mags for the UV photography tomorrow. So the interest was in the number of frames remaining on magazine Mike and magazine Papa, try - trying to determine which of those would be usable for tomorrow's UV photography.

a15_2765106.speaker: Scott
a15_2765106.text: Okay. I think we've got that log in the Flight Plan. Stand by 'til Al finishes his P23s, and we'll take a look.

a15_2765106.speaker: Scott
a15_2765106.text: [I] think we'll use a mag that has some film in it.

a15_2765106.speaker: Scott
a15_2765106.text: I said, at - at any rate, we'll use a mag that has some film in it tomorrow.

a15_2765706.speaker: Parker
a15_2765706.text: Apollo 15, Houston. Requesting Gamma-ray Gain Step, Shield, Off, now, please.

a15_2765706.speaker: Parker
a15_2765706.text: That was a good mark, Al. [Pause.]

a15_2765706.speaker: Worden
a15_2765706.text: Yeah, and it didn't update the state vector very much.

a15_2772852.speaker: Parker
a15_2772852.text: Apollo 15, Houston. You're Go to start to spinup for PTC.

a15_2772852.speaker: Parker
a15_2772852.text: And, Apollo 15, we'd like you to check that the Potable Tank Inlet valve is open, please.

a15_2772852.speaker: Worden
a15_2772852.text: Roger; understand. Potable Tank Inlet valve, open. [Long pause.]

a15_2772852.speaker: Scott
a15_2772852.text: Okay. Listen, potable tank inlet valve is open and has been the whole flight. What prompted the question?

a15_2772852.speaker: Parker
a15_2772852.text: 15, we saw a drop in the potable at the same time that the waste tank was staying stable, and we were - just concerned that it might have gotten out of configuration. We certainly expected it to be open; we just wanted to check it before you went to sleep, so we didn't have to wake you up.

a15_2772852.speaker: Scott
a15_2772852.text: Okay. Understand. Yeah - we're reading potable at 90 percent.

a15_2774352.speaker: Parker
a15_2774352.text: Apollo 15, Houston. No need to acknowledge, but we'd like to put the DSKY to sleep before you guys go to sleep.
